  "proof": "Proof. If H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell)=0, then H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C is the zero vector space, and the zero Hermitian form is positive definite and satisfies the required identity vacuously. Hence assume H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) is nonzero. Since X_k is a nonempty connected variety over the algebraically closed field k, choose x in X_k(k). Let A be the Albanese variety of X_k over k, and let alpha_x:X_k->A be the Albanese morphism with alpha_x(x)=0. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_alb_h1_geometric, phi=alpha_x^*:H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell)->H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism. Let m:A_k x A_k->A_k be the group law and p_1,p_2 the projections. The standard Tate-module description of H^1 of an abelian variety gives m^*=p_1^*+p_2^* on H^1_et(-,Q_ell). For b in A_k(k), write c_b:A_k->A_k for the constant morphism at b; the translation t_b is m o (id,c_b), so t_b^*=(id,c_b)^* o m^*=(id,c_b)^* o p_1^*+(id,c_b)^* o p_2^*=(p_1 o (id,c_b))^*+(p_2 o (id,c_b))^*=id+c_b^*=id, because H^1_et(Spec k,Q_ell)=0. Thus translations act trivially on H^1. If x' is another k-point, then alpha_{x'}=t_{-alpha_x(x')} o alpha_x, so alpha_{x'}^*=alpha_x^*; hence the isomorphism phi is independent of the base point. Let A_0 be the Albanese variety of X over F_{q^m}; its base change to k is A. Let G=Gal(k/F_{q^m}). For tau in G, let tau_X and tau_A be the induced automorphisms of X_k and A_k. The tau-conjugate of alpha_x is tau_A o alpha_x o tau_X^{-1}, which is the Albanese morphism with base point tau(x). By base-point independence its pullback is again phi, so (tau_X^{-1})^* o phi o tau_A^* = phi. Multiplying on the left by tau_X^* and on the right by (tau_A^*)^{-1} gives tau_X^* o phi = phi o tau_A^*. Taking tau to be the q^m-power Frobenius generator gives F_X o phi = phi o F_A, where F_X and F_A are the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius actions on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) and H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell). Therefore F_X=phi o F_A o phi^{-1}. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_515, F_A is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell); by similarity, F_X is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). Now we bound the eigenvalues. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_463_abelian_variety_covered_by_product_of_curves applied to A_0 over F_{q^m}, there exist smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,...,C_r over F_{q^m} and a surjective morphism f:Y=C_1 x ... x C_r -> A_0 over F_{q^m}. Let f_k:Y_k->A_k be its base change. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, applied with the prime power q^m in place of q to the constant sheaf Q_ell on X_k, A_k, and Y_k, the Q_ell-vector spaces H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell), H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell), and H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) are finite-dimensional. We claim f_k^*:H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell)->H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective. Choose y_0 in Y_k(k) and put b=f_k(y_0). Define f_0(y)=f_k(y)-b; then f_0 is a surjective morphism of varieties over k, hence is surjective on k-points, and f_0(y_0)=0. Let B=Alb_{Y_k/k} and let a:Y_k->B be the Albanese morphism with a(y_0)=0. By the universal property of the Albanese variety, there is a homomorphism h:B->A_k with f_0=h o a. Since f_0 is surjective on k-points, h(B(k)) contains A_k(k); the image h

 is a closed subgroup of A_k, and A_k(k) is Zariski dense in A_k, so h(B)=A_k. Thus h is a surjective homomorphism of abelian varieties, hence an isogeny. Let h^t:A_k->B be a dual isogeny. There is a nonzero integer n with h o h^t=[n] on A_k. For every abelian variety E over k, the pullback [n]^*:H^1_et(E_k,Q_ell)->H^1_et(E_k,Q_ell) is multiplication by n: the group-law identity m^*=p_1^*+p_2^* gives [2]^*=2 id, and inductively [n+1]^*=[n]^*+id. Pulling back h o h^t=[n] gives (h^t)^* o h^* = n id on H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell), so h^* is injective because n is invertible in Q_ell. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_alb_h1_geometric, a^*:H^1_et(B,Q_ell)->H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism, so f_0^*=a^* o h^* is injective. Since f_k=t_b o f_0 and translations act trivially on H^1, f_k^*=f_0^*, hence f_k^* is injective. Because f is defined over F_{q^m}, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius morphisms satisfy Fr_A o f_k = f_k o Fr_Y. Taking pullbacks gives f_k^* o F_A = F_Y o f_k^*. Let W_0=im(f_k^*) in H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell). Then W_0 is F_Y-stable, and f_k^* identifies W_0 with H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell) in a way compatible with the Frobenius actions, so the induced action of F_Y on W_0 corresponds to F_A. By the Kunneth formula, H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is the direct sum of H^1_et(C_{i,k},Q_ell) for i=1,...,r, and F_Y is the corresponding direct sum of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius operators on the factors. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/3cb9b7, every eigenvalue of F_Y, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{m/2}; in particular, under the embedding sigma, every eigenvalue alpha of F_Y satisfies |sigma(alpha)|=q^{m/2}. Extend scalars from Q_ell to C via sigma. Let V=H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C, let T=F_Y tensor id, and let W=W_0 tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Then W is a T-stable C-subspace of V, and every root in C of the characteristic polynomial of T has absolute value q^{m/2}. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/e7b3c7, every root in C of the characteristic polynomial of T|_W has absolute value q^{m/2}. Since f_k^* identifies W_0 with H^1_et(A_k,Q_ell) as Frobenius modules, every eigenvalue beta of F_A, viewed via sigma, satisfies |sigma(beta)|=q^{m/2}. Since F_X=phi o F_A o phi^{-1}, every eigenvalue of F_X under sigma also has absolute value q^{m/2}. In particular no eigenvalue of F_X is zero, so F_X lies in GL(H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Finally apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_360 to V=H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell), T=F_X, the embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, and c=q^m. Its hypotheses hold: T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue alpha of T satisfies |sigma(alpha)|^2=q^m. Therefore there exists a positive definite Hermitian form H on H^1_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C such that H((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^m H(x,y) for all x,y. This proves the lemma."
}

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let d,m>=1, let q=p^a be a prime power, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let F_V in GL_K(V), let F_W in GL_K(W), let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with phi F_V=F_W phi, let beta:V x V->K satisfy beta(F_V x,F_V y)=q^{md}beta(x,y), and let beta_W(a,b)=beta(phi^{-1}a,phi^{-1}b). Then beta_W(F_W a,F_W b)=q^{md}beta_W(a,b) for all a,b in W.
proof: Let a,b be arbitrary elements of W. Let psi be the inverse map of phi, and set x=psi(a) and y=psi(b). Then phi(x)=a and phi(y)=b. Since phi F_V=F_W phi, we have F_W a = F_W phi(x) = phi(F_V x) and F_W b = F_W phi(y) = phi(F_V y). By the definition of beta_W, beta_W(F_W a,F_W b)=beta(psi(F_W a),psi(F_W b)). Substituting the previous equalities gives beta(psi(phi(F_V x)),psi(phi(F_V y))). Since psi is the inverse of phi, this is beta(F_V x,F_V y). By the hypothesis on beta, beta(F_V x,F_V y)=q^{md} beta(x,y). Finally, beta(x,y)=beta(psi(a),psi(b))=beta_W(a,b). Hence beta_W(F_W a,F_W b)=q^{md} beta_W(a,b). This completes the proof for arbitrary a,b in W. The characteristic-zero assumption guarantees that the integer q^{md} is a nonzero scalar in K under the canonical map from Z to K; no further properties of beta are needed.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X over F_{q^m}, let i:Y->X be the inclusion, and let F_X and F_Y be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) and H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell), respectively. Then i^*F_X=F_Y i^*.
proof:
Let sigma: k -> k denote the q^m-power field automorphism, sigma(a) = a^{q^m}. Since every element of F_{q^m} satisfies a^{q^m} = a, the automorphism sigma fixes F_{q^m} pointwise; equivalently, sigma is an automorphism of k over the base F_{q^m}.

Step 1 (Definition of the arithmetic Frobenius). By the standard definition of the arithmetic Frobenius — the definition established in the cited lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, which identifies the arithmetic Frobenius on H^i_et(X_k, Q_ell) with the pullback (id_X x sigma)^* for the appropriate power automorphism sigma of k — the same definition applies verbatim over the base F_{q^m} with sigma the q^m-power automorphism. Concretely, writing X_k = X x_{F_{q^m}} k and Y_k = Y x_{F_{q^m}} k, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) is the pullback map
  F_X := (id_X x sigma)^*: H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell),
where (id_X x sigma): X_k -> X_k is the k-morphism acting as the identity on the X-factor and as sigma on the k-factor of the fiber product. Similarly, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is
  F_Y := (id_Y x sigma)^*: H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell).
The pullback map i^*: H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell) attached to the inclusion i: Y -> X is the pullback along the base change i_k: Y_k -> X_k of i to k.

Step 2 (The Frobenius square commutes). We claim that the following square of k-schemes commutes:
  Y_k --i_k--> X_k
  |              |
(id_Y x sigma)  (id_X x sigma)
  v              v
  Y_k --i_k--> X_k
i.e. that i_k o (id_Y x sigma) = (id_X x sigma) o i_k as morphisms Y_k -> X_k.

To verify this, let pr_X: X_k -> X and pr_k: X_k -> k be the two projections defining the fiber product X_k = X x_{F_{q^m}} k, and let pr_Y: Y_k -> Y be the corresponding projection for Y_k. By the definition of (id_X x sigma) we have
  pr_X o (id_X x sigma) = pr_X,   pr_k o (id_X x sigma) = sigma o pr_k,
and similarly pr_Y o (id_Y x sigma) = pr_Y and pr_k o (id_Y x sigma) = sigma o pr_k. Since i_k is the base change of i, we have
  pr_X o i_k = i o pr_Y,   pr_k o i_k = pr_k.
Now compare the two morphisms i_k o (id_Y x sigma) and (id_X x sigma) o i_k, both mapping Y_k to X_k, by their compositions with the projections pr_X and pr_k. For the first:
  pr_X o [i_k o (id_Y x sigma)] = (pr_X o i_k) o (id_Y x sigma) = (i o pr_Y) o (id_Y x sigma) = i o (pr_Y o (id_Y x sigma)) = i o pr_Y,
  pr_k o [i_k o (id_Y x sigma)] = (pr_k o i_k) o (id_Y x sigma) = pr_k o (id_Y x sigma) = sigma o pr_k.
For the second:
  pr_X o [(id_X x sigma) o i_k] = (pr_X o (id_X x sigma)) o i_k = pr_X o i_k = i o pr_Y,
  pr_k o [(id_X x sigma) o i_k] = (pr_k o (id_X x sigma)) o i_k = (sigma o pr_k) o i_k = sigma o (pr_k o i_k) = sigma o pr_k.
Thus both morphisms have identical compositions with pr_X and pr_k. By the universal property of the fiber product X_k = X x_{F_{q^m}} k, the two morphisms Y_k -> X_k are equal. Hence i_k o (id_Y x sigma) = (id_X x sigma) o i_k, and the square commutes.

Step 3 (Functoriality of the pullback in etale cohomology). The etale cohomology functor with Q_ell coefficients is contravariantly functorial with respect to morphisms of schemes: for any commutative square of schemes
  A --f--> B
  |g        |h
  v         v
  C --f'--> D
satisfying f' o g = h o f, the induced pullback maps on etale cohomology satisfy g^* o (f')^* = f^* o h^*. Indeed, by the composition rule for pullbacks, (f' o g)^* = g^* o (f')^* and (h o f)^* = f^* o h^*, and since f' o g = h o f as morphisms A -> D, the two left-hand sides coincide.

Applying this to the commutative square of Step 2 with A = C = Y_k, B = D = X_k, f = f' = i_k, g = (id_Y x sigma), and h = (id_X x sigma), we obtain
  ((id_Y x sigma))^* o (i_k)^* = (i_k)^* o ((id_X x sigma))^*.

Step 4 (Conclusion). Substituting the definitions of Step 1, namely ((id_Y x sigma))^* = F_Y, ((id_X x sigma))^* = F_X, and (i_k)^* = i^*, the equality of Step 3 becomes
  F_Y o i^* = i^* o F_X,
i.e. i^* F_X = F_Y i^*, as claimed. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let d,m>=1, let q=p^a be a prime power, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let F in GL_K(V), let beta:V x V->K satisfy beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}beta(x,y), and for N>=1 put G_N(x,y)=beta(x,F^N y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F^{-N} y). Then G_N(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}G_N(x,y) for all x,y in V and N>=1.
proof:
The context is fully confirmed: this lemma is the basic "similitude propagation" identity $G_N(Fx,Fy) = q^{md}G_N(x,y)$ underlying the entire $G_n$-machinery. My proof is a self-contained direct computation. I have verified the exponent bookkeeping ($F^{-N}\circ F = F^{-N+1}$, a $+1$ shift) and checked it against an explicit 2-dimensional example. No proved lemmas or references are required.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/e57da1",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove the identity G_N(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}G_N(x,y) for all x,y in V and all N>=1 by a direct computation using only the given hypothesis.

Setup and well-definedness. Since char(K)=0, the prime subfield of K is Q, so every positive integer embeds as a nonzero element of K; in particular q^{md} and q^{mdN} (with q=p^a a prime power, d,m>=1, N>=1) are well-defined nonzero scalars of K, and the sign (-1)^d is the scalar 1 or -1 in K. Since F in GL_K(V), F is invertible, so F^{-1} exists and F^{-N}:=(F^{-1})^N is a well-defined K-linear automorphism for every N>=1. The hypothesis is that the K-bilinear form beta:V x V -> K satisfies
    (H)  beta(Fu, Fv) = q^{md} beta(u,v)  for ALL u,v in V.
Because (H) holds for every pair (u,v) in V x V, we may substitute any vectors we like for u and v, in particular vectors that are themselves powers of F applied to given vectors.

Fix N>=1 and fix x,y in V. We expand G_N(Fx,Fy) using the definition G_N(a,b)=beta(a,F^N b)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(a,F^{-N} b) with a=Fx, b=Fy:
    G_N(Fx,Fy) = beta(Fx, F^N(Fy)) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(Fx, F^{-N}(Fy)).

Exponent bookkeeping. Since F is a K-linear automorphism, powers compose by adding exponents: F^a o F^b = F^{a+b} for all integers a,b (for negative exponents this follows from F^{-1} o F = id and induction). Hence
    F^N(Fy) = F^{N} o F (y) = F^{N+1} y,
    F^{-N}(Fy) = F^{-N} o F (y) = F^{-N+1} y.
Substituting these into the expansion gives
    G_N(Fx,Fy) = beta(Fx, F^{N+1} y) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(Fx, F^{-N+1} y).   (*)
Both arguments on the right now have the form F applied to something in the second slot: F^{N+1} y = F(F^N y) and F^{-N+1} y = F(F^{-N} y).

First term. Apply hypothesis (H) with u = x and v = F^N y (both are elements of V, so (H) applies to this pair):
    beta(Fx, F(F^N y)) = q^{md} beta(x, F^N y).
Since F(F^N y) = F^{N+1} y, this reads
    (1)  beta(Fx, F^{N+1} y) = q^{md} beta(x, F^N y).

Second term. Apply hypothesis (H) with u = x and v = F^{-N} y (again both in V):
    beta(Fx, F(F^{-N} y)) = q^{md} beta(x, F^{-N} y).
Since F(F^{-N} y) = F^{-N+1} y, this reads
    (2)  beta(Fx, F^{-N+1} y) = q^{md} beta(x, F^{-N} y).

Conclusion. Substitute (1) and (2) into (*):
    G_N(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} beta(x, F^N y) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} [ q^{md} beta(x, F^{-N} y) ]
                = q^{md} beta(x, F^N y) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} q^{md} beta(x, F^{-N} y)
                = q^{md} beta(x, F^N y) + (-1)^d q^{md(N+1)} beta(x, F^{-N} y),
where in the last step we used q^{mdN} q^{md} = q^{md(N+1)} (ordinary multiplication of the embedded scalars in K). Factoring out the common scalar q^{md}:
    G_N(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} [ beta(x, F^N y) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x, F^{-N} y) ]
                = q^{md} G_N(x, y),
by the definition of G_N(x,y). This completes the proof for arbitrary x,y in V and N>=1.

Remark on validity of the two applications of (H): no additional property of beta (symmetry, nondegeneracy) or of F (semisimplicity) is used; only that (H) holds for every pair (u,v) and that F^a o F^b = F^{a+b}. The critical point is that F^{-N}(Fy)=F^{-N+1}y is a +1 shift (not a -1 shift), so that in both summands the second argument is F applied to a vector, matching the +1 shift of the first argument from x to Fx, which is exactly the form covered by (H)."
}

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let d,m>=1, let q=p^a be a prime power, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let F_V in GL_K(V), let F_W in GL_K(W), let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with phi F_V=F_W phi, let beta:V x V->K, let beta_W(a,b)=beta(phi^{-1}a,phi^{-1}b), and for N>=1 put G_N^V(x,y)=beta(x,F_V^N y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F_V^{-N} y), G_N^W(a,b)=beta_W(a,F_W^N b)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta_W(a,F_W^{-N} b). Then for every N>=1, G_N^V is nondegenerate if and only if G_N^W is nondegenerate.
proof:
We fix an integer N >= 1 for the duration of the proof and show G_N^V is nondegenerate if and only if G_N^W is nondegenerate. Throughout, "nondegenerate" for a function G: Z x Z -> K on a vector space Z means: G is left-nondegenerate (if G(x,y)=0 for every y in Z then x=0) and right-nondegenerate (if G(x,y)=0 for every x in Z then y=0). No bilinearity of beta, G_N^V, or G_N^W is assumed or used.

Step 1 (Conjugacy of powers). Since phi: V -> W is a K-linear isomorphism and phi F_V = F_W phi, we have F_W = phi F_V phi^{-1}. We claim F_W^N = phi F_V^N phi^{-1} for all N >= 1. The case N=1 is the conjugacy relation itself. For the inductive step, F_W^{N+1} = F_W F_W^N = (phi F_V phi^{-1})(phi F_V^N phi^{-1}) = phi F_V (phi^{-1} phi) F_V^N phi^{-1} = phi F_V^{N+1} phi^{-1}. Similarly, since F_V and F_W are invertible, F_W^{-1} = phi F_V^{-1} phi^{-1}, and the same induction gives F_W^{-N} = phi F_V^{-N} phi^{-1} for all N >= 1.

Step 2 (Key identity). We prove that for every a, b in W,
  G_N^W(a,b) = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)).
Indeed, expanding the definition of G_N^W and using the definition beta_W(a,b) = beta(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)):
  G_N^W(a,b) = beta_W(a, F_W^N b) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta_W(a, F_W^{-N} b)
             = beta(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(F_W^N b)) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(F_W^{-N} b)).
By Step 1, F_W^N b = phi F_V^N phi^{-1}(b), so phi^{-1}(F_W^N b) = F_V^N phi^{-1}(b). Likewise phi^{-1}(F_W^{-N} b) = F_V^{-N} phi^{-1}(b). Substituting:
  G_N^W(a,b) = beta(phi^{-1}(a), F_V^N phi^{-1}(b)) + (-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(phi^{-1}(a), F_V^{-N} phi^{-1}(b))
             = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)).
This is the identity we need. Note that at no point did we use bilinearity of beta; we only evaluated beta at specific pairs.

Step 3 (Left nondegeneracy is preserved in both directions).

(3a) G_N^V left-nondegenerate implies G_N^W left-nondegenerate. Suppose G_N^W(a,b) = 0 for every b in W, for some a in W. By the identity of Step 2, G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) = 0 for every b in W. Since phi^{-1}: W -> V is surjective (phi is an isomorphism), as b ranges over W the element phi^{-1}(b) ranges over all of V. Hence G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), y) = 0 for every y in V. By left nondegeneracy of G_N^V, phi^{-1}(a) = 0, so a = phi(phi^{-1}(a)) = phi(0) = 0. Thus G_N^W is left-nondegenerate.

(3b) G_N^W left-nondegenerate implies G_N^V left-nondegenerate. Suppose G_N^V(x,y) = 0 for every y in V, for some x in V. Set a = phi(x) in W. For any b in W, Step 2 gives G_N^W(a,b) = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) = G_N^V(x, phi^{-1}(b)). Since phi^{-1} is surjective, phi^{-1}(b) ranges over all of V as b ranges over W, so G_N^W(a,b) = 0 for every b in W. By left nondegeneracy of G_N^W, a = 0, i.e. phi(x) = 0, so x = 0 (phi is injective). Thus G_N^V is left-nondegenerate.

Step 4 (Right nondegeneracy is preserved in both directions).

(4a) G_N^V right-nondegenerate implies G_N^W right-nondegenerate. Suppose G_N^W(a,b) = 0 for every a in W, for some b in W. By Step 2, G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) = 0 for every a in W. Since phi^{-1} is surjective, phi^{-1}(a) ranges over all of V, so G_N^V(x, phi^{-1}(b)) = 0 for every x in V. By right nondegeneracy of G_N^V, phi^{-1}(b) = 0, so b = 0. Thus G_N^W is right-nondegenerate.

(4b) G_N^W right-nondegenerate implies G_N^V right-nondegenerate. Suppose G_N^V(x,y) = 0 for every x in V, for some y in V. Set b = phi(y) in W. For any a in W, Step 2 gives G_N^W(a,b) = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), y). Since phi^{-1} is surjective, phi^{-1}(a) ranges over all of V, so G_N^W(a,b) = 0 for every a in W. By right nondegeneracy of G_N^W, b = 0, i.e. phi(y) = 0, so y = 0. Thus G_N^V is right-nondegenerate.

Step 5 (Conclusion). From Steps 3 and 4, G_N^V is left-nondegenerate if and only if G_N^W is left-nondegenerate, and G_N^V is right-nondegenerate if and only if G_N^W is right-nondegenerate. Therefore G_N^V is nondegenerate if and only if G_N^W is nondegenerate. Since N >= 1 was arbitrary, the result holds for every N >= 1.

Remark on the argument. The only facts used are: (i) the conjugacy identity G_N^W(a,b) = G_N^V(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) from Step 2, which follows from the definition of G_N^W in terms of beta_W and the relation F_W^N = phi F_V^N phi^{-1}; and (ii) the surjectivity of phi^{-1}, which follows from phi being an isomorphism. No bilinearity of beta, G_N^V, or G_N^W is invoked at any point, so the argument is valid for an arbitrary function beta: V x V -> K, as the hypothesis requires.

statement:
Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=3, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor, xi its cycle class, L cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. Put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_
Q_ell), let U be the open complement of Y in X, let j:U->X, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) and H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell), let delta:H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary, suppose j^* restricts to an isomorphism phi:P^d->ker(delta) of Q_ell[F]-modules, let beta be Poincare duality on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let beta_U(phi x,phi z)=beta(x,z), and for N>=1 put G_N^P(x,y)=beta(x,F^N y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F^{-N} y), G_N^U(a,b)=beta_U(a,F^N b)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta_U(a,F^{-N} b). Then G_N^P(x,y)=G_N^U(phi x,phi y) for all x,y in P^d and N>=1.
proof: Write H=H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), H_U=H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell), P=P^d, Q=ker(delta), and denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius operators on H and H_U by F_X and F_U. By hypothesis phi:P->Q is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules, so for every u in P one has F_U(phi(u))=phi(F_X(u)). Because phi is an isomorphism, the rule beta_U(phi a,phi b)=beta(a,b) is a well-defined bilinear form on Q. First we justify the use of negative powers. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, applied to the F_{q^m}-schemes X and U, the operators F_X and F_U are Q_ell-linear automorphisms of H and H_U. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, applied to the proper variety X over F_{q^m} with the constant sheaf Q_ell and its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, the vector space H is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. Hence P is finite-dimensional, and since phi is an isomorphism onto Q, Q is finite-dimensional. The relation F_U(phi(u))=phi(F_X(u)) shows that F_X(P) is contained in P and F_U(Q) is contained in Q. Because F_X is injective on H, its restriction to P is injective; finite-dimensionality of P then implies that F_X|_P is an automorphism of P. Because F_U is injective on H_U, its restriction to Q is injective; finite-dimensionality of Q then implies that F_U|_Q is an automorphism of Q. Thus F_X^{n}P=P and F_U^{n}Q=Q for every integer n, in particular for n=N and n=-N with N>=1. From F_U phi=phi F_X we obtain by induction F_U^{N} phi=phi F_X^{N} on P for every N>=0. For negative powers, let y in P and put z=F_X^{-1}y, which lies in P. Then F_X z=y, so F_U(phi(z))=phi(y). Since F_U is injective on H_U, the unique element of H_U whose F_U-image is phi(y) is phi(z), and this element is also F_U^{-1}(phi(y)); hence F_U^{-1}(phi(y))=phi(F_X^{-1}y). Iterating gives F_U^{-N} phi(y)=phi(F_X^{-N}y) for every N>=1. Now fix x,y in P and N>=1. By the definition of G_N^U on Q, G_N^U(phi x,phi y)=beta_U(phi x,F_U^{N}phi y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta_U(phi x,F_U^{-N}phi y). Using the commutation relations just proved, F_U^{N}phi y=phi(F_X^{N}y) and F_U^{-N}phi y=phi(F_X^{-N}y). Since F_X^{N}y and F_X^{-N}y lie in P, the second arguments lie in Q=phi(P), where beta_U is defined. By the defining relation beta_U(phi a,phi b)=beta(a,b) for a,b in P, with a=x and b=F_X^{N}y, and then with b=F_X^{-N}y, we get beta_U(phi x,phi(F_X^{N}y))=beta(x,F_X^{N}y) and beta_U(phi x,phi(F_X^{-N}y))=beta(x,F_X^{-N}y). Substituting these two equalities gives G_N^U(phi x,phi y)=beta(x,F_X^{N}y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F_X^{-N}y), which is exactly the definition of G_N^P(x,y). This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth very ample divisor on X over F_{q^m}, let i:Y->X, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of Y, let L:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) be cup product with xi, and let B(x,y)=tr_Y(i^*x cup i^*y) for x,y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell), where tr_Y is the Poincare duality trace. Then the left radical of B equals ker(L).
proof:
I have verified all the lemmas I need. Now I'll write the complete proof. My argument:

1. **Step 1** (via 8735d6, instantiated with the target's \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\)-identification): \(B(x,y) =  eta_D(i^*x, i^*y) =  eta_X(Lx, y)\).
2. **Step 2**: Left radical of \(B\) = \(\{x :  eta_X(Lx, y)=0 \  orall y\}\).
3. **Step 3** (via lemma_77(b), \(n=d+1\)): the pairing \(H^{d+1}	imes H^{d-1}	o\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) is perfect; composing with the target's \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\)-induced isomorphism \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)	o\mathbb Q_\ell\) gives the perfect \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued pairing \( eta_X\), so \( eta_X(Lx,y)=0\  orall y \iff Lx=0\).
4. **Step 4**: Left radical \(= \ker(L)\).

This uses only the target's \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) identification throughout (no \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\)-vs-\(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) mismatch, no 6f8d0c).

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/968c6a",
  "cited_lemmas": ["Miner/16d24b0281973336/8735d6", "eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77"],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that the left radical of B equals ker(L). Let u denote the target's fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1). It determines a Q_ell-linear isomorphism phi: Q_ell(1) -> Q_ell with phi(u)=1, and hence for every integer n a Q_ell-linear identification Q_ell(n) -> Q_ell (for n>0 via phi^{tensor n}, and for n<0 via the dual (phi^{tensor |n|})^* composed with the canonical self-duality Q_ell^* = Q_ell). In particular u induces a Q_ell-linear isomorphism Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell. Write H^s = H^s_et(X_k, Q_ell) and H^s_Y = H^s_et(Y_k, Q_ell).

STEP 1 (B equals the pulled-back Poincare pairing). We apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/8735d6. That lemma is a general statement: for a smooth projective geometrically connected X of pure dimension d>=2 over F_{q^m}, a smooth very ample divisor D defined over F_{q^m} with inclusion i, and an identification of Tate twists with Q_ell, if xi is the cycle class of D, L is cup product with xi, beta_X: H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell is the Poincare duality pairing, and beta_D: H^{d-1}_et(D_k,Q_ell) x H^{d-1}_et(D_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell is the Poincare duality pairing, then beta_X(Lx,y) = beta_D(i^*x, i^*y) for all x,y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell). The lemma holds for any identification of Tate twists with Q_ell (equivalently, for any nonzero element of Q_ell(1)); we instantiate it with D = Y and with the target's identification given by u. This is a valid instantiation because the target's identification (fixing the nonzero element u of Q_ell(1)) is exactly an identification of Tate twists with Q_ell. We obtain, for all x,y in H^{d-1}:
    beta_X(Lx, y) = beta_D(i^*x, i^*y).   (1)
Here beta_X is the canonical Poincare duality pairing (a,y) -> tr_X(a cup y) (which by the Poincare duality trace tr_X: H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d) lands in Q_ell(-d)) composed with the u-induced isomorphism Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell, and beta_D is the canonical Poincare duality pairing (a,b) -> tr_Y(a cup b) (landing in Q_ell(-(d-1))) composed with the u-induced isomorphism Q_ell(-(d-1)) -> Q_ell.

By the target's definition, B(x,y) = tr_Y(i^*x cup i^*y) is precisely beta_D(i^*x, i^*y): it is the Poincare duality trace on Y_k applied to i^*x cup i^*y, composed with the identification of Tate twists with Q_ell given by u. Combining this with (1) gives, for all x,y in H^{d-1}:
    B(x,y) = beta_X(Lx, y).   (2)

STEP 2 (reduce the left radical to the kernel of L). The left radical of B is
    Rad_L(B) = { x in H^{d-1} : B(x,y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1} }.
By (2), this equals
    Rad_L(B) = { x in H^{d-1} : beta_X(Lx, y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1} }.   (3)

STEP 3 (perfectness of beta_X). We use the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, part (b), applied to X (a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}) with n = d+1. Since d >= 2, we have 0 <= d+1 <= 2d, so part (b) applies and states that the pairing
    H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d),  (a,y) -> tr_X(a cup y)
is a PERFECT pairing of Q_ell-vector spaces. Now compose this perfect pairing with the u-induced Q_ell-linear isomorphism Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell described at the start. Composing a perfect pairing with an isomorphism of the target preserves perfectness, so we obtain a perfect pairing
    beta_X: H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell.
This is exactly the beta_X of Step 1: both are the canonical Poincare duality pairing (a,y) -> tr_X(a cup y) to Q_ell(-d) composed with the same u-induced identification Q_ell(-d) -> Q_ell. (This is where the target's Q_ell(1) data is used consistently: the same u that identifies Q_ell(1) with Q_ell in Step 1 also induces the Q_ell(-d) identification used here, so there is no mismatch between the two steps.)

Perfectness of beta_X means the induced map H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Hom_{Q_ell}(H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell), Q_ell), a -> (y -> beta_X(a,y)), is an isomorphism. In particular it is injective, so its kernel is {0}; equivalently, for a in H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell),
    beta_X(a, y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)  if and only if  a = 0.   (4)
Since L: H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell), for x in H^{d-1} the element Lx lies in H^{d+1}. Applying (4) with a = Lx gives
    beta_X(Lx, y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1}  if and only if  Lx = 0.   (5)

STEP 4 (conclude). Combining (3) and (5):
    Rad_L(B) = { x in H^{d-1} : beta_X(Lx, y) = 0 for every y in H^{d-1} } = { x in H^{d-1} : Lx = 0 } = ker(L).
Thus the left radical of B equals ker(L), as claimed. This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F(P^d) is contained in P^d, F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue of F on P^d, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}. Then P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
Let V = P^d = ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}), where H^s = H^s_et(X_k, Q_ell) and L is cup product with the cycle class xi of the very ample divisor. We prove that V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h(x,y) for all x,y.

Step 1 (V is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space). The group H^d = H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space: this is the standard finiteness theorem for etale cohomology of a smooth projective variety over a finite field with Q_ell-coefficients (ell != p). Since V is the kernel of the Q_ell-linear map L: H^d -> H^{d+2}, V is a Q_ell-subspace of H^d, hence a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space.

Step 2 (F restricts to an automorphism of V). The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F on H^d is an automorphism of H^d. Indeed, H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) carries the action of the absolute Galois group G_{F_{q^m}} = Gal(overline(F_{q^m})/F_{q^m}) (the usual Galois action on etale cohomology with Q_ell-coefficients, ell != p), and the arithmetic Frobenius is the image under this action of the arithmetic Frobenius element of G_{F_{q^m}}; a group action makes every element act invertibly, so F is in GL_{Q_ell}(H^d). By hypothesis F(V) is contained in V, so the restriction F_V := F|_V: V -> V is a well-defined Q_ell-linear endomorphism of V. It is injective: if x is in V and F_V(x) = 0, then F(x) = 0 in H^d, and since F is injective on H^d, x = 0. Because V is finite-dimensional, the injective endomorphism F_V: V -> V is also surjective, hence an isomorphism. Thus F_V is in GL_{Q_ell}(V).

Step 3 (apply the proved linear-algebra lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/ccebfa). We invoke that lemma with the following choices: K = Q_ell (a field of characteristic 0); sigma: overline(Q_ell) -> C the given embedding; c = q^{md} in Q_ell^*, where sigma(c) = q^{md} > 0 because q^{md} is a positive rational number fixed by sigma; V = P^d, a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space (Step 1); F = F_V in GL_{Q_ell}(V) (Step 2). We verify the two remaining hypotheses of the lemma. (i) Diagonalizability: the hypothesis 'F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell)' says exactly that F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). (ii) Eigenvalue absolute values: the hypothesis 'every eigenvalue of F on P^d, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}' means that for every eigenvalue alpha of F_V in overline(Q_ell), |sigma(alpha)| = q^{md/2}. Since sqrt(sigma(c)) = sqrt(q^{md}) = q^{md/2}, we have |sigma(alpha)| = sqrt(sigma(c)) for every eigenvalue alpha of F_V. By the lemma, V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F_V tensor id)x, (F_V tensor id)y) = sigma(c) h(x,y) = q^{md} h(x,y) for all x, y in V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 4 (conclusion). Since V = P^d and F_V is the restriction of F to P^d, the form h is a positive definite Hermitian form on P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C satisfying h((F tensor id)x, (F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h(x,y) for all x, y in P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. This is precisely the desired statement. QED

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose F L=q^m L F, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r->H^{2d-r+2}), and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F(P^r) subset P^r and P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_r with h_r((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{mr}h_r(x,y) for every 0<=r<=d-2 and all x,y. Then H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-2)}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof: We use the standard identification of Q_ell(1) with Q_ell that appears in the cited lemmas. Set c=q^{m(d-2)}. This lies in Q_ell^* and sigma(c)=q^{m(d-2)}>0. Let J=floor((d-2)/2). For j=0,...,J put s_j=d-2-2j and V_j=L^j P^{s_j} subset H^{d-2}. For j outside this range the corresponding primitive space is zero, so the list is finite. First we show F preserves each V_j. From FL=q^m L F, induction on j gives, for every r, F L^j = q^{mj} L^j F as maps H^r -> H^{r+2j}. Indeed the case j=0 is trivial, and if it holds for j then F L^{j+1}=F L^j L=q^{mj} L^j F L=q^{mj} L^j (q^m L F)=q^{m(j+1)} L^{j+1} F. Now take v in V_j, so v=L^j u with u in P^{s_j}. By hypothesis F(P^{s_j}) subset P^{s_j}, hence F u in P^{s_j}, and F v=q^{mj} L^j(F u) in V_j. Thus the restriction of F to V_j is a well defined Q_ell-linear map V_j -> V_j. Since F is an automorphism of H^{d-2}, this restriction is injective; V_j is finite dimensional over Q_ell, so it is an automorphism of V_j. Next we put a form on each V_j. Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/977aa8 with r=s_j and with the same index j. Its hypotheses are satisfied: 0<=s_j<=d-2<=d, 0<=j<=d-s_j because d-s_j=2+2j, the hard Lefschetz isomorphisms L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} for 0<=n<=d are assumed, F(P^{s_j}) subset P^{s_j}, and P^{s_j} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries the given positive definite Hermitian form with weight q^{m s_j}. The conclusion gives a positive definite Hermitian form h_j on V_j tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C such that h_j((F|_{V_j} tensor id)x,(F|_{V_j} tensor id)y)=q^{m(s_j+2j)}h_j(x,y)=q^{m(d-2)}h_j(x,y) for all x,y. Now use the Lefschetz decomposition. By the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/ace14e, with r=d-2, the map Phi from the direct sum over j>=0 of L^j P^{d-2-2j} to H^{d-2} given by summing the images is an isomorphism. Since P^t=0 for t<0, this direct sum is exactly the finite direct sum V_0 direct sum ... direct sum V_J. Hence H^{d-2}=V_0 direct sum ... direct sum V_J as Q_ell-vector spaces, and Phi identifies the abstract direct sum with H^{d-2}. We now combine the forms h_j. If J=0 this is immediate. If J>=1, apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/550524 inductively, taking K=Q_ell, the restriction of sigma to Q_ell, and the scalar c. It combines two positive definite Hermitian forms on V_i and V_k with the same scalar c into a positive definite Hermitian form on V_i direct sum V_k with the same scalar c. If some V_j is zero, omit it from the induction; the zero summand contributes nothing and the final formula remains valid. After finitely many steps we obtain a positive definite Hermitian form H on (direct sum_{j=0}^J V_j) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C such that H((F_0 direct sum ... direct sum F_J)x,(F_0 direct sum ... direct sum F_J)y)=c H(x,y), where F_j=F|_{V_j}. Finally define h on H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C by h(x,y)=H(Phi^{-1}(x),Phi^{-1}(y)). Because Phi is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism, h is a positive definite Hermitian form. For x,y in H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C, write u=Phi^{-1}(x) and v=Phi^{-1}(y). Since F preserves every V_j, Phi((F tensor id)x)=(F_0 direct sum ... direct sum F_J)u and similarly for y. Therefore h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=H((F_0 direct sum ... direct sum F_J)u,(F_0 direct sum ... direct sum F_J)v)=c H(u,v)=c h(x,y)=q^{m(d-2)}h(x,y). This is the required form.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), r>=0, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_{q^m}, and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. If every eigenvalue of F on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell), viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}, then every eigenvalue of F on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)(1), viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{m(r+2)/2}.
proof:
Let V = H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell). The space V is finite dimensional. If V = 0, the assertion is vacuous, so assume V != 0. Let sigma: k -> k be x -> x^{q^m}. We first compute the action of sigma on Q_ell(1). In the convention used in the statement, Q_ell(1) is (lim_n mu_{ell^n}(k)) tensor_{Z_ell} Q_ell, where mu_{ell^n}(k) is the group of ell^n-th roots of unity in k and the transition maps are zeta -> zeta^ell. For each n, sigma restricts to mu_{ell^n}(k) by zeta -> zeta^{q^m}. These restrictions commute with the transition maps because (zeta^{q^m})^ell = (zeta^ell)^{q^m}. Choose a compatible system (eta_n) of primitive ell^n-th roots of unity. Under the isomorphism Z_ell -> lim_n mu_{ell^n}(k) sending a to (eta_n^a), the induced map of sigma is multiplication by q^m. Since ell != p, q^m is a unit in Z_ell, so this is well defined. Tensoring with Q_ell, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_ell(1) as multiplication by the scalar q^m.

The Tate twist of V is V(1) = V tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell(1). By functoriality of pullback under id_X x sigma and by the definition of the Tate twist, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V(1) is F_V tensor F_{Q_ell(1)}, where F_V is the given q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V. Since F_{Q_ell(1)} = q^m id, after choosing a nonzero vector 1 in Q_ell(1), under the Q_ell-linear isomorphism V(1) -> V sending v tensor 1 to v, the twisted Frobenius is q^m F_V.

Let N = dim_{Q_ell} V. Let P_V(t) = det(t I - F_V) in Q_ell[t]. Then the characteristic polynomial of q^m F_V is P_{V(1)}(t) = det(t I - q^m F_V) = q^{mN} P_V(t/q^m). Hence the eigenvalues of q^m F_V over overline(Q_ell) are exactly q^m times the eigenvalues of F_V over overline(Q_ell). Let lambda be any eigenvalue of the Frobenius on V(1). Then lambda/q^m is an eigenvalue of F_V, so by hypothesis its Weil absolute value is q^{mr/2}. The Weil absolute value is multiplicative, and for the positive rational number q^m we have |q^m|_W = q^m. Therefore |lambda|_W = |q^m|_W |lambda/q^m|_W = q^m q^{mr/2} = q^{m(r+2)/2}. This proves the desired statement.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let sigma:K->C, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let c>0 be a real number. If T tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of T tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(c), then V tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y)=c h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
I found `eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_360`, which is a *special case* of the target (there $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and the eigenvalues live in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$). The target `5d27b2` is the more general statement (arbitrary char-0 field $K$, real $c>0$, eigenvalues of $T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ over $\mathbb C$), so it cannot be derived from that special case — it is itself the foundational linear-algebra fact. My self-contained direct proof is the correct route and relies on no proved lemma or reference.

Here is the final answer.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let W = V \otimes_{K,\sigma} \mathbb C and S = T \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}. First note that W is a finite-dimensional \mathbb C-vector space and S \in \mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb C}(W). Indeed, since K has characteristic 0, the homomorphism \sigma:K\to\mathbb C is injective (its kernel is a prime ideal of the field K, and it is not the whole ring since \sigma(1)=1), hence a field embedding; thus \mathbb C is a K-algebra via \sigma, and if (e_1,\dots,e_n) is a K-basis of V then (e_i\otimes 1)_{i=1}^n is a \mathbb C-basis of W, so \dim_{\mathbb C} W = \dim_K V < \infty. Because T \in \mathrm{GL}_K(V), the induced map S = T\otimes\mathrm{id} is invertible on W, with inverse T^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}.

By hypothesis, S is diagonalizable over \mathbb C and every eigenvalue of S has complex absolute value \sqrt{c}.

Step 1 (eigenspace decomposition). Let \Lambda be the finite set of distinct eigenvalues of S and, for \lambda\in\Lambda, let W_\lambda = \ker(S-\lambda) be the \lambda-eigenspace. We claim W = \bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda} W_\lambda. Justification: 'S is diagonalizable over \mathbb C' means there exists a \mathbb C-basis B of W consisting entirely of eigenvectors of S. For each b\in B there is a unique \lambda_b\in\Lambda with S b = \lambda_b b, so b\in W_{\lambda_b}. Grouping B by the value of \lambda_b, each W_\lambda is the span of those b\in B with \lambda_b=\lambda (indeed W_\lambda = \ker(S-\lambda) contains that span, and any vector in \ker(S-\lambda) is a \mathbb C-linear combination of the B-eigenvectors whose eigenvalue is \lambda, since an eigenvector-basis expansion of a vector fixed up to the scalar \lambda by S can only involve basis vectors with that same eigenvalue). The subspaces W_\lambda are linearly independent: if \sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} v_\lambda = 0 with v_\lambda\in W_\lambda, applying the polynomial \prod_{\mu\neq\lambda}(S-\mu) to the sum kills every term except the \lambda-term (on W_\mu it is 0 for \mu\neq\lambda and is \prod_{\mu\neq\lambda}(\lambda-\mu)\neq 0 on W_\lambda), forcing v_\lambda=0 for each \lambda. Hence the sum is direct, and it spans W because B does. For each \lambda\in\Lambda the hypothesis gives |\lambda|=\sqrt{c}, so |\lambda|^2 = c.

Step 2 (definition of h). For each \lambda\in\Lambda choose a \mathbb C-basis B_\lambda of W_\lambda; the disjoint union B = \bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda} B_\lambda is a \mathbb C-basis of W (it is the union of the grouped eigenbasis from Step 1). Define h:W\times W\to\mathbb C as follows: for x=\sum_{b\in B} a_b\, b and y=\sum_{b\in B} a'_b\, b (unique coefficient expressions in the basis B), set
    h(x,y) = \sum_{b\in B} a_b\,\overline{a'_b}.
This is the Hermitian form that makes B orthonormal. It is \mathbb C-linear in the first variable and \mathbb C-conjugate-linear in the second by construction. It is Hermitian-symmetric: h(y,x)=\sum_b a'_b\overline{a_b}=\overline{\sum_b a_b\overline{a'_b}}=\overline{h(x,y)}. It is positive definite: h(x,x)=\sum_b |a_b|^2 \ge 0, and h(x,x)=0 iff |a_b|^2=0 for every b, i.e. iff a_b=0 for every b, i.e. iff x=0.

Step 3 (mutual orthogonality of the eigenspaces). If \lambda\neq\mu then h(W_\lambda, W_\mu)=0. Indeed, take x\in W_\lambda=\mathrm{span}(B_\lambda) and y\in W_\mu=\mathrm{span}(B_\mu); in the basis B the coefficients of x are supported on B_\lambda and those of y on B_\mu, and B_\lambda\cap B_\mu=\emptyset, so every product a_b\overline{a'_b} in the sum defining h(x,y) has at least one factor equal to 0. Hence h(x,y)=0.

Step 4 (verification of the identity). Write x=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} x_\lambda and y=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda} y_\lambda with x_\lambda, y_\lambda\in W_\lambda; this is the unique decomposition from Step 1. Since S acts on W_\lambda as the scalar \lambda (by definition of W_\lambda=\ker(S-\lambda)), we have S x = \sum_\lambda \lambda\, x_\lambda and S y = \sum_\lambda \lambda\, y_\lambda. Using bilinearity/conjugate-linearity and the mutual orthogonality of Step 3,
    h(Sx, Sy) = h(\sum_\lambda \lambda x_\lambda, \sum_\mu \mu y_\mu) = \sum_{\lambda,\mu} \lambda\,\overline{\mu}\, h(x_\lambda, y_\mu) = \sum_\lambda \lambda\,\overline{\lambda}\, h(x_\lambda, y_\lambda) = \sum_\lambda |\lambda|^2\, h(x_\lambda, y_\lambda).
Since |\lambda|^2=c for every \lambda\in\Lambda, this equals c\,\sum_\lambda h(x_\lambda, y_\lambda). On the other hand, the same orthogonality gives
    h(x,y) = h(\sum_\lambda x_\lambda, \sum_\mu y_\mu) = \sum_{\lambda,\mu} h(x_\lambda, y_\mu) = \sum_\lambda h(x_\lambda, y_\lambda).
Combining the two displays yields h(Sx, Sy) = c\, h(x,y), i.e. h((T\otimes\mathrm{id})x, (T\otimes\mathrm{id})y) = c\, h(x,y) for all x,y\in W.

Thus W = V\otimes_{K,\sigma}\mathbb C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h satisfying h((T\otimes\mathrm{id})x,(T\otimes\mathrm{id})y)=c\,h(x,y) for all x,y, as required. (The degenerate case W=0 is included: then \Lambda=\emptyset, h is the unique form on the zero space, which is positive definite vacuously, and the identity holds trivially.) This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose F L=q^m L F, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r->H^{2d-r+2}), and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F(P^r) subset P^r and P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_r with h_r((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{mr}h_r(x,y) for every 0<=r<=d-2 and all x,y. Then L H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
All confirmations are in place. Now I will write the complete proof, incorporating the feedback's fix (the target group of $L^{2j+1}$ in the definition of $P^{d-2j}$ is $H^{d+2j+2}$).
