  "cited_lemmas": ["Miner/16d24b0281973336/6a1acf", "Miner/16d24b0281973336/977aa8"],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Setup and notation. Let H^s = H^s_et(X_k, Q_ell). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (so F denotes the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius operator on each H^s), let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, and let L: H^s -> H^{s+2} be cup product with xi. We are given: (i) L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d; (ii) F L = q^m L F, i.e. F_{n+2} o L = q^m L o F_n for every n; (iii) for every 0 <= r <= d-2, F(P^r) is contained in P^r and P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_r with h_r((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{mr} h_r(x,y) for all x,y, where P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2}).

Step 1 (Lefschetz decomposition of L H^{d-2}). We apply lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/6a1acf. Its hypotheses are exactly the present ones: q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, xi the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, and the Lefschetz isomorphisms L^{d-n}: H^n -> H^{2d-n} for 0 <= n <= d (the identification of Tate twists with Q_ell in its statement is a harmless convention, since no twisted cohomology appears in the conclusion). With P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}: H^r -> H^{2d-r+2}) as in the target, the lemma gives that L H^{d-2} is the direct sum of the subspaces L^j P^{d-2j} for j = 1, ..., floor(d/2):

    L H^{d-2} = direct sum over j=1..floor(d/2) of L^j P^{d-2j}  (as Q_ell-subspaces of H^d).

For each j in this range, substituting r = d-2j into the definition of P^r gives, with the correct target cohomology group:

    P^{d-2j} = ker(L^{d-(d-2j)+1}: H^{d-2j} -> H^{2d-(d-2j)+2}) = ker(L^{2j+1}: H^{d-2j} -> H^{d+2j+2}).

Thus each summand L^j P^{d-2j} is the image of P^{d-2j} under L^j, hence a Q_ell-subspace of H^{d-2j+2j} = H^d, and the displayed decomposition is a direct sum. The index range is consistent: j runs from 1 to floor(d/2), so r = d-2j runs from d-2 down to 0 (if d is even) or 1 (if d is odd), in particular 0 <= r <= d-2 for every summand.

Step 2 (F-stability of the summands). First we establish, by induction on j >= 1, that F L^j = q^{mj} L^j F (both sides being maps H^n -> H^{n+2j} for all n). For j = 1 this is exactly the hypothesis F L = q^m L F. If it holds for j, then

    F L^{j+1} = (F L^j) L = q^{mj} L^j (F L) = q^{mj} L^j (q^m L F) = q^{m(j+1)} L^{j+1} F,

which completes the induction.

Now fix j in {1, ..., floor(d/2)} and put r = d - 2j, so 0 <= r <= d-2. Let x be an arbitrary element of L^j P^r. By definition of the image L^j P^r, x = L^j y for some y in P^r. Using the identity of the preceding paragraph,

    F x = (F L^j) y = q^{mj} L^j (F y).

Since r <= d-2, the target hypothesis (iii) applies to this r and gives F(P^r) contained in P^r, hence F y is in P^r, and therefore F x = q^{mj} L^j(F y) lies in L^j P^r. As x was arbitrary, F(L^j P^r) is contained in L^j P^r for every j = 1, ..., floor(d/2).

Step 3 (Hermitian forms on the summands). Fix j in {1, ..., floor(d/2)} and put r = d - 2j. We verify the hypotheses of lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/977aa8 with this r and this j: (a) 0 <= r <= d, since 0 <= r <= d-2; (b) 0 <= j <= d - r, since d - r = d - (d - 2j) = 2j and j >= 1 implies j <= 2j; (c) F(P^r) is contained in P^r, which is the target hypothesis (iii) for this r (valid because r <= d-2); (d) P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_r with h_r((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{mr} h_r(x,y), again the target hypothesis (iii). (The convention in 977aa8 of fixing a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identifying Tate twists with Q_ell is a convention internal to that lemma's statement; its conclusion concerns only the un-twisted space L^j P^r tensor C, so it applies here without change.) By 977aa8, L^j P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C = L^j P^{d-2j} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_j with

    h_j((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{m(r+2j)} h_j(x,y) = q^{md} h_j(x,y)

for all x,y, where the second equality uses r + 2j = (d-2j) + 2j = d.

Step 4 (gluing on the direct sum). Since L H^{d-2} = direct sum over j=1..floor(d/2) of L^j P^{d-2j} is a direct sum of Q_ell-vector spaces, tensoring with C over Q_ell via sigma preserves the direct sum, so every x in L H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C has a unique decomposition x = sum over j of x_j with x_j in L^j P^{d-2j} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Define

    h(x,y) = sum over j=1..floor(d/2) of h_j(x_j, y_j).

We verify all required properties:

(1) Well-definedness: the decomposition x = sum x_j is unique, so h is independent of any choice of decomposition.

(2) C-linearity in the first variable and conjugate-linearity in the second: each h_j is C-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second, and a finite sum of such functions is as well.

(3) Hermitian symmetry: h(y,x) = sum_j h_j(y_j, x_j) = sum_j conjugate(h_j(x_j, y_j)) = conjugate(h(x,y)), using the Hermitian symmetry of each h_j.

(4) Positive definiteness: for any x, h(x,x) = sum_j h_j(x_j, x_j) is a finite sum of nonnegative real numbers (each h_j is positive definite), hence h(x,x) >= 0. If h(x,x) = 0, then h_j(x_j, x_j) = 0 for every j, and by positive definiteness of each h_j this forces x_j = 0 for every j, hence x = 0.

(5) Weight property: by Step 2 each summand L^j P^{d-2j} is F-stable. Therefore, for x = sum_j x_j, the j-th component of (F tensor id)x is (F tensor id)x_j, i.e. (F tensor id)x = sum_j (F tensor id)x_j. Hence, using the weight property of each h_j from Step 3,

    h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = sum_j h_j((F tensor id)x_j, (F tensor id)y_j) = sum_j q^{md} h_j(x_j, y_j) = q^{md} h(x,y).

Thus h is a positive definite Hermitian form on L H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C satisfying h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h(x,y) for all x,y, which is exactly the desired conclusion. The argument is uniform for all d >= 2; in the endpoint case d = 2 the sum has the single term j = 1 with r = 0, where P^0 = ker(L^3: H^0 -> H^6) = H^0 (since H^6 = 0 for a 2-dimensional variety), and the target hypothesis (iii) applies at r = 0 as required. This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let K be a field, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let T_V in GL_K(V), let T_W in GL_K(W), let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with phi T_V = T_W phi, let beta:V x V->K, let beta_W(a,b)=beta(phi^{-1}a, phi^{-1}b), let r be an integer, and let c in K^*. For N>=1 put G_N^V(x,y)=beta(x, T_V^N y)+(-1)^r c^N beta(x, T_V^{-N} y) and G_N^W(a,b)=beta_W(a, T_W^N b)+(-1)^r c^N beta_W(a, T_W^{-N} b). Then G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = G_N^V(v, w) for all v, w in V and all N>=1.
proof:
The target is a purely algebraic pullback identity. Per the reviser's guidance, it is self-contained: no proved lemma or reference is needed. I verified the route (conjugation of powers through φ, then direct computation applying T_W^{±N} only to the second argument of β_W). No search hit is required.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/d1c848",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = G_N^V(v, w) for all v, w in V and all N>=1. The argument is entirely algebraic: it uses only the definitions, the isomorphism property of phi, and the intertwining relation phi T_V = T_W phi (i.e. phi o T_V = T_W o phi). No field embedding, complex structure, positivity, or characteristic-0 assumption is used.

Step 1 (positive powers commute through phi). We claim T_W^N o phi = phi o T_V^N for every N>=1. For N=1 this is exactly the hypothesis T_W o phi = phi o T_V. Assume the claim for some N>=1. Then, using associativity of composition,
  T_W^{N+1} o phi = T_W o (T_W^N o phi) = T_W o (phi o T_V^N) = (T_W o phi) o T_V^N = (phi o T_V) o T_V^N = phi o (T_V o T_V^N) = phi o T_V^{N+1},
where the second equality is the inductive hypothesis, the third is associativity, the fourth is the hypothesis again, and the fifth is associativity. This completes the induction, so T_W^N o phi = phi o T_V^N for all N>=1.

Step 2 (negative powers commute through phi). First derive T_W^{-1} o phi = phi o T_V^{-1}: starting from T_W o phi = phi o T_V, compose on the left by T_W^{-1} to get phi = T_W^{-1} o phi o T_V, then compose on the right by T_V^{-1} to obtain phi o T_V^{-1} = T_W^{-1} o phi. Now claim T_W^{-N} o phi = phi o T_V^{-N} for every N>=1. For N=1 this is the identity just derived. Assume it for some N>=1. Then, again by associativity,
  T_W^{-(N+1)} o phi = T_W^{-1} o (T_W^{-N} o phi) = T_W^{-1} o (phi o T_V^{-N}) = (T_W^{-1} o phi) o T_V^{-N} = (phi o T_V^{-1}) o T_V^{-N} = phi o (T_V^{-1} o T_V^{-N}) = phi o T_V^{-(N+1)},
using the inductive hypothesis and the N=1 case. This completes the induction, so T_W^{-N} o phi = phi o T_V^{-N} for all N>=1.

Step 3 (conjugation). Composing the identities of Steps 1 and 2 on the left by phi^{-1} (which exists because phi is an isomorphism) gives, for every N>=1,
  phi^{-1} o T_W^N o phi = T_V^N   and   phi^{-1} o T_W^{-N} o phi = T_V^{-N}.
Equivalently, for any w in V, T_W^N(phi(w)) = phi(T_V^N(w)) and T_W^{-N}(phi(w)) = phi(T_V^{-N}(w)).

Step 4 (the pullback identity). Fix v, w in V and N>=1. By the definition of G_N^W, the powers T_W^{+N} and T_W^{-N} are applied to the second argument only, so
  G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = beta_W(phi(v), T_W^N(phi(w))) + (-1)^r c^N beta_W(phi(v), T_W^{-N}(phi(w))).
By Step 3, T_W^N(phi(w)) = phi(T_V^N(w)) and T_W^{-N}(phi(w)) = phi(T_V^{-N}(w)), so
  G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = beta_W(phi(v), phi(T_V^N(w))) + (-1)^r c^N beta_W(phi(v), phi(T_V^{-N}(w))).
Now apply the definition beta_W(a,b) = beta(phi^{-1}(a), phi^{-1}(b)) to each term, pulling phi^{-1} through to both slots (this is legitimate because phi^{-1} o phi = id_V): in the first term phi^{-1}(phi(v)) = v and phi^{-1}(phi(T_V^N(w))) = T_V^N(w); in the second term phi^{-1}(phi(v)) = v and phi^{-1}(phi(T_V^{-N}(w))) = T_V^{-N}(w). Hence
  G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = beta(v, T_V^N(w)) + (-1)^r c^N beta(v, T_V^{-N}(w)).
The right-hand side is, by definition, G_N^V(v, w). Therefore G_N^W(phi(v), phi(w)) = G_N^V(v, w), as required.

Remark on the direction of the computation: at no point is T_W^{+N} or T_W^{-N} pushed through phi^{-1} onto the first argument of beta. The definition of G_N^W applies T_W^{+N} and T_W^{-N} only to the second argument, and the pullback through phi^{-1} is applied argument-wise to both slots of beta_W, which is exactly the definition of beta_W. This is the only place the intertwining relation is used, via Steps 1-3. This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let sigma:K->C, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let c in K^* with sigma(c)>0. If V tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y)=c h(x,y) for all x,y, then T tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of T tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c)).
proof:
Proof. Let W = V tensor_{K,sigma} C and let A = T tensor id, the C-linear automorphism of W induced by T. The hypothesis reads h(Ax, Ay) = sigma(c) h(x, y) for all x, y in W, where sigma(c) > 0 is a positive real number (the element c in K acts on W through sigma).

Step 1 (Reduction to an isometry). Let s = sqrt(sigma(c)) > 0 be the positive real square root. Set B = s^{-1} A. Then B is C-linear and, for all x, y in W,
h(Bx, By) = h(s^{-1} Ax, s^{-1} Ay) = s^{-1} overline{s^{-1}} h(Ax, Ay) = s^{-2} sigma(c) h(x, y) = h(x, y),
where we used that s is real (so overline{s^{-1}} = s^{-1}) and the hypothesis h(Ax, Ay) = sigma(c) h(x, y) = s^2 h(x, y). Thus B is an isometry for h.

If B is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue of modulus 1, then A = s B is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of A has modulus s = sqrt(sigma(c)). It therefore suffices to prove the following claim.

Claim. Let (W, h) be a finite-dimensional complex vector space with a positive definite Hermitian form h, and let B in GL(W) be a C-linear isometry, i.e., h(Bx, By) = h(x, y) for all x, y in W. Then B is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of B has complex absolute value 1.

Step 2 (The adjoint). Recall the conventions: h is C-linear in its first variable and C-conjugate-linear in its second, so h(alpha x, beta y) = alpha overline{beta} h(x, y), and h(x, y) = overline{h(y, x)}. For each y in W, the map x -> h(Bx, y) is a C-linear functional on W (C-linearity of h in its first variable and C-linearity of B). Because h is positive definite it is nondegenerate, so the map z -> (x -> h(x, z)) from W onto the space of C-linear functionals on W is bijective; hence there exists a unique vector B* y in W such that
h(Bx, y) = h(x, B* y) for all x in W.
This defines a map B*: W -> W.

We verify B* is C-linear. For alpha in C and y in W, for every x in W,
h(Bx, alpha y) = overline{alpha} h(Bx, y) = overline{alpha} h(x, B* y) = h(x, alpha B* y),
using C-conjugate-linearity of h in its second variable in the first and last equalities. By uniqueness of the representing vector, B* (alpha y) = alpha B* y. For additivity, for y1, y2 in W and every x in W,
h(Bx, y1 + y2) = h(Bx, y1) + h(Bx, y2) = h(x, B* y1) + h(x, B* y2) = h(x, B* y1 + B* y2),
so B* (y1 + y2) = B* y1 + B* y2. Thus B* is C-linear.

Step 3 (B is unitary). For all x, y in W,
h(x, y) = h(Bx, By) = h(x, B* (B y)),
where the last equality applies the defining relation with first argument Bx and second argument By. Since h is nondegenerate, B* B y = y for every y, i.e., B* B = I.

From B* B = I, B is injective (B x = 0 implies x = B* B x = 0), and since W is finite-dimensional, B is surjective, hence invertible. As B* is a left inverse of the invertible map B, we get B* = B^{-1}, and therefore also B B* = I. Thus B is unitary: B* B = B B* = I and B* = B^{-1}.

Step 4 (Sublemma on eigenvectors). Let v in W, v != 0, be an eigenvector of B with eigenvalue lambda, i.e., B v = lambda v. Then |lambda| = 1 and B* v = overline{lambda} v.

Proof of the sublemma.
(i) |lambda| = 1. By the isometry property,
||B v||^2 = h(B v, B v) = h(v, v) = ||v||^2.
On the other hand, B v = lambda v, so
||B v||^2 = h(lambda v, lambda v) = lambda overline{lambda} h(v, v) = |lambda|^2 ||v||^2.
Hence |lambda|^2 ||v||^2 = ||v||^2. Since v != 0, ||v||^2 = h(v, v) > 0, so |lambda|^2 = 1, i.e., |lambda| = 1. In particular lambda != 0.

(ii) B* v = overline{lambda} v. Since B* is C-linear,
B* B v = B* (B v) = B* (lambda v) = lambda B* v.
By unitarity (B B* = B* B),
B (B* v) = B* B v = lambda B* v,
so the vector B* v is an eigenvector of B with eigenvalue lambda (or is 0).

Now compute two identities. First, applying the defining relation with first argument v and second argument B v,
h(B v, B v) = h(v, B* (B v)) = h(v, B* B v) = h(v, lambda B* v) = overline{lambda} h(v, B* v),
where the last equality uses C-conjugate-linearity of h in its second variable. The left side equals h(v, v) = ||v||^2, so
overline{lambda} h(v, B* v) = ||v||^2.  (1)
Second, applying the defining relation with first argument v and second argument v,
h(B v, v) = h(v, B* v).
The left side is h(lambda v, v) = lambda h(v, v) = lambda ||v||^2 (C-linearity of h in its first variable), so
h(v, B* v) = lambda ||v||^2.  (2)

Now set u = B* v / overline{lambda}, which is well-defined since |lambda| = 1 implies overline{lambda} != 0.

First, ||u|| = ||v||. Indeed, B* is itself an isometry: for any x, y in W, writing x = B a and y = B b (possible since B is surjective), we have h(B* x, B* y) = h(a, b) = h(B a, B b) = h(x, y). Hence
||u||^2 = ||B* v / overline{lambda}||^2 = (1/|overline{lambda}|^2) ||B* v||^2 = ||B* v||^2 = ||v||^2,
so ||u|| = ||v||.

Next, compute h(u, v):
h(u, v) = h(B* v / overline{lambda}, v) = (1/overline{lambda}) h(B* v, v).
By conjugate symmetry and (2), h(B* v, v) = overline{h(v, B* v)} = overline{lambda ||v||^2} = overline{lambda} ||v||^2 (the last equality because ||v||^2 is real). Therefore
h(u, v) = (1/overline{lambda}) overline{lambda} ||v||^2 = ||v||^2.

We thus have h(u, v) = ||v||^2 and ||u|| = ||v||. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives |h(u, v)| <= ||u|| ||v|| = ||v||^2, and we have equality |h(u, v)| = ||v||^2 = ||u|| ||v||. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz for a positive definite Hermitian form holds if and only if u and v are C-linearly dependent: if u, v were linearly independent, then for any C-basis e_1, e_2 of span(u, v) the Gram matrix (h(e_i, e_j)) would be positive definite, hence its determinant ||u||^2 ||v||^2 - |h(u, v)|^2 would be strictly positive, contradicting the determinant being 0; if u, v are dependent, say u = alpha v, then |h(u, v)| = |alpha| ||v||^2 = ||u|| ||v||.

Hence u = alpha v for some alpha in C. Then
||v||^2 = h(u, v) = h(alpha v, v) = alpha h(v, v) = alpha ||v||^2,
using C-linearity of h in its first variable, so alpha = 1. Therefore u = v, i.e., B* v / overline{lambda} = v, i.e., B* v = overline{lambda} v. This proves the sublemma.

Step 5 (Diagonalizability by induction). We prove by induction on n = dim W that every isometry on an n-dimensional complex vector space with a positive definite Hermitian form is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue of modulus 1.

Base case n = 0: vacuous. Base case n = 1: for any nonzero e in W, B e = lambda e for some lambda in C (B is a scalar on a one-dimensional space), and the sublemma (applied to the eigenvector e) gives |lambda| = 1; B is diagonalizable with its single eigenvalue of modulus 1.

Inductive step. Assume the statement for all dimensions at most n, and let dim W = n + 1. Since W is a complex vector space and B is a C-linear endomorphism, the characteristic polynomial of B with respect to any basis is a nonconstant polynomial in C[t], which has a root by the fundamental theorem of algebra; hence B has an eigenvalue lambda with a nonzero eigenvector v. By the sublemma, |lambda| = 1 and B* v = overline{lambda} v.

Let U = v^perp = {x in W : h(x, v) = 0}. The functional x -> h(x, v) is nonzero (its value at v is h(v, v) != 0), so U has codimension 1, i.e., dim U = n.

We show U is B-invariant. Let x in U, so h(x, v) = 0. Then, using the defining relation for B* and C-conjugate-linearity of h in its second variable,
h(B x, v) = h(x, B* v) = h(x, overline{lambda} v) = overline{overline{lambda}} h(x, v) = lambda h(x, v) = 0.
Hence B x in U, so B(U) subset U.

Thus B|_U is an isometry on (U, h|_U), where h|_U is positive definite as the restriction of a positive definite form. By the inductive hypothesis, B|_U is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue of modulus 1: there exists a C-basis u_1, ..., u_n of U with B u_i = mu_i u_i and |mu_i| = 1 for each i = 1, ..., n.

Since v notin U and dim U = n = dim W - 1, the set {v, u_1, ..., u_n} is a C-basis of W. In this basis, B is represented by the diagonal matrix diag(lambda, mu_1, ..., mu_n), because B v = lambda v and B u_i = mu_i u_i. Hence B is diagonalizable over C and its eigenvalues lambda, mu_1, ..., mu_n all have modulus 1. This completes the induction and proves the claim.

Step 6 (Conclusion). By the claim, B is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue of modulus 1. Write B = P D P^{-1} with D = diag(beta_1, ..., beta_n) and |beta_i| = 1 for each i. Then
A = s B = s P D P^{-1} = P (s D) P^{-1} = P diag(s beta_1, ..., s beta_n) P^{-1}.
Thus A = T tensor id is diagonalizable over C, and its eigenvalues are s beta_1, ..., s beta_n, each of complex absolute value |s| |beta_i| = s = sqrt(sigma(c)).

This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose F L=q^m L F, and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If H^{d-2} tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-2)}h(x,y) for all x,y, then F on L H^{d-2} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of F on L H^{d-2} satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = q^{md/2}.
proof: Let V=H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_ell) and W=L(V) subset H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). By the standard finiteness theorem for etale cohomology of smooth projective varieties over finite fields, V is finite-dimensional over Q_ell; since W is the image of the Q_ell-linear map L:V->H^d, W is also finite-dimensional. The hypothesis F L=q^m L F implies F(W) subset W: if w=L(v), then F(w)=F(L(v))=q^m L(F(v)) in W. Thus F restricts to endomorphisms F_V of V and F_W of W. First F_V is invertible: if F_V(v)=0, then 0=h(F_V v,F_V v)=q^{m(d-2)}h(v,v). Since h is positive definite, h(v,v)=0 forces v=0 in V (the natural map V->V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C is injective). Hence F_V is injective, and finite-dimensionality of V gives surjectivity, so F_V in GL_{Q_ell}(V). Next F_W is surjective: for w=L(v) in W, put u=q^{-m}F_V^{-1}(v) in V and w'=L(u) in W; then F_W(w')=F(L(u))=q^m L(F(u))=q^m L(q^{-m}v)=L(v)=w. Since W is finite-dimensional, F_W is invertible. Now apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_468 with T=F_V, c=q^{m(d-2)}, and iota=sigma. The number c lies in Q_{>0} subset Q_ell^x, sigma(c)>0, and h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C satisfying h((F_V tensor id)x,(F_V tensor id)y)=sigma(c)h(x,y). Therefore F_V is diagonalizable over Qbar_l and every eigenvalue alpha of F_V in Qbar_l satisfies |sigma(alpha)|^2=sigma(c)=q^{m(d-2)}, i.e. |sigma(alpha)|=q^{m(d-2)/2}. Let Vbar=V tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_l and Wbar=W tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_l, and let Lbar=L tensor id:Vbar->H^d tensor Qbar_l. We have Wbar=Lbar(Vbar): indeed every element of Wbar is a finite sum w_i tensor a_i with w_i=L(v_i) in W, hence equals Lbar(sum v_i tensor a_i), and the reverse inclusion is clear. By the diagonalizability just obtained, F_V tensor id on Vbar is diagonalizable over Qbar_l. Let alpha_1,...,alpha_r be its distinct eigenvalues and write Vbar=direct sum_i Vbar_{alpha_i}, where Vbar_{alpha_i}=ker((F_V tensor id)-alpha_i id). For vbar in Vbar_{alpha_i}, using the base-changed relation (F tensor id)Lbar=q^m Lbar(F_V tensor id), we get (F_W tensor id)(Lbar(vbar))=(F tensor id)(Lbar(vbar))=q^m Lbar(F_V tensor id vbar)=q^m alpha_i Lbar(vbar). Thus Lbar(Vbar_{alpha_i}) is contained in the (possibly zero) eigenspace E_{q^m alpha_i}=ker((F_W tensor id)-q^m alpha_i id) of F_W tensor id. Since Wbar=Lbar(Vbar)=sum_i Lbar(Vbar_{alpha_i}), Wbar is spanned by eigenvectors of F_W tensor id; because Wbar is finite-dimensional, F_W tensor id is diagonalizable over Qbar_l, and therefore F_W is diagonalizable over Qbar_l. It remains to identify the eigenvalues. Let mu be an eigenvalue of F_W tensor id and let 0 neq wbar in Wbar be an eigenvector. Write wbar=sum_i wbar_i with wbar_i in Lbar(Vbar_{alpha_i}) subset E_{q^m alpha_i}. Because F_W tensor id is diagonalizable, Wbar is the direct sum of its nonzero eigenspaces. The numbers q^m alpha_i are pairwise distinct, since the alpha_i are distinct and q^m neq 0. Hence the nonzero subspaces among the E_{q^m alpha_i} are distinct direct summands in this decomposition. Applying the decomposition to 0=(F_W tensor id - mu id)(wbar)=sum_i (q^m alpha_i - mu)wbar_i forces (q^m alpha_i - mu)wbar_i=0 for every i. Since wbar neq 0, some wbar_i is nonzero, so mu=q^m alpha_i for some i. Finally, |sigma(mu)|=|sigma(q^m alpha_i)|=q^m |sigma(alpha_i)| because sigma fixes Q and q^m>0. By the eigenvalue estimate for F_V, |sigma(alpha_i)|=q^{m(d-2)/2}. Therefore |sigma(mu)|=q^m q^{m(d-2)/2}=q^{md/2}. This proves that F on L H^{d-2}=W is diagonalizable over Qbar_l and every eigenvalue mu of F on W satisfies |sigma(mu)|=q^{md/2}.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let sigma:K->C with sigma(K) subset R, let r be an integer, let c in K^* with sigma(c)>0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let beta:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(y,x)=(-1)^r beta(x,y) and beta(Tx,Ty)=c beta(x,y). For N>=1 put G_N(x,y)=beta(x,T^N y)+(-1)^r c^N beta(x,T^{-N} y). If G_N is positive definite on V tensor_{K,sigma} C for every N>=1, then T tensor id is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue having complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c)).
proof:
We set V_C = V \otimes_{K,\sigma} C and T_C = T \otimes \mathrm{id}_{V_C}. We construct a positive definite Hermitian form h on V_C satisfying h(T_C x, T_C y) = \sigma(c)\, h(x,y) for all x,y \in V_C, and then apply lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea.

**Step 1: The conjugation on V_C.**
We define a map \overline{\cdot}: V_C \to V_C on simple tensors by \overline{v \otimes a} = v \otimes \bar{a} (where \bar{a} is the usual complex conjugate of a \in C), and extend it additively to all of V_C. We verify well-definedness. The defining relation of the tensor product is (kv) \otimes a = v \otimes \sigma(k) a for k \in K, v \in V, a \in C. We compute both sides of the image under the proposed bar:
\overline{(kv) \otimes a} = (kv) \otimes \bar{a} = v \otimes \sigma(k)\, \bar{a} \quad (\text{tensor relation}),
\overline{v \otimes \sigma(k) a} = v \otimes \overline{\sigma(k)\, a} = v \otimes \overline{\sigma(k)}\, \bar{a}.
Since \sigma(K) \subseteq \mathbb{R}, we have \sigma(k) \in \mathbb{R} = \overline{\sigma(k)}, so the two expressions coincide. Hence \overline{\cdot} is well-defined.

The map \overline{\cdot} is an involution: \overline{\overline{v \otimes a}} = \overline{v \otimes \bar{a}} = v \otimes \overline{\bar{a}} = v \otimes a.

The map \overline{\cdot} is C-conjugate-linear: for \lambda \in C and a simple tensor z = v \otimes a,
\overline{\lambda z} = \overline{v \otimes (\lambda a)} = v \otimes \overline{\lambda a} = v \otimes \bar{\lambda}\, \bar{a} = \bar{\lambda}\, \overline{v \otimes a} = \bar{\lambda}\, \overline{z}.
By additivity this holds for all z \in V_C.

**Step 2: The C-bilinear form G_1^C and its symmetry.**
Since G_1: V \times V \to K is K-bilinear, it extends uniquely to a C-bilinear form G_1^C: V_C \times V_C \to C given on simple tensors by
G_1^C(v \otimes a,\, w \otimes b) = \sigma(G_1(v,w))\, a\, b.

We first prove that G_1 is symmetric on V. Recall G_1(x,y) = \beta(x, Ty) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y).

We use two identities derived from \beta(Ta, Tb) = c\, \beta(a,b):
(i)\quad \beta(x, Ty) = c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y),
obtained by substituting a = T^{-1}x, b = y into \beta(Ta, Tb) = c\, \beta(a,b):
\beta(T(T^{-1}x),\, Ty) = c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y), i.e.\ \beta(x, Ty) = c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y).

(ii)\quad \beta(Tx, y) = c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y),
obtained by substituting a = x, b = T^{-1}y into \beta(Ta, Tb) = c\, \beta(a,b):
\beta(Tx,\, T(T^{-1}y)) = c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y), i.e.\ \beta(Tx, y) = c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y).

Now compute G_1(y, x):
G_1(y, x) = \beta(y, Tx) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(y, T^{-1}x).

For the first term, by the symmetry \beta(u,v) = (-1)^r \beta(v,u):
\beta(y, Tx) = (-1)^r \beta(Tx, y) = (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y) \quad (\text{using identity (ii)}).

For the second term, by the symmetry:
\beta(y, T^{-1}x) = (-1)^r \beta(T^{-1}x, y),
so\ \, (-1)^r c\, \beta(y, T^{-1}x) = (-1)^r c\, (-1)^r \beta(T^{-1}x, y) = c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y).

Therefore:
G_1(y, x) = (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y) + c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y).

On the other hand, using identity (i):
G_1(x, y) = \beta(x, Ty) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y) = c\, \beta(T^{-1}x, y) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y).

Thus G_1(y, x) = G_1(x, y) for all x, y \in V; G_1 is symmetric.

By C-bilinearity, G_1^C is symmetric on V_C: G_1^C(z_1, z_2) = G_1^C(z_2, z_1) for all z_1, z_2 \in V_C.

We also record the conjugation formula: for all x, y \in V_C,
\overline{G_1^C(x, y)} = G_1^C(\bar{x}, \bar{y}).
Proof: for simple tensors x = v \otimes a, y = w \otimes b,
\overline{G_1^C(x, y)} = \overline{\sigma(G_1(v,w))\, a\, b} = \sigma(G_1(v,w))\, \bar{a}\, \bar{b} \quad (\text{since } \sigma(G_1(v,w)) \in \mathbb{R}),
G_1^C(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = G_1^C(v \otimes \bar{a},\, w \otimes \bar{b}) = \sigma(G_1(v,w))\, \bar{a}\, \bar{b}.
The two agree, and by C-bilinearity of G_1^C and additivity of \overline{\cdot}, the formula extends to all x, y \in V_C.

**Step 3: The Hermitian form h.**
Define h: V_C \times V_C \to C by h(x, y) = G_1^C(x, \bar{y}).

C-linearity in the first argument: h(\lambda x, y) = G_1^C(\lambda x, \bar{y}) = \lambda\, G_1^C(x, \bar{y}) = \lambda\, h(x,y).
C-conjugate-linearity in the second argument: h(x, \lambda y) = G_1^C(x, \overline{\lambda y}) = G_1^C(x, \bar{\lambda}\, \bar{y}) = \bar{\lambda}\, G_1^C(x, \bar{y}) = \bar{\lambda}\, h(x,y).

Hermitian symmetry: for all x, y \in V_C,
h(y, x) = G_1^C(y, \bar{x}) = G_1^C(\bar{x}, y) \quad (\text{by symmetry of } G_1^C)
= \overline{G_1^C(x, \bar{y})} \quad (\text{by the conjugation formula with } a = x,\, b = \bar{y}: \overline{G_1^C(x, \bar{y})} = G_1^C(\bar{x}, \overline{\bar{y}}) = G_1^C(\bar{x}, y))
= \overline{h(x, y)}.

Thus h is a Hermitian form on V_C: C-linear in the first slot, C-conjugate-linear in the second, with h(y,x) = \overline{h(x,y)}.

**Step 4: Positivity of h.**
For x \in V_C, h(x, x) = G_1^C(x, \bar{x}). We first verify this is real: by the conjugation formula and symmetry of G_1^C,
G_1^C(x, \bar{x}) = G_1^C(\bar{x}, x) = \overline{G_1^C(x, \bar{x})},
so G_1^C(x, \bar{x}) \in \mathbb{R}. By the hypothesis with N = 1, G_1^C(x, \bar{x}) > 0 for every nonzero x \in V_C. Hence h is positive definite.

**Step 5: The scaling identity for G_1^C.**
We show G_1(Tx, Ty) = c\, G_1(x, y) for all x, y \in V.

G_1(Tx, Ty) = \beta(Tx, T^2 y) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(Tx, y).

First term: \beta(Tx, T^2 y) = \beta(Tx, T(Ty)) = c\, \beta(x, Ty), using \beta(Ta, Tb) = c\, \beta(a,b) with a = x, b = Ty.

Second term: \beta(Tx, y) = \beta(Tx, T(T^{-1}y)) = c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y), using \beta(Ta, Tb) = c\, \beta(a,b) with a = x, b = T^{-1}y.

Therefore:
G_1(Tx, Ty) = c\, \beta(x, Ty) + (-1)^r c^2\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y) = c\bigl[\beta(x, Ty) + (-1)^r c\, \beta(x, T^{-1}y)\bigr] = c\, G_1(x, y).

Extending to V_C by C-bilinearity: for all x, y \in V_C,
G_1^C(T_C x,\, T_C y) = \sigma(c)\, G_1^C(x, y).
(Verification on simple tensors: G_1^C(T_C(v \otimes a),\, T_C(w \otimes b)) = G_1^C((Tv) \otimes a,\, (Tw) \otimes b) = \sigma(G_1(Tv, Tw))\, a\, b = \sigma(c\, G_1(v,w))\, a\, b = \sigma(c)\, \sigma(G_1(v,w))\, a\, b = \sigma(c)\, G_1^C(v \otimes a,\, w \otimes b).)

**Step 6: Commutation of \overline{\cdot} with T_C.**
We show \overline{T_C y} = T_C \bar{y} for all y \in V_C.

For a simple tensor y = v \otimes a:
\overline{T_C y} = \overline{(Tv) \otimes a} = (Tv) \otimes \bar{a} = T_C(v \otimes \bar{a}) = T_C \bar{y}.

For a general y = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (w_j \otimes b_j):
\overline{T_C y} = \overline{T_C\bigl(\sum_j (w_j \otimes b_j)\bigr)}
= \overline{\sum_j T_C(w_j \otimes b_j)} \quad (T_C \text{ is C-linear, hence additive})
= \overline{\sum_j ((Tw_j) \otimes b_j)}
= \sum_j \overline{(Tw_j) \otimes b_j} \quad (\overline{\cdot} \text{ is additive})
= \sum_j (Tw_j) \otimes \bar{b_j} \quad (\text{definition of } \overline{\cdot} \text{ on simple tensors})
= \sum_j T_C(w_j \otimes \bar{b_j}) \quad (\text{definition of } T_C)
= T_C\bigl(\sum_j (w_j \otimes \bar{b_j})\bigr) \quad (T_C \text{ is C-linear, hence additive})
= T_C\bigl(\overline{\sum_j (w_j \otimes b_j)}\bigr) \quad (\overline{\cdot} \text{ is additive})
= T_C \bar{y}.

**Step 7: The scaling of h.**
For all x, y \in V_C:
h(T_C x,\, T_C y) = G_1^C(T_C x,\, \overline{T_C y})
= G_1^C(T_C x,\, T_C \bar{y}) \quad (\text{Step 6: } \overline{T_C y} = T_C \bar{y})
= \sigma(c)\, G_1^C(x, \bar{y}) \quad (\text{Step 5: scaling identity})
= \sigma(c)\, h(x, y).

**Step 8: Application of the diagonalizability lemma.**
We have shown that V_C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T \otimes \mathrm{id})x,\, (T \otimes \mathrm{id})y) = \sigma(c)\, h(x,y) for all x, y \in V_C, and \sigma(c) > 0. By lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea, T \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of T \otimes \mathrm{id} has complex absolute value \sqrt{\sigma(c)}.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d and beta|_{P^d} is nondegenerate. For N>=1 put G_N^P(x,y)=beta(x,F^N y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F^{-N} y). If G_N^P is positive definite on P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C for every N>=1, then F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) with every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), having Weil absolute value q^{md/2}.
proof: Set V=P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). If V=0 the assertion is vacuous, so assume V is nonzero. It is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. Let F_V be the restriction of F to V. We first show F_V is invertible. By lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7, beta(Fu,Fv)=q^{md} beta(u,v) for all u,v in H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). If F_V x=0 with x in V, then for every y in V, 0=beta(F_V x,F_V y)=q^{md} beta(x,y). Since q^{md} is nonzero and beta restricted to V is nondegenerate, x=0. Thus F_V is injective, and because V is finite-dimensional, F_V is an automorphism of V; in particular F^{-1} maps V to V. Let V_C=V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C, and let bar denote complex conjugation on the C factor. For the C-bilinear extension Ghat_1 of sigma composed with G_1^P, define h(v,w)=Ghat_1(v,bar w) for v,w in V_C. Explicitly, if v=sum_i x_i tensor a_i and w=sum_j y_j tensor b_j, then h(v,w)=sum_{i,j} sigma(G_1^P(x_i,y_j)) a_i bar(b_j). By the hypothesis for N=1, with its standard Hermitian interpretation, h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V_C; only the case N=1 of the hypothesis is needed, and we do not evaluate G_1^P(x,x) on eigenvectors over overline(Q_ell). Next we prove the scaling relation. Because F_V is Q_ell-linear, bar(F_V w)=F_V bar(w). For x,y in V, using the definition G_1^P(a,b)=beta(a,F b)+(-1)^d q^{md} beta(a,F^{-1} b), we compute G_1^P(F_V x,F_V y)=beta(F_V x,F_V^2 y)+(-1)^d q^{md} beta(F_V x,y). By lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7 twice, beta(F_V x,F_V^2 y)=q^{md} beta(x,F_V y) and beta(F_V x,y)=q^{md} beta(x,F_V^{-1} y). Hence G_1^P(F_V x,F_V y)=q^{md} beta(x,F_V y)+(-1)^d q^{2md} beta(x,F_V^{-1} y)=q^{md} G_1^P(x,y). Therefore Ghat_1(F_V x tensor 1,F_V y tensor 1)=sigma(q^{md} G_1^P(x,y))=q^{md} Ghat_1(x tensor 1,y tensor 1), since sigma fixes the rational number q^{md}. By C-bilinearity of Ghat_1, this gives Ghat_1(F_V v,F_V bar w)=q^{md} Ghat_1(v,bar w) for all v,w in V_C. Consequently h((F_V tensor id)v,(F_V tensor id)w)=Ghat_1(F_V v,bar(F_V w))=Ghat_1(F_V v,F_V bar w)=q^{md} Ghat_1(v,bar w)=q^{md} h(v,w). Now apply lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_468 with T=F_V, c=q^{md}, and iota=sigma. The hypotheses are satisfied: V is finite-dimensional over Q_ell, F_V is in GL(V), c is a positive rational number, and h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V_C with h((F_V tensor id)v,(F_V tensor id)w)=sigma(c) h(v,w) for all v,w. The conclusion is that F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue alpha of F_V satisfies |sigma(alpha)|^2=sigma(c)=q^{md}. Taking square roots gives |sigma(alpha)|=q^{md/2}, which is the Weil absolute value of alpha. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected curve on X, and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{-m}h(x,y), then F is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) on H^3_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof: Let U = H^1_et(Y_k, Q_ell), V = H^1_et(X_k, Q_ell), H3 = H^3_et(X_k, Q_ell), and W = U(-1). Write F_X, F_Y, F_W for the action of the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on these spaces. Step 1. Frobenius is invertible, so F_W is in GL_{Q_ell}(W). By the hypothesis, W tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F_W tensor id)x, (F_W tensor id)y) = q^{-m} h(x,y). Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea with K = Q_ell, T = F_W, and c = q^{-m}. Since sigma fixes Q, sigma(q^{-m}) = q^{-m} > 0, so F_W tensor id is diagonalizable over C. Let mu_W(t) be the minimal polynomial of F_W over Q_ell. If mu_W had a repeated factor over Q_ell, its image under sigma would have a repeated factor over C, contradicting diagonalizability over C. Hence mu_W is squarefree. Over the algebraic closure overline(Q_ell), mu_W splits into distinct linear factors, so F_W is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). Let lambda range over the distinct eigenvalues of F_W in overline(Q_ell), and let E_lambda = ker(F_W - lambda). Then W is the direct sum of the E_lambda. Step 2. We construct a surjective map g: W -> H3 that is equivariant for Frobenius up to a nonzero scalar. Choose a nonzero element u of Q_ell(1) and identify all Tate twists with Q_ell by u^n -> 1. Let j: U -> H3 be the Gysin map i_! after this identification. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/50af72 (applied with the prime power q^m), j is surjective. Let alpha: W -> U be the identification fixing a nonzero element of Q_ell(-1). Put g = j alpha. Since alpha is an isomorphism and j is surjective, g is surjective. We claim that there exists c in Q_ell^* such that F_X g = c g F_W. First, let < , >_X : H3 x V -> Q_ell and < , >_Y : U x U -> Q_ell be the Poincare duality pairings followed by the above identifications of Q_ell(-2) and Q_ell(-1) with Q_ell. They are perfect. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, the un-identified Poincare duality pairings are Frobenius-equivariant with nonzero scalars; since the identifications are Q_ell-linear, the identified pairings are Frobenius-equivariant up to nonzero scalars s_X and s_Y in Q_ell^*: <F_X a, F_X b>_X = s_X <a,b>_X and <F_Y a, F_Y b>_Y = s_Y <a,b>_Y. By the defining property of the Gysin map (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_gysin_projection_divisor, applied with the prime power q^m and n=1), there is a nonzero scalar lambda_0 in Q_ell^* such that for all a in U and b in V, < j(a), b >_X = lambda_0 < a, i^* b >_Y. By eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/f527bc, the restriction map i^*: V -> U is equivariant for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius: F_Y i^* = i^* F_X. Now fix a in U. For every b in V, < F_X j(a), F_X b >_X = s_X < j(a), b >_X = s_X lambda_0 < a, i^* b >_Y. On the other hand, < j(F_Y a), F_X b >_X = lambda_0 < F_Y a, i^* F_X b >_Y = lambda_0 < F_Y a, F_Y i^* b >_Y = lambda_0 s_Y < a, i^* b >_Y. Therefore < F_X j(a), F_X b >_X = (s_X / s_Y) < j(F_Y a), F_X b >_X. Since F_X: V -> V is invertible, as b ranges over V, F_X b ranges over V. Hence for every b' in V, < F_X j(a) - (s_X/s_Y) j(F_Y a), b' >_X = 0. Perfectness of < , >_X in the first variable gives F_X j(a) = (s_X/s_Y) j(F_Y a). Thus F_X j = c_1 j F_Y with c_1 = s_X/s_Y in Q_ell^*. Next, the one-dimensional Q_ell-vector space Q_ell(-1) carries the Frobenius action by multiplication by some nonzero scalar t in Q_ell^*. For the identification alpha, this means alpha F_W = t F_Y alpha, equivalently F_Y alpha = t^{-1} alpha F_W. Put c_2 = t^{-1} in Q_ell^*. Finally, F_X g = F_X j alpha = c_1 j F_Y alpha = c_1 c_2 j alpha F_W = c g F_W, where c = c_1 c_2 is nonzero. Only this nonvanishing of c is used below. Step 3. Let E'_mu be the eigenspace of F_X on H3 for an eigenvalue mu in overline(Q_ell). If w in E_lambda, then F_X g(w) = c g(F_W w) = c lambda g(w). Thus g(E_lambda) is contained in E'_{c lambda} (with the zero vector allowed). Since g is surjective, H3 = sum_lambda g(E_lambda) subset sum_lambda E'_{c lambda}. Therefore H3 is spanned by eigenvectors of F_X. Choosing a basis of each g(E_lambda) inside the corresponding eigenspace gives a spanning set of eigenvectors of F_X; hence F_X is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let sigma:K->C with sigma(K) subset R, let r be an integer, let c in K^* with sigma(c)>0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let beta:V x V->K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(y,x)=(-1)^r beta(x,y) and beta(Tx,Ty)=c beta(x,y). For N>=1 put G_N(x,y)=beta(x,T^N y)+(-1)^r c^N beta(x,T^{-N}y). If G_N is positive definite on V tensor_{K,sigma}C for every N>=1, then V tensor_{K,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y)=sigma(c)h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
Let W = V \otimes_{K,\sigma} C and write S = T \otimes \mathrm{id} \in \mathrm{GL}_\mathbb{C}(W). We prove that W carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h(Sx, Sy) = \sigma(c) h(x,y) for all x, y \in W.

Step 1 (diagonalizability and eigenvalue absolute values). We apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/40c2fd. We verify its hypotheses one by one against the hypotheses of the present lemma:
(1) K is a field of characteristic 0 — given.
(2) \sigma: K \to \mathbb{C} with \sigma(K) \subset \mathbb{R} — given (this is the added hypothesis that makes the positivity condition below well-defined).
(3) r is an integer — given.
(4) c \in K^* with \sigma(c) > 0 — given.
(5) V is a finite-dimensional K-vector space and T \in \mathrm{GL}_K(V) — given.
(6) \beta: V \times V \to K is a nondegenerate bilinear form with \beta(y,x) = (-1)^r \beta(x,y) and \beta(Tx,Ty) = c\,\beta(x,y) — given.
(7) For every N \geq 1, G_N(x,y) = \beta(x, T^N y) + (-1)^r c^N \beta(x, T^{-N} y) is positive definite on W. Since \sigma(K) \subset \mathbb{R}, this is the standard convention shared by the present lemma and by 40c2fd, namely \sigma(G_N(v,v)) > 0 for every nonzero v \in V; the two statements use the identical hypothesis, so the condition is satisfied verbatim.
All hypotheses of 40c2fd are therefore met, and its conclusion applies: S = T \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalizable over \mathbb{C}, and every eigenvalue of S has complex absolute value \sqrt{\sigma(c)}.

Step 2 (construction of the Hermitian form). Put c_0 := \sigma(c) \in \mathbb{R}. By hypothesis \sigma(c) > 0, so c_0 is a positive real number. We now apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2 with the data (K, \sigma, V, T) and the positive real number c_0. Its hypotheses are:
(a) K is a field of characteristic 0 — given.
(b) \sigma: K \to \mathbb{C} — given (no restriction on the image is required in 5d27b2).
(c) V is a finite-dimensional K-vector space and T \in \mathrm{GL}_K(V) — given.
(d) c_0 > 0 is a real number — shown above.
(e) T \otimes \mathrm{id} is diagonalizable over \mathbb{C} and every eigenvalue of T \otimes \mathrm{id} has complex absolute value \sqrt{c_0} — exactly the conclusion of Step 1, since \sqrt{c_0} = \sqrt{\sigma(c)}.
Therefore 5d27b2 applies and yields: W = V \otimes_{K,\sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h (a genuine sesquilinear form: \mathbb{C}-linear in the first variable, conjugate-\mathbb{C}-linear in the second, with h(y,x) = \overline{h(x,y)} and h(x,x) > 0 for all nonzero x) such that h((T \otimes \mathrm{id})x, (T \otimes \mathrm{id})y) = c_0\, h(x,y) for all x, y \in W. Since c_0 = \sigma(c), this is precisely h((T \otimes \mathrm{id})x, (T \otimes \mathrm{id})y) = \sigma(c)\, h(x,y) for all x, y \in W.

This is exactly the desired conclusion.

Remark on the previous attempt (addressing the verifier's points). The present proof does not use the \mathbb{C}-bilinear scalar extension of G_1 (or of \beta) as a Hermitian form: a \mathbb{C}-bilinear form on a nonzero complex vector space cannot be positive definite (g(ix,ix) = -g(x,x)), and it is not sesquilinear, so no polarization or real-valuedness argument on it is valid. The form h is not constructed from G_1 at all; it is supplied by the proved lemma 5d27b2, whose proof constructs a genuine positive definite sesquilinear Hermitian form from the diagonalizability and eigenvalue-absolute-value data. That data is supplied by the proved lemma 40c2fd, whose hypotheses are identical to those of the present lemma (including \sigma(K) \subset \mathbb{R}), so the application of 40c2fd is justified directly and no intermediate use of 45d6ea with an invalid form is made. All steps are thus supported by proved lemmas with verified matching hypotheses.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let sigma:K->C, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let F_V and F_W be K-linear automorphisms, let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with phi F_V=F_W phi, and let c in K^* with sigma(c)>0. If W tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F_W tensor id)a,(F_W tensor id)b)=c h(a,b) for all a,b in W tensor_{K,sigma} C, then F_V tensor id is diagonalizable over C with every eigenvalue having complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c)).
proof: Let C_W denote W tensor_{K,sigma} C and let C_V denote V tensor_{K,sigma} C. Since C_W is obtained from W by extension of scalars via sigma, multiplication by c in K^* on C_W is the same as multiplication by sigma(c) in C, and by hypothesis sigma(c)>0. Thus the given identity may be read as h((F_W tensor id)a,(F_W tensor id)b)=sigma(c) h(a,b) for all a,b in C_W. The argument below is also valid in the zero-dimensional case, where the conclusion is vacuous. Let Phi: C_V -> C_W be the C-linear isomorphism induced by phi. On simple tensors it is given by Phi(v tensor z)=phi(v) tensor z, and its inverse is induced by phi^{-1}. We first check that Phi intertwines the two scalar extensions of F_V and F_W. For a simple tensor v tensor z in C_V, Phi((F_V tensor id)(v tensor z)) = Phi(F_V v tensor z) = phi(F_V v) tensor z. Since phi F_V = F_W phi, this equals F_W phi(v) tensor z = (F_W tensor id)(phi(v) tensor z) = (F_W tensor id)Phi(v tensor z). By C-linearity, the same identity holds for every x in C_V: Phi((F_V tensor id)x) = (F_W tensor id)Phi(x). Now define a form h_V on C_V by h_V(x,y)=h(Phi x, Phi y). We verify that h_V is a positive definite Hermitian form. For Hermitian symmetry, h_V(y,x)=h(Phi y,Phi x)=conjugate(h(Phi x,Phi y))=conjugate(h_V(x,y)), using that h is Hermitian. For positive definiteness, if x is nonzero in C_V, then Phi x is nonzero in C_W because Phi is an isomorphism; hence h_V(x,x)=h(Phi x,Phi x)>0. If x=0, then h_V(x,x)=0. Finally, for all x,y in C_V, h_V((F_V tensor id)x,(F_V tensor id)y) = h(Phi((F_V tensor id)x), Phi((F_V tensor id)y)) = h((F_W tensor id)Phi(x), (F_W tensor id)Phi(y)) = c h(Phi(x),Phi(y)) = c h_V(x,y), where c acts on C_V through sigma, i.e. as sigma(c)>0. Therefore C_V carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_V satisfying h_V((F_V tensor id)x,(F_V tensor id)y)=c h_V(x,y) for all x,y. We may now apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea with T=F_V. Since F_V is a K-linear automorphism of V and c in K^* satisfies sigma(c)>0, the lemma gives that F_V tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of F_V tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c)). This is exactly the desired conclusion.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d. Put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and suppose F L=q^m L F and F(P^d) subset P^d. Then H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)=L H^{d-2}_et(X_k,Q_ell) ⊕ P^d as a direct sum of Q_ell[F]-submodules.
proof: Let H^s denote H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Put Q=q^m and view X as a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_Q; the algebraic closure of F_Q is the same field k, and the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius is exactly the given q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F. The divisor whose class is xi is defined over F_Q. By the hard Lefschetz hypothesis with n=d-2, the map L^2:H^{d-2}->H^{d+2} is an isomorphism. Consequently L:H^{d-2}->H^d is injective: if L(a)=0, then L^2(a)=L(L(a))=0, and injectivity of L^2 gives a=0. Now apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_decomposition_criterion with base prime power Q in place of q. Its hypotheses are satisfied: d>=2, L is injective, and L^2 is an isomorphism. Therefore H^d = P^d ⊕ L(H^{d-2}) as a direct sum of Q_ell-vector spaces. It remains to verify that the two summands are stable under F. By assumption F(P^d) is contained in P^d. For the other summand, let y be in L(H^{d-2}) and write y=L(a) with a in H^{d-2}. Then F(y)=F(L(a))=(F L)(a)=(q^m L F)(a)=q^m L(F(a)), which lies in L(H^{d-2}) because F(a) is in H^{d-2}. Hence F(L(H^{d-2})) is contained in L(H^{d-2}). Since F is a Q_ell-linear automorphism, both P^d and L(H^{d-2}) are Q_ell[F]-submodules of H^d. The vector-space direct sum is therefore a direct sum in the category of Q_ell[F]-modules: the sum map and the projection maps are F-equivariant because each summand is F-stable. Thus H^d = L(H^{d-2}) ⊕ P^d as a direct sum of Q_ell[F]-submodules.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), r>=2, d>=2r, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor, i:Y->X. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) identifying Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of Y, let L be cup product with xi, and let i_1!:H^{d-2}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1)->H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) be the usual Gysin map. Let i_{r,!}:H^{d-2r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-r)->H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) be the composition by cup product with (i^*xi)^{r-1} followed by i_1!. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. If i^*:H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-2r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism and L^r:H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) is injective, then i_{r,!} is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules from H^{d-2r}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-r) onto L^r H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof: Let V = H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_l) and W = H^{d-2r}_et(Y_k,Q_l). Write alpha for the pullback i^*:V -> W. By hypothesis alpha is an isomorphism. After the fixed identification Q_l(1)=Q_l, write W_{-r}=H^{d-2r}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-r) and let alpha_{-r}:V_{-r}->W_{-r} be the same pullback on underlying Q_l-vector spaces; it is also an isomorphism. Let c:W_{-r}->H^{d-2}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) be cup product with (i^*xi)^{r-1}, where (i^*xi)^{r-1} is viewed in H^{2r-2}_et(Y_k,Q_l(r-1)), and let g:H^{d-2}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1)->H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) be i_{1,!}. Then i_{r,!}=g c. First prove the identity i_{r,!} alpha_{-r}=L^r. For x in V_{-r}, c(alpha_{-r}x)=alpha_{-r}x cup (i^*xi)^{r-1}. By functoriality of pullback and cup product this equals i^*(x cup xi^{r-1})=i^*(L^{r-1}x), where L^{r-1} is the usual iterated cup product on X viewed under the fixed identification of Tate twists. Applying g and using the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/1f2e4b, which says g i^*=L (with i^* understood followed by the fixed identification of H^{d-2}(Y) with H^{d-2}(Y)(-1)), gives g c alpha_{-r}x=L(L^{r-1}x)=L^r x. Thus i_{r,!} alpha_{-r}=L^r, where the right hand side is the usual L^r after identifying V_{-r} with V. Now let z in W_{-r} satisfy i_{r,!}z=0. Since alpha_{-r} is onto, z=alpha_{-r}x for a unique x. Then 0=i_{r,!}z=L^r x. The hypothesis says L^r is injective, so x=0, hence z=0. Thus i_{r,!} is injective. For the image, if z in W_{-r}, write z=alpha_{-r}x. Then i_{r,!}z=L^r x, so i_{r,!}(W_{-r}) is contained in L^r V. Conversely, every element of L^r V is of the form L^r x, and by the identity it equals i_{r,!}(alpha_{-r}x). Hence i_{r,!}(W_{-r})=L^r V=L^r H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_l). Therefore i_{r,!} is a Q_l-linear isomorphism from W_{-r} onto L^r H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_l). It remains to check the Frobenius module structure. The pullback alpha_{-r} is a morphism of Q_l[F]-modules because etale cohomology is functorial and the closed immersion i commutes with the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. The map c is a morphism of Q_l[F]-modules: the cycle class xi of the F_{q^m}-rational divisor Y is fixed by F in H^2_et(X_k,Q_l(1)), so (i^*xi)^{r-1} is fixed by F in H^{2r-2}_et(Y_k,Q_l(r-1)), and cup product with an F-stable class is F-linear. The Gysin map g is a morphism of Q_l[F]-modules by functoriality of Gysin maps for smooth closed immersions. Hence i_{r,!}=g c is a morphism of Q_l[F]-modules. Since i_{r,!} is a bijective Q_l[F]-linear map onto L^r H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_l), it is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules. This also shows L^r H^{d-2r}_et(X_k,Q_l) is F-stable: if y is in that subspace, y=i_{r,!}z for some z, and F_X y=i_{r,!}(F_Y z) lies again in the subspace. This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), n>=1, Y smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension n over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) identifying Tate twists with Q_ell. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If F on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mn/2}, then H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(n-2)}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof: Let V = H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) and let T be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V. Put W = V(-1) = V tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell(-1). Since Y is smooth projective, V and W are finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces, and Frobenius is an automorphism of each. By definition of the Tate twist, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_ell(1) as multiplication by q^m, hence on Q_ell(-1) as multiplication by q^{-m}; under the fixed identification of Tate twists with Q_ell, the Frobenius F_W on W is therefore q^{-m}T. By hypothesis T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). Since q^{-m} is a nonzero scalar in Q_ell, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248 implies that q^{-m}T, i.e. F_W, is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). Now apply lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/477ab8. Its hypotheses are satisfied because every eigenvalue of T on V, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mn/2}. Hence every eigenvalue alpha of F_W on W, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{m(n-2)/2}. By the definition of Weil absolute value, an algebraic number with Weil absolute value r has complex absolute value r under every complex embedding, in particular under the chosen embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C; thus |sigma(alpha)| = q^{m(n-2)/2} for every eigenvalue alpha of F_W. Set c = q^{m(n-2)} in Q_ell^*. Then sigma(c) = q^{m(n-2)} > 0 and sqrt(sigma(c)) = q^{m(n-2)/2}. Therefore F_W is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of the finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space W, it is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue alpha of F_W satisfies |sigma(alpha)| = sqrt(sigma(c)). Lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/ccebfa now gives a positive definite Hermitian form h on W tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C such that h((F_W tensor id)x,(F_W tensor id)y) = sigma(c) h(x,y) = q^{m(n-2)} h(x,y) for all x,y in W tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Since W = H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1), this is exactly the required form.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, and let bar be the C-semilinear involution on P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C induced by complex conjugation. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d and beta|_{P^d} is nondegenerate. For N>=1 put G_N^P(x,y)=beta(x,F^N y)+(-1)^d q^{mdN} beta(x,F^{-N} y), extended C-bilinearly to P^d tensor C. If for every N>=1 and every nonzero x in P^d tensor C, G_N^P(x,bar x) != 0, then P^d tensor C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
Set V = P^d, a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, and write V_C = V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C (the tensor product taken with C regarded as a Q_ell-vector space via the restriction of sigma to Q_ell). Let F_V = F|_V, let beta_V = beta|_{V x V}, let beta_C be the C-bilinear extension of beta_V to V_C x V_C -> C, and let G_N^P_C be the C-bilinear extension of G_N^P to V_C x V_C -> C. Let bar denote the C-semilinear involution on V_C induced by complex conjugation on C, i.e. bar(sum_i v_i tensor c_i) = sum_i v_i tensor c_i^bar. Note that sigma: overline(Q_ell) -> C is a field homomorphism with sigma(1)=1, hence an injective field embedding, and its restriction sigma|_{Q_ell}: Q_ell -> C is likewise an embedding.

Trivial case. If V = 0, then V_C = 0, and the unique Hermitian form on the zero space (the zero form) is positive definite (the condition h(x,x)>0 for nonzero x is vacuous) and satisfies h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h(x,y) (vacuously, as there are no vectors). The conclusion holds, so assume V != 0.

Step 1. F_V is an automorphism of V. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) (its inverse is the corresponding power of the geometric Frobenius). By hypothesis F(V) subset V. Because F is injective, dim F(V) = dim V; since F(V) is a subspace of V of the same dimension as V, we get F(V) = V. Hence F_V: V -> V is a Q_ell-linear automorphism, and F_V^{-N} is defined for every N>=1 (so the definition of G_N^P makes sense on V).

Step 2. Scaling of beta_V. By the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7, beta(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x,y in H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). Restricting to V, we have beta_V(F_V x, F_V y) = q^{md} beta_V(x,y) for all x,y in V. (Equivalently, F_V is a q^{md}-similitude of beta_V.)

Step 3. F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). We invoke the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/359fb9. We verify its hypotheses in our situation (where d>=2 satisfies the lemma's d>=1): X is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}; xi is the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L is cup product with xi, and P^d = ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}) by construction; F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius and beta the Poincare pairing. The remaining hypotheses are: (i) F preserves V — true by Step 1; (ii) beta|_V is nondegenerate — true by the hypothesis of the present lemma; (iii) beta(Fx,Fy) = q^{md} beta(x,y) on V — true by Step 2; (iv) for every nonzero x in V there exists n>=1 with beta(x, F^n x) + (-1)^d q^{mdn} beta(x, F^{-n} x) != 0. We verify (iv) with n=1.

Let x in V, x != 0. The inclusion V -> V_C sends x to x tensor 1, which is nonzero. Applying the hypothesis of the present lemma with N=1 to the nonzero element x tensor 1 in V_C gives G_1^P_C(x tensor 1, bar(x tensor 1)) != 0. Since complex conjugation fixes 1 in C, bar(x tensor 1) = x tensor bar(1) = x tensor 1, so G_1^P_C(x tensor 1, x tensor 1) != 0. Now G_1^P_C is the C-bilinear extension of the Q_ell-bilinear form G_1^P(u,v) = beta(u, F v) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta(u, F^{-1} v) on V, so G_1^P_C(x tensor 1, x tensor 1) = sigma(G_1^P(x,x)) = sigma(beta(x, F x) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta(x, F^{-1} x)), where the last quantity lies in Q_ell. Because sigma is injective, sigma(G_1^P(x,x)) != 0 forces G_1^P(x,x) = beta(x, F x) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta(x, F^{-1} x) != 0 in Q_ell. This is exactly the required inequality with n=1. Hence condition (iv) holds.

By Miner/16d24b0281973336/359fb9, the unipotent part U of F_V in its Jordan-Chevalley decomposition (over the characteristic-0 field Q_ell) is the identity. In characteristic 0 an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is diagonalizable over an algebraic closure if and only if its unipotent part in the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition is the identity; therefore F_V is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell).

Step 4. F_C is diagonalizable over C. Let V' = V tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) and let F' = F tensor id_{overline(Q_ell)}: V' -> V'. Since F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), its base change F' is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell): choose an overline(Q_ell)-basis e_1,...,e_r of V' of eigenvectors of F' with F' e_i = alpha_i e_i for alpha_i in overline(Q_ell).

Consider the canonical change-of-base-field isomorphism of C-vector spaces
  Psi: V' tensor_{overline(Q_ell)} C -> V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C = V_C,
  Psi((w tensor a) tensor c) = w tensor (sigma(a) c),
where w in V', a in overline(Q_ell), c in C, and the right-hand side is obtained by viewing w in V tensor_{Q_ell} C and multiplying the C-coefficient by sigma(a) c. This is the standard isomorphism arising from the associativity of tensor products over fields; it is an isomorphism of C-vector spaces and requires no dimension argument. Because e_1,...,e_r form an overline(Q_ell)-basis of V', the elements e_1 tensor 1, ..., e_r tensor 1 form a C-basis of V' tensor_{overline(Q_ell)} C, and hence Psi(e_1 tensor 1), ..., Psi(e_r tensor 1) form a C-basis of V_C.

We verify that Psi intertwines F' tensor id_C and F_C = F tensor id_C. For (w tensor a) tensor c in V' tensor_{overline(Q_ell)} C:
  Psi((F' tensor id_C)((w tensor a) tensor c)) = Psi((F'(w tensor a)) tensor c) = F'(w tensor a) tensor sigma(a) c.
Since F' = F tensor id_{overline(Q_ell)}, F'(w tensor a) = F w (with F applied to the V-component of w). Thus the right side equals (F w) tensor sigma(a) c. On the other hand,
  F_C(Psi((w tensor a) tensor c)) = F_C(w tensor sigma(a) c) = (F w) tensor sigma(a) c.
So Psi (F' tensor id_C) = F_C Psi, i.e. F_C = Psi (F' tensor id_C) Psi^{-1}.

Since F' is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), its base change F' tensor id_C is diagonalizable over C (if F' = P D P^{-1} with D diagonal over overline(Q_ell), then F' tensor id_C = (P tensor 1)(D tensor 1)(P tensor 1)^{-1} with D tensor 1 diagonal over C). Therefore F_C is diagonalizable over C. Its eigenvalues are the images under sigma of the eigenvalues of F', namely sigma(alpha_1), ..., sigma(alpha_r). Concretely, for each i, F_C(Psi(e_i tensor 1)) = (F e_i) tensor 1 = e_i tensor sigma(alpha_i) = sigma(alpha_i) Psi(e_i tensor 1), so Psi(e_i tensor 1) is a nonzero eigenvector of F_C with eigenvalue sigma(alpha_i), and these form a C-basis of V_C.

Step 5. Every eigenvalue of F_C has complex absolute value q^{md/2}. Let y in V_C be a nonzero eigenvector of F_C with eigenvalue lambda in C, so F_C y = lambda y.

First, F_C commutes with bar. Indeed, F_C = F tensor id_C and bar = id_V tensor bar_C where bar_C is complex conjugation on C, and (F tensor id_C)(id_V tensor bar_C) = F tensor bar_C = (id_V tensor bar_C)(F tensor id_C). Hence for every z in V_C, F_C bar(z) = bar(F_C z). Applying this to y:
  F_C bar(y) = bar(F_C y) = bar(lambda y) = bar(lambda) bar(y),
where bar(lambda) is the complex conjugate of lambda. Similarly, since F_C^{-1} also commutes with bar and F_C^{-1} y = lambda^{-1} y,
  F_C^{-1} bar(y) = bar(F_C^{-1} y) = bar(lambda^{-1} y) = bar(lambda^{-1}) bar(y).

By the hypothesis of the present lemma with N=1 applied to the nonzero vector y in V_C, we have G_1^P_C(y, bar(y)) != 0. Using the C-bilinearity of G_1^P_C and beta_C:
  G_1^P_C(y, bar(y)) = beta_C(y, F_C bar(y)) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta_C(y, F_C^{-1} bar(y))
  = beta_C(y, bar(lambda) bar(y)) + (-1)^d q^{md} beta_C(y, bar(lambda^{-1}) bar(y))
  = bar(lambda) beta_C(y, bar(y)) + (-1)^d q^{md} bar(lambda^{-1}) beta_C(y, bar(y))
  = (bar(lambda) + (-1)^d q^{md} bar(lambda^{-1})) beta_C(y, bar(y)).
Since this product is nonzero, both factors are nonzero; in particular beta_C(y, bar(y)) != 0.

Now extend Step 2 C-bilinearly to V_C: beta_C(F_C u, F_C v) = q^{md} beta_C(u, v) for all u,v in V_C. Taking u = y and v = bar(y):
  beta_C(F_C y, F_C bar(y)) = q^{md} beta_C(y, bar(y)).
Substituting F_C y = lambda y and F_C bar(y) = bar(lambda) bar(y) and using the C-bilinearity of beta_C:
  lambda bar(lambda) beta_C(y, bar(y)) = q^{md} beta_C(y, bar(y)).
Since beta_C(y, bar(y)) != 0, we may cancel it to obtain lambda bar(lambda) = q^{md}. Because lambda bar(lambda) = |lambda|^2 (the product of a complex number with its conjugate), it follows that |lambda|^2 = q^{md}, hence |lambda| = q^{md/2}.

Since y was an arbitrary nonzero eigenvector of F_C, every eigenvalue lambda of F_C satisfies |lambda| = q^{md/2}.

Step 6. Conclusion. Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2 with: K = Q_ell (a field of characteristic 0); sigma: K -> C the restriction of the given embedding overline(Q_ell) -> C; V = P^d (a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space); T = F_V, which lies in GL_{Q_ell}(V) by Step 1; and c = q^{md}, a positive real number. By Step 4, T tensor id = F_C is diagonalizable over C; by Step 5, every eigenvalue of F_C has complex absolute value q^{md/2} = sqrt(q^{md}) = sqrt(c). Therefore, by Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2, V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C = P^d tensor C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F_C tensor id)x, (F_C tensor id)y) = c h(x,y) = q^{md} h(x,y) for all x,y in P^d tensor C.

This is exactly the desired conclusion. QED.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s(Z)=H^s_et(Z_k,Q_ell). Let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, let U be the open complement of Y in X, let j:U->X, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) identifying Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of Y, let L be cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n(X)->H^{2d-n}(X) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, put P^d=ker(L:H^d(X)->H^{d+2}(X)), let delta:H^d(U)->H^{d-1}(Y)(-1) be the Gysin boundary, let phi:P^d->ker(delta) be the restriction of j^*, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d(X), and let beta_U be the bilinear form on ker(delta) defined by beta_U(phi(x),phi(z))=beta(x,z). Then beta_U(Fa,Fb)=q^{md} beta_U(a,b) for all a,b in ker(delta).
proof:
I have everything I need. The proof rests on two proved lemmas whose hypotheses match the target exactly:

- **Miner/16d24b0281973336/60c7d1**: φ = j^*|_{P^d}: P^d → ker(δ) is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ[F]-modules.
- **Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7**: β(Fx,Fy) = q^{md}β(x,y) for all x,y ∈ H^d(X).

The conclusion follows by transporting β_U back to P^d along φ.

{
  "lemma_id": "Miner/16d24b0281973336/56b37c",
  "cited_lemmas": ["Miner/16d24b0281973336/60c7d1", "Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7"],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that beta_U(Fa,Fb)=q^{md} beta_U(a,b) for all a,b in ker(delta).\n\nStep 1 (phi is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules). The hypotheses of the target lemma are exactly the hypotheses of the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/60c7d1: q=p^a, ell!=p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X over F_{q^m}, U the open complement of Y with j:U->X, a fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1) identifying Tate twists with Q_ell, xi the cycle class of Y, L cup product with xi, L^{d-n}:H^n(X)->H^{2d-n}(X) an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, P^d=ker(L:H^d(X)->H^{d+2}(X)), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and delta:H^d(U)->H^{d-1}(Y)(-1) the Gysin boundary. Therefore, by Miner/16d24b0281973336/60c7d1, the restriction phi=j^*|_{P^d}:P^d->ker(delta) is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules.\n\nFrom this we extract three facts. (i) Bijectivity: phi is bijective, so every element of ker(delta) is uniquely of the form phi(x) with x in P^d. This is precisely what makes the bilinear form beta_U on ker(delta) well-defined: for a=phi(x), b=phi(z) in ker(delta), the value beta_U(a,b)=beta(x,z) depends only on a and b, because the preimages x and z are unique. (ii) Frobenius commutes with phi: since phi is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules, F(phi(x))=phi(F x) for every x in P^d. (iii) F preserves ker(delta): for a=phi(x) in ker(delta), F a = F(phi(x)) = phi(F x), which lies in phi(P^d)=ker(delta); hence Fa in ker(delta) for every a in ker(delta), and likewise Fb in ker(delta).\n\nStep 2 (Frobenius scaling of the Poincare pairing). By the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7 (whose hypotheses d>=1, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, beta the Poincare duality pairing on H^d(X), and F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius are all satisfied by the present data, since d>=2), we have beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x,y in H^d(X).\n\nStep 3 (conclusion). Let a,b be arbitrary elements of ker(delta). By (i) there exist unique x,z in P^d with a=phi(x) and b=phi(z). By (iii), Fa and Fb lie in ker(delta), so beta_U(Fa,Fb) is defined; by (ii), Fa=phi(Fx) and Fb=phi(Fz). Now compute, using the definition of beta_U, the commutation (ii), and the scaling of Step 2:\nbeta_U(Fa,Fb) = beta_U(phi(Fx),phi(Fz)) = beta(Fx,Fz) = q^{md} beta(x,z) = q^{md} beta(phi(x),phi(z)) = q^{md} beta_U(a,b).\nThe first equality uses Fa=phi(Fx), Fb=phi(Fz); the second is the definition of beta_U applied to the pair (phi(Fx),phi(Fz)); the third is Step 2 applied to x,z in H^d(X); the fourth rewrites beta(x,z)=beta(phi(x),phi(z)) using a=phi(x), b=phi(z) and the definition of beta_U.\n\nThus beta_U(Fa,Fb)=q^{md} beta_U(a,b) for all a,b in ker(delta), as required."
