Let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, let U be the open complement of Y in X, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) identifying Tate twists with Q_ell, let xi be the cycle class of Y, let L be cup product with xi, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, let delta:H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary, and let phi:P^d->ker(delta) be a Q_ell[F]-isomorphism. Let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose ker(delta) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_U with h_U((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h_U(x,y) for all x,y in ker(delta) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Then P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_P with h_P((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h_P(x,y) for all x,y in P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.
proof:
Setup. Let V := P^d = ker(L: H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ell)) and W := ker(delta), a subspace of H^d_et(U_k, Q_ell); both are finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces. Since phi: P^d -> ker(delta) is by hypothesis an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules, the data include Q_ell-linear endomorphisms G := F|_V of V and F_W := F|_W of W satisfying phi(Gv) = F_W(phi(v)) for every v in V, and phi: V -> W is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism with inverse phi^{-1}: W -> V. We work with these restrictions abstractly; no statement about L, cup products, the Gysin sequence, or the invertibility of G or F_W is needed. Write V_sigma := P^d tensor_{Q_ell, sigma} C and W_sigma := ker(delta) tensor_{Q_ell, sigma} C, where sigma restricted to Q_ell is the embedding under which C is a Q_ell-vector space; pure tensors v tensor t (v in V, t in C) span V_sigma. Likewise the endomorphisms G and F_W extend to C-linear maps (G tensor id) on V_sigma and (F_W tensor id) on W_sigma by (G tensor id)(v tensor t) = Gv tensor t and (F_W tensor id)(w tensor t) = F_W w tensor t; on V_sigma the notation (F tensor id) in the conclusion denotes exactly G tensor id. Fix once and for all the following convention for Hermitian forms (the one used throughout the DAG): a Hermitian form h on a C-vector space is C-conjugate-linear in the first variable, C-linear in the second, satisfies h(x,y) = conjugate(h(y,x)), and is positive definite if h(x,x) > 0 for every nonzero x. The hypothesis applies to h_U under exactly this convention: h_U is a positive definite Hermitian form on W_sigma with h_U((F_W tensor id)u, (F_W tensor id)v) = q^{md} h_U(u,v) for all u,v in W_sigma, where q^{md} is the positive real number identified with its image under sigma. Hence h_U(au, u') = conjugate(a) h_U(u, u'), h_U(u, bu') = b h_U(u, u'), h_U(u, u') = conjugate(h_U(u', u)), h_U(z, z) > 0 for z != 0, and h_U(0,0) = 0 by linearity in the second slot.

Step 1: the C-linear extension of phi. Let Phi: V_sigma -> W_sigma be the unique C-linear map with Phi(v tensor t) = phi(v) tensor t, and let Psi: W_sigma -> V_sigma be the unique C-linear map with Psi(w tensor t) = phi^{-1}(w) tensor t. On pure tensors: Psi(Phi(v tensor t)) = Psi(phi(v) tensor t) = phi^{-1}(phi(v)) tensor t = v tensor t, and Phi(Psi(w tensor t)) = Phi(phi^{-1}(w) tensor t) = phi^{-1}(w) tensor t = w tensor t... more precisely Phi(Psi(w tensor t)) = phi(phi^{-1}(w)) tensor t = w tensor t. Both Psi o Phi: V_sigma -> V_sigma and Phi o Psi: W_sigma -> W_sigma agree with the identity map on pure tensors, and both are C-linear; since pure tensors span V_sigma and W_sigma, Psi o Phi = id_{V_sigma} and Phi o Psi = id_{W_sigma}. Thus Phi is a C-linear isomorphism with inverse Psi; in particular Phi is injective, so Phi(x) = 0 implies x = 0.

Step 2: definition of h_P. Define h_P: V_sigma x V_sigma -> C by h_P(x, y) = h_U(Phi(x), Phi(y)). This is a well-defined function of two arguments: Phi is a C-linear map V_sigma -> W_sigma (already a well-defined object on the whole tensor product space), and h_U is a fixed function on W_sigma x W_sigma, so the pullback h_U o (Phi x Phi) is defined on all of V_sigma x V_sigma; no conjugation map on V_sigma is used or needed, and no separate check of compatibility with the tensor relations is required beyond the C-linearity of Phi already established in Step 1.

Step 3: sesquilinearity and Hermitian symmetry. For a, b in C and x, x', y, y' in V_sigma, using C-linearity of Phi and the corresponding properties of h_U under the fixed convention: h_P(x + x', y) = h_U(Phi(x) + Phi(x'), Phi(y)) = h_P(x, y) + h_P(x', y); h_P(x, y + y') = h_P(x, y) + h_P(x, y'); h_P(a x, y) = h_U(a Phi(x), Phi(y)) = conjugate(a) h_U(Phi(x), Phi(y)) = conjugate(a) h_P(x, y); h_P(x, b y) = h_U(Phi(x), b Phi(y)) = b h_P(x, y). Thus h_P is conjugate-linear in the first slot and linear in the second. Finally h_P(x, y) = h_U(Phi(x), Phi(y)) = conjugate(h_U(Phi(y), Phi(x))) = conjugate(h_P(y, x)), so h_P is Hermitian in particular h_P(x, x) = conjugate(h_P(x, x)) is a real number for all x.

Step 4: positive definiteness. For x in V_sigma, h_P(x, x) = h_U(Phi(x), Phi(x)). If x = 0 then h_P(x, x) = h_U(0, 0) = 0. If x != 0, then Phi(x) != 0 because Phi is injective (Step 1), so the hypothesis on h_U gives h_U(Phi(x), Phi(x)) > 0, and hence h_P(x, x) > 0. Therefore h_P is positive definite.

Step 5: the Frobenius scaling. First record the intertwining of the extended maps: for pure tensors, (F_W tensor id)(Phi(v tensor t)) = (F_W tensor id)(phi(v) tensor t) = F_W(phi(v)) tensor t = phi(Gv) tensor t = Phi(Gv tensor t) = Phi((G tensor id)(v tensor t)); both sides of the identity (F_W tensor id) o Phi = Phi o (G tensor id) are C-linear maps V_sigma -> W_sigma equal on pure tensors, which span V_sigma, so the identity holds on all of V_sigma. Now for all x, y in V_sigma, by the definition of h_P, the intertwining relation just proved, the hypothesis on h_U applied to u = Phi(x), v = Phi(y), and again the definition of h_P: h_P((F tensor id)x, (F tensor id)y) = h_P((G tensor id)x, (G tensor id)y) = h_U(Phi((G tensor id)x), Phi((G tensor id)y)) = h_U((F_W tensor id)Phi(x), (F_W tensor id)Phi(y)) = q^{md} h_U(Phi(x), Phi(y)) = q^{md} h_P(x, y). Here q^{md} is a positive integer, hence a positive real number with the same image under sigma, so the scalar in the C-valued equality is unambiguous.

Conclusion. h_P is a positive definite Hermitian form on P^d tensor_{Q_ell, sigma} C = V_sigma satisfying h_P((F tensor id)x, (F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h_P(x, y) for all x, y in V_sigma, which is exactly the asserted conclusion. Note that the whole argument uses only: that phi is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism whose C-linear extension Phi is a C-linear isomorphism, that phi intertwines the two F-restrictions, and the hypothesis on h_U; no conjugation of elements of V_sigma was ever introduced, and no properties of L, the Gysin boundary, or the ambient Frobenius were invoked.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let r be an integer, let c in K^*, let beta: V x V -> K be a bilinear form with beta(y,x) = (-1)^r beta(x,y) for all x,y in V, let T in GL_K(V) with beta(Tx,Ty) = c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V, and let N >= 1. Then the bilinear form G_N on V defined by G_N(x,y) = beta(x,T^N y) + (-1)^r c^N beta(x,T^{-N}y) is symmetric and satisfies G_N(x,x) = 2 beta(x,T^N x) for all x in V.
proof:
Let K be a field of characteristic 0, V a finite-dimensional K-vector space, r an integer, c in K^*, beta: V x V -> K a bilinear form with beta(y,x) = (-1)^r beta(x,y) for all x,y in V, T in GL_K(V) with beta(Tx,Ty) = c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V, and N >= 1. Write T^N for the N-fold composition of T and T^{-N} = (T^{-1})^N, both well-defined K-linear automorphisms of V since T is invertible. Define G_N(x,y) := beta(x,T^N y) + (-1)^r c^N beta(x,T^{-N}y). First, G_N is a bilinear form on V: fixing y, the maps x -> beta(x,T^N y) and x -> beta(x,T^{-N}y) are K-linear because T^N and T^{-N} are K-linear and beta is linear in its first argument; the same argument with the arguments swapped gives linearity in the second variable. We now prove the two claimed identities. (Remark: every step below uses only the field axioms, the graded symmetry of beta, and the similitude property, so in particular no use is made of the characteristic beyond that stated.)

Step 1 (iterating the similitude). Claim: for each integer n >= 1 and all x,y in V,
(1_n)  beta(x, T^n y) = c^n beta(T^{-n}x, y).
Proof by induction on n. Base case n = 1: since T is invertible, x = T(T^{-1}x), so applying the similitude identity beta(Tu,Tv) = c beta(u,v) to the pair (u,v) = (T^{-1}x, y) gives beta(x, Ty) = beta(T(T^{-1}x), T y) = c beta(T^{-1}x, y), which is (1_1). Inductive step: assume (1_n). Apply the similitude to the pair (u,v) = (T^{-1}x, T^n y): beta(x, T^{n+1}y) = beta(T(T^{-1}x), T(T^n y)) = c beta(T^{-1}x, T^n y). Now apply (1_n) with x replaced by T^{-1}x: beta(T^{-1}x, T^n y) = c^n beta(T^{-n} T^{-1}x, y) = c^n beta(T^{-(n+1)}x, y). Combining, beta(x, T^{n+1}y) = c^{n+1} beta(T^{-(n+1)}x, y), which is (1_{n+1}). Induction is complete, and for our fixed N we obtain
(1)  beta(x, T^N y) = c^N beta(T^{-N}x, y)  for all x,y in V.

Step 2 (inverse similitude for T^{-1}). Let u,v in V be arbitrary and write u = Tu', v = Tv' for some u',v' in V, possible because T is surjective. Then beta(u,v) = beta(Tu', Tv') = c beta(u',v'), so beta(u',v') = c^{-1} beta(u,v), where c^{-1} is the multiplicative inverse of c in K^*. In other words,
(2)  beta(T^{-1}u, T^{-1}v) = c^{-1} beta(u,v)  for all u,v in V.
Applying the argument of Step 1 with T replaced by T^{-1} (which satisfies the similitude (2) with scalar c^{-1}) yields, for every n >= 1 and all x,y in V,
(3)  beta(x, T^{-n}y) = c^{-n} beta(T^n x, y).
Specializing to n = N gives
(4)  beta(x, T^{-N}y) = c^{-N} beta(T^N x, y)  for all x,y in V.

Step 3 (symmetry of G_N). Let x,y in V. Apply the graded symmetry beta(a,b) = (-1)^r beta(b,a) to the second argument of the right-hand side of (1):
(5)  beta(x, T^N y) = c^N beta(T^{-N}x, y) = (-1)^r c^N beta(y, T^{-N}x).
Apply graded symmetry to the second argument of the right-hand side of (4):
(6)  beta(x, T^{-N}y) = c^{-N} beta(T^N x, y) = (-1)^r c^{-N} beta(y, T^N x).
Substitute (5) and (6) into the definition of G_N(x,y):
G_N(x,y) = (-1)^r c^N beta(y, T^{-N}x) + (-1)^r c^N [(-1)^r c^{-N} beta(y, T^N x)]
= (-1)^r c^N beta(y, T^{-N}x) + (-1)^{2r} (c^N c^{-N}) beta(y, T^N x).
Since (-1)^{2r} = ((-1)^2)^r = 1 in K and c^N c^{-N} = 1 (scalar multiplication is commutative and associative in K), this simplifies to
G_N(x,y) = (-1)^r c^N beta(y, T^{-N}x) + beta(y, T^N x).
On the other hand, by the definition of G_N with the roles of x and y interchanged,
G_N(y,x) = beta(y, T^N x) + (-1)^r c^N beta(y, T^{-N}x).
Addition in K is commutative, so the two displayed expressions coincide. Hence G_N(x,y) = G_N(y,x) for all x,y in V, i.e., G_N is symmetric.

Step 4 (the diagonal identity). Let x in V. From (1) with y = x:
(7a)  beta(x, T^N x) = c^N beta(T^{-N}x, x).
By graded symmetry, beta(T^{-N}x, x) = (-1)^r beta(x, T^{-N}x); substituting into (7a) gives
(7)  beta(x, T^N x) = (-1)^r c^N beta(x, T^{-N}x).
Now evaluate G_N on the diagonal:
G_N(x,x) = beta(x, T^N x) + (-1)^r c^N beta(x, T^{-N}x)
= beta(x, T^N x) + beta(x, T^N x)        (using (7) to identify the second summand)
= 2 beta(x, T^N x),
where 2 denotes 1+1 in K. (From (7) one also reads off G_N(x,x) = 2(-1)^r c^N beta(x, T^{-N}x), consistent with the stated identity.)

Both required identities, G_N(x,y) = G_N(y,x) and G_N(x,x) = 2 beta(x, T^N x) for all x,y in V, are therefore established, completing the proof. Note, as the statement's hypotheses indicate and the argument confirms, that this is a purely algebraic reduction: it proves the identities and the symmetry of G_N, and does not assert any positivity of G_N, which would require additional geometric input.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell) and fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1). Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, suppose FL=q^mLF on H^{d-2}->H^d and on H^d->H^{d+2}, and assume that for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety Z of dimension <d over F_{q^m} and every r>=0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r(Z_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) with eigenvalues of Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Let P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}). If the restriction of F to P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) with eigenvalues of Weil absolute value q^{md/2}, then F on H^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}.
proof: Fix an arbitrary embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell) to C. Put V=H^d, V_1=image(L:H^{d-2} to H^d), and V_2=P^d=ker(L:H^d to H^{d+2}). The space H^d is finite dimensional over Q_ell, and the q^m arithmetic Frobenius F on V is an automorphism, since it is the action of a Galois element; write F_i for the restriction of F to V_i. By lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/cb62f7, because hard Lefschetz holds for L and because FL=q^mLF for the maps H^{d-2} to H^d and H^d to H^{d+2}, we have V=V_1 direct sum V_2 as Q_ell[F]-modules. Hence F preserves V_1 and V_2, and each F_i is an automorphism of its summand, with the statement understood vacuously if a summand is zero. We first analyze V_1. All hypotheses of lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/9a382b are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d, hard Lefschetz holds for L, the commutation relation FL=q^mLF holds, and the assumed inductive hypothesis on every smooth projective geometrically connected Z of dimension less than d over F_{q^m} is exactly the hypothesis required in that lemma. Therefore V_1 tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_1 such that h_1((F_1 tensor id)x,(F_1 tensor id)y)=q^{md} h_1(x,y) for all x,y. If V_1 is nonzero, apply lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/503846 with K=Q_ell, Kbar=overline(Q_ell), c=q^{md}, and T=F_1. Since sigma(c)=q^{md}>0, this lemma gives that F_1 is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of F_1 satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=sqrt(q^{md})=q^{md/2}. If V_1 is zero, the same conclusion is vacuous. For V_2, the target hypothesis directly says that F_2=F|_{P^d} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}; in the convention used in the cited linear algebra lemmas, this means |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2} for the chosen embedding sigma, and the statement is vacuous if V_2=0. It remains to combine. If one of V_1 and V_2 is zero, the desired conclusion follows immediately from the corresponding part already established: if V_1=0 then V=V_2 and the target hypothesis applies to all of V; if V_2=0 then V=V_1 and the result follows from the preceding paragraph. If both summands are nonzero, apply lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/8bfe65 with K=Q_ell, V=H^d=V_1 direct sum V_2, T=F, and R=q^{md/2}. The two restrictions T|_{V_1}=F_1 and T|_{V_2}=F_2 are both diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue of either restriction satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=R. Therefore F is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue lambda of F on H^d satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2}. The embedding sigma was arbitrary, and the arguments above apply to any embedding of overline(Q_ell) into C. Hence every eigenvalue of F on H^d has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell) and fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1). Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, suppose FL=q^mLF on H^{d-2}->H^d and on H^d->H^{d+2}, and assume that for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety Z of dimension <d over F_{q^m} and every r>=0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r(Z_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) with eigenvalues of Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Then F on im(L:H^{d-2}->H^d) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}.
proof: Proof. Put V=im(L:H^{d-2}->H^d). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, applied with base field F_{q^m} (replace q by q^m) to the constant sheaf Q_l on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius, each H^r=H^r_et(X_k,Q_l) is finite-dimensional over Q_l; hence V is a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space. Next apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable to X regarded as a smooth projective variety over F_{q^m}; in that lemma replace the prime power q by q^m=p^{am}. The given very ample divisor is F_{q^m}-rational, with cycle class xi. The lemma gives F L = q^m L F on every cohomological degree, in particular for the maps H^{d-2}->H^d and H^d->H^{d+2}; the degree-specific assumptions in the target are therefore redundant for what follows. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, applied with base field F_{q^m}, the arithmetic Frobenius F is a Q_l-linear automorphism of every H^r. From F L = q^m L F on H^{d-2}->H^d we obtain F^{-1} L = q^{-m} L F^{-1}. If v=Lx belongs to V, then F v = q^m L(F x) belongs to V and F^{-1} v = q^{-m} L(F^{-1}x) belongs to V. Hence V is stable under F and F^{-1}, and T=F|_V is an element of GL(V). There exist embeddings of Qbar_l into C; let tau:Qbar_l->C be an arbitrary such embedding. The hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/9a382b do not depend on the chosen embedding except for the explicit parameter sigma. Therefore we may apply it with sigma=tau. Its assumptions are the hard Lefschetz isomorphisms for L, the full commutation F L = q^m L F, and the assumed diagonalizability and Weil absolute value q^{mr/2} on all smooth projective geometrically connected varieties Z of dimension < d over F_{q^m}; all are satisfied in the present setting. It yields a positive definite Hermitian form h_tau on V tensor_{Q_l,tau} C such that h_tau((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md} h_tau(x,y) for all x,y. Put c=q^{md} in Q_l^*. Since c is a positive rational number, tau(c)=q^{md}>0. Finally apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/503846 with K=Q_l, Kbar=Qbar_l, sigma=tau, V=V, T=T, c=c, and h=h_tau. This lemma gives that T is diagonalizable over Qbar_l and that every eigenvalue lambda of T in Qbar_l satisfies |tau(lambda)|=sqrt(tau(c))=q^{md/2}. Since tau was arbitrary, every eigenvalue of F on V has Weil absolute value q^{md/2}. In particular T is diagonalizable over Qbar_l. This proves the desired statement.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), and d>=2. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth geometrically connected divisor on X, put U=X\Y, and let delta:H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary map. Suppose delta is F-equivariant, where F is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Let t be the nonzero scalar by which F acts on Q_ell(-1), and let sigma be an embedding overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of that action satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{m(d-1)/2}. Then im(delta) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 h(x,y) for all x,y in im(delta) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.
proof:
Set K = Q_ell, W := H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k,Q_ell), V := H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) = W tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell(-1), and write F for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. On W the Frobenius is F_W; on Q_ell(-1) it is multiplication by the nonzero scalar t; hence on V the Frobenius is T := F|_V with T(w tensor s) = F_W(w) tensor (t s) = t (F_W tensor id)(w tensor s). Thus T is the nonzero scalar t times the Q_ell-linear operator (F_W tensor id) on V.

Step 1 (T diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell); spectral value; invertibility). By hypothesis F_W is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), so W tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) has a basis w_1,...,w_n with F_W(w_i)=lambda_i w_i and |sigma(lambda_i)| = q^{m(d-1)/2} for each i (the spectral hypothesis). The Tate twist Q_ell(-1) is 1-dimensional over Q_ell; fix a nonzero e in Q_ell(-1). Then {w_i tensor e : 1<=i<=n} is a basis of V tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) = (W tensor Q_ell(-1)) tensor overline(Q_ell), and T(w_i tensor e) = F_W(w_i) tensor (t e) = lambda_i w_i tensor (t e) = (lambda_i t)(w_i tensor e). Hence T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and its eigenvalues are exactly the mu_i = lambda_i t. For each i, |sigma(mu_i)| = |sigma(lambda_i t)| = |sigma(lambda_i)| |sigma(t)| = q^{m(d-1)/2} |sigma(t)|, using that sigma is an embedding (hence multiplicative) and that the complex absolute value is multiplicative. In particular every mu_i is nonzero because |sigma(mu_i)|>0, so T is invertible; equivalently T in GL_{Q_ell}(V). (Directly, T = t (F_W tensor id) with t != 0 and F_W an automorphism of W.)

Step 2 (T tensor id diagonalizable over C; eigenvalue modulus sqrt(c)). Set c := q^{m(d-1)} |sigma(t)|^2; this is a positive real because q^{m(d-1)}>0 and |sigma(t)|^2>0 (t!=0 implies sigma(t)!=0). Passing to scalars over C via sigma, we have V tensor_{Q_ell} C = (V tensor overline(Q_ell)) tensor_{overline(Q_ell)} C. The vectors w_i tensor e, now regarded in V tensor C, still form a basis and still satisfy (T tensor id)(w_i tensor e) = sigma(lambda_i t)(w_i tensor e), since the scalar lambda_i t in overline(Q_ell) maps to sigma(lambda_i t) in C under the extension-of-scalars map. Hence T tensor id is diagonalizable over C, with eigenvalues sigma(lambda_i t). Moreover |sigma(lambda_i t)| = q^{m(d-1)/2}|sigma(t)| = sqrt( q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 ) = sqrt(c), so every eigenvalue of T tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(c).

Step 3 (a positive definite Hermitian form on V tensor C). We now invoke the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2 with K = Q_ell (char 0), the embedding sigma|_{Q_ell}: Q_ell -> C (the restriction of the given embedding overline(Q_ell)->C), the finite-dimensional K-space V, the operator T in GL_{Q_ell}(V) from Step 1, and the positive real c from Step 2. Its hypotheses hold: T tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of T tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(c). Therefore V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_0 with h_0((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = c h_0(x,y) for all x,y in V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 4 (im(delta) tensor C is T-stable). Let F_U be the q^m-Frobenius on H^d_{et}(U_k,Q_ell). The hypothesis 'delta is F-equivariant' means T o delta = delta o F_U. Let z in im(delta); then z = delta(u) for some u in H^d_{et}(U_k,Q_ell), and T z = T delta(u) = delta(F_U u). Since F_U u lies in H^d_{et}(U_k,Q_ell), delta(F_U u) lies in im(delta). Hence T(im(delta)) subset im(delta). Since delta is Q_ell-linear, im(delta) is a Q_ell-subspace of V, so (im(delta)) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C is a C-subspace of V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C and, by the preceding line, it is (T tensor id)-stable.

Step 5 (restrict the form). Let h be the restriction of h_0 to the C-subspace (im(delta)) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. It is positive definite: if 0 != x in (im(delta)) tensor C, then x != 0 as a vector of V tensor C, so h(x,x)=h_0(x,x)>0. The similitude identity of Step 3 holds for all x,y in V tensor C, hence a fortiori for all x,y in (im(delta)) tensor C:
 h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = h_0((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = c h_0(x,y) = c h(x,y) = q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 h(x,y).
Because T = F|_V, the restriction of (T tensor id) to (im(delta)) tensor C is precisely (F tensor id) on (im(delta)) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Therefore h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y) = q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 h(x,y) for all x,y in im(delta) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C, which is the desired conclusion. (No numerical value of t is asserted; the similitude is written in terms of the given scalar t, and the argument is uniform in d>=2 with no special case.)

statement: Let ell be a prime, let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C be an embedding, let V be a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, let T in GL_Q_ell(V), let N>=1 and R>0. If T^N is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of T^N satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=R^N, then T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue mu of T satisfies |sigma(mu)|=R.
proof: If dim V=0, the statement is vacuous, so assume dim V>0. Let K=Qbar_ell and let W=V tensor_{Q_ell} K. Denote by barT the induced automorphism of W. It is enough to prove the assertion for barT, because diagonalizability over K and the eigenvalues of T over K are precisely the diagonalizability and eigenvalues of barT, and sigma is an embedding of K into C. The field K has characteristic 0 and is algebraically closed. First we prove that barT is diagonalizable. Since barT is invertible, its eigenvalues lambda_1,...,lambda_s in K are nonzero. Let W_j be the generalized eigenspace for lambda_j. The generalized eigenspaces form a direct sum decomposition W = W_1 direct sum ... direct sum W_s. On W_j, write barT|_{W_j} = lambda_j (I + A_j), where A_j is nilpotent. Define S|_{W_j} = lambda_j id_{W_j} and U|_{W_j} = I + A_j. Then S is diagonalizable, because it acts as a scalar on each summand W_j. The operator U is unipotent, because U-I is a direct sum of nilpotent operators and hence nilpotent. Also S and U commute, and barT = S U. Taking N-th powers gives barT^N = S^N U^N. The operator S^N is diagonalizable, because it acts as the scalar lambda_j^N on W_j. The operator U^N is unipotent, because U^N-I is a polynomial in the nilpotent operator U-I. The two operators S^N and U^N commute. We now show U^N=I. Since S^N is diagonalizable, W is the direct sum of the eigenspaces W_alpha of S^N, where alpha runs over the set {lambda_j^N}. Because S^N and U^N commute, every W_alpha is stable under U^N: if S^N v=alpha v, then S^N(U^N v)=U^N(S^N v)=alpha U^N v. The restriction of barT^N to W_alpha is alpha times U^N|_{W_alpha}. Since barT^N is diagonalizable and W_alpha is stable under barT^N, the restriction barT^N|_{W_alpha} is diagonalizable, because its minimal polynomial divides the minimal polynomial of barT^N, which is a product of distinct linear factors. Hence alpha U^N|_{W_alpha} is diagonalizable. The operator U^N|_{W_alpha} is unipotent, so all its eigenvalues are 1; therefore alpha U^N|_{W_alpha} has only the eigenvalue alpha. A diagonalizable operator with only one eigenvalue is scalar: its minimal polynomial divides the distinct linear polynomial x-alpha, so the operator equals alpha id. Thus U^N|_{W_alpha}=id_{W_alpha} for every alpha, and hence U^N=I. Since U is unipotent and U^N=I, the minimal polynomial of U is a power (x-1)^m and also divides x^N-1. In characteristic 0, x^N-1 has a simple factor x-1 because its derivative N x^(N-1) is nonzero at x=1. Hence m<=1, so the minimal polynomial of U is x-1, and U=I. Therefore barT=S is diagonalizable over K. Finally, let mu_1,...,mu_r be the eigenvalues of barT in K. Since barT is diagonalizable, we may choose a basis of eigenvectors in which barT=diag(mu_1,...,mu_r); then barT^N=diag(mu_1^N,...,mu_r^N). By hypothesis, for each i, |sigma(mu_i^N)|=R^N. Because sigma is a field embedding, sigma(mu_i^N)=sigma(mu_i)^N, so |sigma(mu_i)|^N=R^N. Since T is invertible, each mu_i is nonzero, and |sigma(mu_i)| is a positive real number. Taking the unique positive real N-th root gives |sigma(mu_i)|=R. This proves that T is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell and that every eigenvalue of T satisfies the required absolute value condition.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and let r be an integer with 0<=r<=d. Suppose that F on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Then F on H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{m(2d-r)/2}.
proof: Let L = overline(Q_l). Put V = H^r_et(X_k, Q_l) and W = H^{2d-r}_et(X_k, Q_l). Let T be the restriction of F to V and let S be the restriction of F to W. Since T is diagonalizable over L by hypothesis and every eigenvalue of T has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}, every eigenvalue of T is nonzero. A diagonalizable endomorphism all of whose eigenvalues are nonzero is invertible, so T^{-1} is defined (and the statement is vacuous if V = 0). Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_271 with the prime power q^m in place of q, so that the Frobenius in that lemma is exactly our q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Taking n = r, that lemma gives a Q_l-linear isomorphism Psi : W -> Hom_{Q_l}(V, Q_l) = V^* such that for every w in W, Psi(S w) = (q^m)^d ((T^{-1})^vee)(Psi(w)). In other words, S = Psi^{-1} o (q^{md} (T^{-1})^vee) o Psi, where the factor (q^m)^d = q^{md} is the scalar by which the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_l(-d). If dim V = 0, then V^* = 0 and the isomorphism Psi forces dim W = 0; the zero-space endomorphism is diagonalizable over L and has no eigenvalues, so we are done. Assume dim V = N > 0. Choose a basis e_1, ..., e_N of V_L = V tensor_{Q_l} L such that T e_i = lambda_i e_i for i = 1, ..., N, with lambda_i in L. The hypothesis gives |sigma(lambda_i)| = q^{mr/2} for any embedding sigma : L -> C. Let e_i^* be the dual basis of V_L^* = V^* tensor_{Q_l} L. Because T e_i = lambda_i e_i, we have T^{-1} e_i = lambda_i^{-1} e_i, and therefore ((T^{-1})^vee)(e_i^*) = e_i^* o T^{-1} = lambda_i^{-1} e_i^*. Hence the map q^{md} (T^{-1})^vee is diagonal on the basis e_1^*, ..., e_N^* of V_L^*, with eigenvalues mu_i = q^{md} / lambda_i for i = 1, ..., N. The equality S = Psi^{-1} o (q^{md} (T^{-1})^vee) o Psi remains valid after extending scalars to L, and Psi is still an isomorphism W_L -> V_L^*. For each i set v_i = Psi^{-1}(e_i^*). The vectors v_1, ..., v_N form a basis of W_L, and S v_i = mu_i v_i. Thus S is diagonalizable over L, and its eigenvalues are precisely mu_1, ..., mu_N, with the same algebraic multiplicities as lambda_1, ..., lambda_N. Finally, for each i, |sigma(mu_i)| = |sigma(q^{md})| / |sigma(lambda_i)| = q^{md} / q^{mr/2} = q^{md - mr/2} = q^{m(2d-r)/2}. Since sigma was arbitrary, this is the Weil absolute value of mu_i. Therefore F on H^{2d-r}_et(X_k, Q_l) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_l), has Weil absolute value q^{m(2d-r)/2}.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, d>=3, let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, let U be the open complement of Y in X, let k = overline(F_q), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius action, and let delta: H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary. Suppose F on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue has Weil absolute value q^{m(d-1)/2}. Then F on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) preserves im(delta), and F on im(delta) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue has Weil absolute value q^{m(d-3)/2}.
proof:
Set V = H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l). Since Y is a smooth very ample divisor in a smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of dimension d, Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d-1.

Let sigma:k->k be c->c^{q^m}. For Z equal to X, Y, or U, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on Z_k is id_Z x Spec sigma. Since sigma is an automorphism of k, Spec sigma is an isomorphism with inverse Spec(sigma^{-1}), so the induced pullback on etale cohomology is an automorphism. Denote these automorphisms by F_U on H^d_et(U_k,Q_l), F_V on V, and F_Y on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1).

Fix a nonzero element tau in Q_l(1) and use it to identify the Tate twist Q_l(-1) with Q_l. Under this identification the Gysin boundary becomes a Q_l-linear map Delta: H^d_et(U_k,Q_l) -> V. If another nonzero element tau' is chosen, Delta' = c Delta for some c in Q_l^*, so im(Delta') = im(Delta); hence the subspace whose stability is proved is independent of the choice of tau.

Let s be the scalar by which the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on Q_l(-1). We use the standard Tate-twist normalization (the one in which the cited lemmas are stated) that the scalar on Q_l(1) is q^m and hence s = q^{-m}. This standard fact is, for example, proved by applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_258 with the prime power q^m to the smooth projective geometrically connected curve P^1 over F_{q^m}; it gives the scalar q^m on the Tate twist appearing in H^2 of a curve, which is a copy of Q_l(1) in this convention. In particular s is nonzero, and under the chosen identification F_Y = s F_V = q^{-m} F_V.

Now apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/d22a5d to X, Y, U with the chosen tau. It gives F_Y Delta = Delta F_U. Since F_U is an automorphism of H^d_et(U_k,Q_l), for y = Delta(x) in im(Delta) we have F_Y(y) = Delta(F_U(x)) in im(Delta), and every element of im(Delta) is of this form because F_U is onto. Thus F_Y(im(Delta)) = im(Delta). Translating back from the chosen identification to the actual twisted space, F on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) preserves im(delta).

By hypothesis, F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l). Since q^{-m} is a nonzero scalar in Q_l, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_248 the scalar multiple F_Y = q^{-m} F_V is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l). Let W = im(Delta), viewed as a Q_l-subspace of V after the chosen identification. If W = 0, the conclusions about the restriction are vacuous. If W is nonzero, then F_Y(W) = W and F_Y|_W is an automorphism of W. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_440, the restriction F_Y|_W is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l).

It remains to determine the Weil absolute values of the eigenvalues of the restriction. Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/477ab8 with n = d-1 to Y over F_{q^m}, using the same fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1). Its hypothesis is exactly that every eigenvalue of F_V on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l) has Weil absolute value q^{m(d-1)/2}; its conclusion is that every eigenvalue of F_Y on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) has Weil absolute value q^{m(d-3)/2}. No embedding of overline(Q_l) into C is needed; the Weil absolute value is the one named in the cited lemma.

Over overline(Q_l), the diagonalizability of F_Y gives a decomposition V_bar = direct sum over mu of E_mu, where E_mu is the mu-eigenspace. Let W_bar = W tensor over Q_l overline(Q_l). Because F_Y(W_bar) = W_bar and the spectral projections onto the E_mu are polynomials in F_Y, W_bar is the direct sum of the subspaces W_bar intersect E_mu. Therefore any eigenvalue of F_Y|_W is one of the mu, i.e. an eigenvalue of F_Y on the whole space. By the preceding sentence its Weil absolute value is q^{m(d-3)/2}.

Thus F on H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) preserves im(delta), and the restriction of F to im(delta) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l) with every eigenvalue of Weil absolute value q^{m(d-3)/2}.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell), fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, suppose FL=q^mLF, and let r be an integer with 0<=r<=d. Put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r->H^{2d-r+2}). Suppose that F on H^r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Then F on P^r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.
proof: Let Q = q^m = p^{am}. Since ell != p, Q is invertible in Q_ell. View X as a smooth projective, hence proper, variety over F_Q; then k = overline(F_Q) = overline(F_q), and the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius in the statement is the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius. Write H^n for H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) and let F_n be the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n. No descent to F_q is used. First, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied with the prime power Q and with K equal to the constant sheaf Q_ell with its natural Frobenius isomorphism, each H^n is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. Second, by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a applied with the prime power Q, each F_n is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of H^n for every n; in particular F_r is in GL_{Q_ell}(H^r), and F_{2d-r+2} is injective. Let M = d-r+1. Write L_n for the degree-2 part of L in degree n, i.e. L_n:H^n->H^{n+2}. The assumption FL = Q L F means that for every n for which the maps are defined, F_{n+2} L_n = Q L_n F_n; this is the degree-wise form of the stated relation, and it is used in every intermediate degree needed below. We prove by induction on j that, as maps H^r -> H^{r+2j}, F_{r+2j} L^j = Q^j L^j F_r, and hence, because Q is invertible, L^j F_r = Q^{-j} F_{r+2j} L^j. The case j=0 is the identity. If the formula holds for j, then F_{r+2j+2} L^{j+1} = F_{r+2j+2} L_{r+2j} L^j = Q L_{r+2j} F_{r+2j} L^j = Q L_{r+2j} (Q^j L^j F_r) = Q^{j+1} L^{j+1} F_r. This is the induction step, and it uses the degree-wise commutation relation on H^{r+2j}. For j=M we obtain L^M F_r = Q^{-M} F_{r+2M} L^M, where r+2M = 2d-r+2. Since L is Q_ell-linear, L^M is Q_ell-linear, and P^r = ker(L^M: H^r -> H^{r+2M}) is a Q_ell-linear subspace of H^r. If x in P^r, then L^M x = 0, so L^M(F_r x) = Q^{-M} F_{r+2M}(L^M x) = 0; hence F_r(P^r) is contained in P^r. Conversely, if x in P^r, choose z = F_r^{-1} x in H^r. Then x = F_r z, and 0 = L^M x = L^M(F_r z) = Q^{-M} F_{r+2M}(L^M z). Since F_{r+2M} is injective, L^M z = 0, so z in P^r and x = F_r z. Therefore F_r(P^r) = P^r, and P^r is an F_r-stable Q_ell-subspace. By the finiteness just established, H^r is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. The hypothesis says that F_r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_440, applied to V = H^r, T = F_r, and W = P^r, the restriction F|_{P^r} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). Finally, let mu be an eigenvalue of F|_{P^r} in overline(Q_ell). If P^r = 0 there are no eigenvalues, so there is nothing to check. Otherwise choose a nonzero eigenvector v in P^r tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) with F v = mu v. Under the natural inclusion (which remains injective after tensoring with overline(Q_ell)), the same v is nonzero and satisfies F v = mu v, so mu is also an eigenvalue of F on H^r. By the hypothesis on H^r, every eigenvalue of F on H^r, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Therefore mu has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. This holds for every eigenvalue of F|_{P^r}, and the lemma is proved.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=3, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, let U be the open complement of Y in X, let j:U->X, fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), let xi be the cycle class of Y, let L be cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), and let delta:H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then the restriction of j^* to P^d is an F-equivariant isomorphism P^d -> ker(delta).
proof:
We prove that the restriction of j^* to P^d is an F-equivariant isomorphism P^d → ker(δ).

**Step 1: F(ξ) = q^m ξ, hence FL = q^m LF.**

The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F: X_k → X_k is a flat morphism: X is smooth over F_{q^m}, so X_k is smooth over k, and the absolute Frobenius of a smooth scheme over a field is flat (it is a local complete intersection map of relative dimension 0, equivalently, locally F is given by a flat endomorphism of regular local rings).

The cycle class map c: (effective Cartier divisors on X_k) → H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell(1)) is compatible with flat pullback: for a flat morphism f: X' → X_k and a Cartier divisor D on X_k, one has f^* c(D) = c(f^{-1}D) where f^{-1}D denotes the scheme-theoretic preimage (a standard property of the étale cycle class map,参见 e.g. the compatibility of the first Chern class with flat pullback).

Applying this to F: X_k → X_k and D = Y, we obtain
  F^* c(Y) = c(F^{-1}Y).

We now compute F^{-1}Y scheme-theoretically. On an étale open neighbourhood of a point of Y, write Y = V(s) where s is a local equation of Y in the structure sheaf O_X (possible because Y is an effective Cartier divisor, being smooth of codimension 1). The morphism F acts on functions by raising to the q^m-th power: F^*s = s^{q^m}. Therefore
  F^{-1}Y = V(F^*s) = V(s^{q^m}).
Since s is a local equation of the reduced Cartier divisor Y (i.e., s is not a zero-divisor and defines Y with multiplicity 1 at each point), the function s^{q^m} defines the same support with multiplicity q^m. Concretely, if at a generic point of Y the valuation of s is 1, then the valuation of s^{q^m} is q^m. Thus
  F^{-1}Y = q^m · Y
as effective Cartier divisors.

By additivity of the cycle class map (c(D + D') = c(D) + c(D') for effective Cartier divisors),
  c(F^{-1}Y) = c(q^m · Y) = q^m c(Y).

Combining: F^* c(Y) = q^m c(Y) in H^2_et(X_k, Q_ℓ(1)).

Under the fixed identification of Q_ℓ(1) with Q_ℓ (given by the chosen nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1)), the cycle class c(Y) corresponds to ξ ∈ H^2_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). Since Q_ℓ(1) is a constant sheaf on X_k (all ℓ-power roots of unity lie in k = ℓ̄_p), the Frobenius pullback F^* acts identically on the sheaf Q_ℓ(1) as on Q_ℓ, and the above equality translates directly to
  F^* ξ = q^m ξ  in H^2_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).

Since F^* is a ring homomorphism on the cohomology ring (it is compatible with the cup product: F^*(α ∪ β) = F^*α ∪ F^*β), for the cup-product maps L: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{n+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) defined by L(α) = ξ ∪ α, we have for all α ∈ H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ):
  F^* L(α) = F^*(ξ ∪ α) = F^*ξ ∪ F^*α = q^m (ξ ∪ F^*α) = q^m L(F^*α).
Therefore F^* L = q^m L F^*, i.e., FL = q^m LF, for both relevant maps L: H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) and L: H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).

**Step 2: ker(j^*) = L·H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).**

Consider the Gysin (long exact) sequence for the closed immersion i: Y → X with open complement U = X \ Y and j: U → X. For a divisor of codimension 1, the relevant portion is
  H^{d-2}_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1) → H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1) → H^{d+1}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ),
where the first map is the Gysin map i_!: H^{d-2}_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1) → H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ), the second map is j^*: H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ), and the third map is the Gysin boundary δ: H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1).

By exactness at H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ):
  ker(j^*) = im(i_!).

We now apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/e1f71d. Its hypotheses are verified as follows: X is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d ≥ 3 (hence d ≥ 2) over F_{q^m}; Y is a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, and since Y is a divisor defined over F_{q^m} (as X is over F_{q^m} and Y is a divisor on X), Y is F_{q^m}-rational; the Lefschetz-type hypothesis L^{d-n}: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for 0 ≤ n ≤ d is exactly the hypothesis of the target lemma; and FL = q^m LF was established in Step 1. The conclusion of e1f71d is:
  im(i_!: H^{d-2}_et(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1) → H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ)) = L · H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ),
where the right-hand side is the image of the cup-product map L: H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).

Therefore:
  ker(j^*: H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ)) = L · H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).   (∗)

**Step 3: Injectivity of j^* on P^d.**

Recall P^d = ker(L: H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ)).

Let x ∈ P^d ∩ ker(j^*). By (∗), x = L(y) for some y ∈ H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). Since x ∈ P^d, L(x) = 0, hence L^2(y) = L(L(y)) = L(x) = 0. But by the Lefschetz-type hypothesis with n = d − 2, the map
  L^2: H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ)
is an isomorphism. Therefore y = 0, and x = L(0) = 0.

Thus P^d ∩ ker(j^*) = {0}, and j^* restricted to P^d is injective.

**Step 4: Surjectivity of j^* onto ker(δ).**

Let u ∈ ker(δ) ⊂ H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ). By exactness of the Gysin sequence at H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ), there exists x ∈ H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) with j^*(x) = u.

Consider L(x) ∈ H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). By the Lefschetz-type hypothesis with n = d − 2, L^2: H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) → H^{d+2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism, so there exists a unique y ∈ H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) with L^2(y) = L(x).

Set x' = x − L(y) ∈ H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ). Then
  L(x') = L(x) − L^2(y) = L(x) − L(x) = 0,
so x' ∈ P^d.

Moreover, L(y) ∈ L · H^{d-2}_et(X_k, Q_ℓ) = ker(j^*) by (∗), so j^*(L(y)) = 0. Therefore
  j^*(x') = j^*(x) − j^*(L(y)) = j^*(x) − 0 = u.

Hence every u ∈ ker(δ) lies in j^*(P^d), and j^* is surjective onto ker(δ).

**Step 5: F-equivariance.**

We show that j^*|_{P^d}: P^d → ker(δ) commutes with the action of F.

(a) F(P^d) ⊆ P^d. Let x ∈ P^d, so L(x) = 0. From FL = q^m LF we have F(L(x)) = q^m L(F(x)). Substituting L(x) = 0: 0 = q^m L(F(x)). Since q^m ≠ 0 in Q_ℓ, L(F(x)) = 0, so F(x) ∈ P^d.

(b) F(ker(δ)) ⊆ ker(δ). The Gysin sequence is natural with respect to the morphism F: X_k → X_k (which restricts to F: U_k → U_k and F: Y_k → Y_k, since F^{-1}Y = q^m·Y has the same underlying closed subset Y, so F maps U to U and Y to Y). By the functoriality of the long exact sequence of the pair (X_k, U_k), the diagram
  H^d(U_k) → H^{d-1}(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1)
  ↓F          ↓F
  H^d(U_k) → H^{d-1}(Y_k, Q_ℓ)(-1)
commutes, i.e., δ ∘ F = F ∘ δ on H^d_et(U_k, Q_ℓ). If u ∈ ker(δ), then δ(F(u)) = F(δ(u)) = F(0) = 0, so F(u) ∈ ker(δ).

(c) j^* commutes with F. The diagram of schemes
  U_k → X_k
  ↓F     ↓F
  U_k → X_k
commutes (j ∘ F = F ∘ j since F(U_k) = U_k). By functoriality of étale cohomology pullback, the induced diagram on cohomology
  H^d(X_k) → H^d(U_k)
  ↓F          ↓F
  H^d(X_k) → H^d(U_k)
commutes, i.e., j^* ∘ F = F ∘ j^* on H^d_et(X_k, Q_ℓ).

Combining (a), (b), and (c): for x ∈ P^d,
  j^*(F(x)) = F(j^*(x)),
where F(x) ∈ P^d by (a) and j^*(x) ∈ ker(δ) by definition. Thus the square
  P^d → ker(δ)
  ↓F     ↓F
  P^d → ker(δ)
commutes, and j^*|_{P^d} is F-equivariant.

**Conclusion.**

Steps 3 and 4 establish that j^*|_{P^d}: P^d → ker(δ) is an isomorphism of Q_ℓ-vector spaces. Step 5 shows it is F-equivariant. Hence the restriction of j^* to P^d is an F-equivariant isomorphism P^d → ker(δ). ∎

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected curve on S, let U be the open complement of Y in S, let j:U->S, write H^s=H^s_et(S_k,Q_ell), fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), let L be cup product with the cycle class of Y, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, suppose L^2:H^0->H^4 and L:H^1->H^3 are isomorphisms and F L=q^m L F, put P^2=ker(L:H^2->H^4), and let delta:H^2_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) be the Gysin boundary. Then j^* restricts to an F-equivariant isomorphism P^2 -> ker(delta), where F acts on H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) and on H^2_et(U_k,Q_ell).
proof: Let i:Y -> S be the inclusion and set d=2. The fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1) gives the identifications used by the cited lemmas. First, the Lefschetz hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/470d25 are satisfied: for n=0, L^2:H^0 -> H^4 is an isomorphism by assumption; for n=1, L:H^1 -> H^3 is an isomorphism by assumption; for n=2, L^0 is the identity map H^2 -> H^2, hence an isomorphism. The scalar relation required by that lemma is F L = q^m L F, exactly the relation given in the statement; no rearrangement of F and L is used. Next, we verify the Gysin image condition. The divisor Y is smooth, very ample, and defined over F_{q^m}, so Miner/16d24b0281973336/1f2e4b applies to X=S, d=2, and Y. Let theta: H^0(Y_k,Q_l) -> H^0(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) be the chosen identification. The lemma gives i_! theta i^* = L as a map H^0(S_k,Q_l) -> H^2(S_k,Q_l). Since S and Y are geometrically connected, H^0(S_k,Q_l)=Q_l and H^0(Y_k,Q_l)=Q_l. The pullback i^* sends the constant 1 on S to the constant 1 on Y, so under the scalar identifications i^* is the identity map Q_l -> Q_l, and theta i^* is also the identity under the identification of H^0(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) with Q_l. For a in H^0(S_k,Q_l), L a = i_! theta i^* a, so L H^0(S_k,Q_l) is contained in im(i_!). Conversely, let b in H^0(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) and choose b_0 in H^0(Y_k,Q_l) such that theta(b_0)=b. Since i^* is surjective, choose a in H^0(S_k,Q_l) with i^* a = b_0. Then theta i^* a = theta(b_0)=b, so i_! b = i_! theta i^* a = L a, hence im(i_!) is contained in L H^0(S_k,Q_l). Therefore im(i_!:H^0(Y_k,Q_l)(-1) -> H^2(S_k,Q_l)) = L H^0(S_k,Q_l). Now all hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/470d25 are met with X=S, d=2, U the complement of Y, P^2=ker(L:H^2 -> H^4), and delta the Gysin boundary. The lemma yields that the restriction phi of j^* to P^2 is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules onto ker(delta). This is exactly an F-equivariant Q_l-linear isomorphism P^2 -> ker(delta), which is the desired conclusion.

statement:
Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=3, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, let

L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on etale cohomology, suppose FL=q^mLF, and put P=ker(L^2:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+3}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). Then H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is the direct sum of im(L:H^{d-3}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)) and P as a Q_ell[F]-module.
proof:
Write H^n := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) and F_n := F|_{H^n}. Set W := im(L_{d-3}: H^{d-3} -> H^{d-1}) and P := ker(L^2: H^{d-1} -> H^{d+3}), where L_{n} denotes cup product with xi as a map H^n -> H^{n+2} and L^2 := L_{d+1} o L_{d-1}. Since d >= 3, the degrees d-3 and d+3 lie in the range [0, 2d], so all spaces and maps below are defined.

Step 1 (finiteness and invertibility of Frobenius). Since X is smooth and projective over F_{q^m}, it is in particular proper over F_{q^m}. The prime power q^m = p^{am} has the same characteristic as q, and overline(F_{q^m}) = overline(F_q) = k. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the prime power q^m in the place of its q (so its "q-power arithmetic Frobenius" is exactly our q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius), X proper over F_{q^m}, k = overline(F_{q^m}), and the constant sheaf K = Q_ell on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, we obtain: for every integer n, H^n is finite-dimensional over Q_ell, and the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_n: H^n -> H^n is a Q_ell-linear automorphism. In particular F_{d-3}, F_{d-1}, F_{d+3} are automorphisms, so they are bijective and their inverses exist. We will also use throughout that q^m and q^{2m} are nonzero elements of Q_ell, since ell != p and Q_ell has characteristic 0.

Step 2 (hard Lefschetz at n = d-3). Since d >= 3, we have 0 <= d-3 <= d, so the hypothesis applies at n = d-3: L^{d-(d-3)} = L^3: H^{d-3} -> H^{2d-(d-3)} = H^{d+3} is an isomorphism. Hence L^3 is both surjective and injective.

Step 3 (sum: H^{d-1} = W + P). Let x be any element of H^{d-1}. By surjectivity of L^3 (Step 2), there exists a unique y in H^{d-3} such that L^3 y = L^2 x. Then, computing in H^{d+3},
  L^2(Ly - x) = L(L(Ly)) - L(Lx) = L^3 y - L^2 x = 0,
so Ly - x in P, and since P is a linear subspace, x - Ly in P. Also Ly in W by definition of W. Thus x = Ly + (x - Ly) is a sum of an element of W and an element of P, proving H^{d-1} = W + P as Q_ell-vector spaces.

Step 4 (trivial intersection: W cap P = {0}). Let z in W cap P, so z = Ly for some y in H^{d-3}. Then
  0 = L^2 z (since z in P) = L^2(Ly) = L^3 y,
and by injectivity of L^3 (Step 2), y = 0. Hence z = Ly = 0, so W cap P = {0}. Together with Step 3, this gives H^{d-1} = W direct sum P as Q_ell-vector spaces.

Step 5 (W is stable under F_{d-1} and F_{d-1}^{-1}). The hypothesis FL = q^m LF, applied to the map L_{d-3}: H^{d-3} -> H^{d-1}, reads
  F_{d+1?} no: F_{d-1} o L_{d-3} = q^m L_{d-3} o F_{d-3}.   (*)
Since F_{d-3} is surjective (Step 1) and q^m != 0 in Q_ell,
  F_{d-1}(W) = F_{d-1}(L_{d-3}(H^{d-3})) = q^m L_{d-3}(F_{d-3}(H^{d-3})) = q^m L_{d-3}(H^{d-3}) = q^m W = W,
where in the second equality we used (*) and in the third surjectivity of F_{d-3}. Hence F_{d-1}(W) = W, and therefore W is stable under both F_{d-1} and F_{d-1}^{-1}. For reference, the inverse action on W is explicit: for w = L_{d-3} y with y in H^{d-3} and z := F_{d-3}^{-1}(y), equation (*) gives F_{d-1}(L_{d-3} z) = q^m L_{d-3}(F_{d-3} z) = q^m w, so F_{d-1}^{-1}(w) = q^{-m} L_{d-3} z in W (note the scalar q^{-m} multiplies L_{d-3} z).

Step 6 (P is stable under F_{d-1} and F_{d-1}^{-1}). The commutation relation holds in every degree, so in particular
  F_{d+1} o L_{d-1} = q^m L_{d-1} o F_{d-1}      (degree d-1)
  F_{d+3} o L_{d+1} = q^m L_{d+1} o F_{d+1}      (degree d+1).
Iterating, in H^*(H^{d-1} -> H^{d+3}):
  F_{d+3} o L^2 = F_{d+3} o L_{d+1} o L_{d-1} = (q^m L_{d+1} o F_{d+1}) o L_{d-1} = q^m L_{d+1} o (F_{d+1} o L_{d-1}) = q^m L_{d+1} o (q^m L_{d-1} o F_{d-1}) = q^{2m} L_{d+1} o L_{d-1} o F_{d-1} = q^{2m} L^2 o F_{d-1}.
Thus we have
  (dagger)  F_{d+3} o L^2 = q^{2m} L^2 o F_{d-1}.
Forward direction: let p in P. Applying (dagger) to p gives
  0 = F_{d+3}(L^2 p) = q^{2m} L^2(F_{d-1}(p)).
Since q^{2m} != 0 in Q_ell (ell != p), it follows L^2(F_{d-1}(p)) = 0, i.e., F_{d-1}(p) in P. Hence F_{d-1}(P) is contained in P.
Backward direction: since F_{d-1} is an automorphism (Step 1), we may right-compose (dagger) with F_{d-1}^{-1} to obtain
  F_{d+3} o L^2 o F_{d-1}^{-1} = q^{2m} L^2.
For p in P, this gives
  F_{d+3}(L^2(F_{d-1}^{-1}(p))) = q^{2m} L^2(p) = q^{2m} * 0 = 0.
Since F_{d+3} is injective (Step 1), L^2(F_{d-1}^{-1}(p)) = 0, i.e., F_{d-1}^{-1}(p) in P. Hence F_{d-1}^{-1}(P) is contained in P. Therefore P is stable under both F_{d-1} and F_{d-1}^{-1}.

Step 7 (conclusion). The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_{d-1} is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of H^{d-1} (Step 1), so H^{d-1} is a module over the group algebra Q_ell[F] = Q_ell[t, t^{-1}], with t acting as F_{d-1}. Steps 3-4 show H^{d-1} = W direct sum P as Q_ell-vector spaces, and Steps 5-6 show that both W and P are stable under F_{d-1} and F_{d-1}^{-1}, i.e., W and P are sub-Q_ell[F]-modules of H^{d-1}. Consequently the direct-sum decomposition H^{d-1} = W direct sum P is a direct sum as Q_ell[F]-modules. This proves that H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) is the direct sum of im(L: H^{d-3}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell)) and P = ker(L^2: H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d+3}_et(X_k, Q_ell)) as a Q_ell[F]-module, as required.

statement: Let K be a field with embedding sigma:K->C, let c in K^*, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let b:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form with b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y). Let n>=1 and let G_n(x,y)=b(x,T^n y)+c^n b(x,T^{-n} y). If there exists a K-basis of V in which the matrix of the C-bilinear extension of G_n to V tensor_{K,sigma} C is a positive definite Hermitian matrix, then T^n+c^n T^{-n} is invertible over K.
proof:
Let d := dim_K V. If d = 0, then V = 0 and T^n + c^n T^{-n} is the unique endomorphism 0 -> 0, which is invertible; the claim holds. Assume d >= 1 from now on.

Step 1 (choice of basis and matrices). By the hypothesis, fix a K-basis (e_1,...,e_d) of V in which the matrix of the C-bilinear extension G_n^C of G_n to V_C := V tensor_{K,sigma} C (basis e_1 tensor 1, ..., e_d tensor 1) is a positive definite Hermitian matrix; denote that matrix by A_n. Let S = (s_{ij}) be the d x d K-matrix of b, s_{ij} = b(e_i, e_j), and let M = (m_{ij}) be the matrix of T in the column convention, i.e. T(e_j) = sum_i m_{ij} e_i for each j.

Step 2 (S, the inverse, and powers).
(a) S is invertible. If v = (v_1,...,v_d)^t in K^d satisfies S v = 0, then for each i, 0 = (S v)_i = sum_j s_{ij} v_j = b(e_i, sum_j v_j e_j). Put v' := sum_j v_j e_j in V. Then b(e_i, v') = 0 for all i, hence b(w, v') = 0 for every w in V, and nondegeneracy of b forces v' = 0, so v = 0. The kernel of S is trivial; S is square; hence S is invertible over K.

(b) Composition rule. Let L, R in End_K(V) have matrices P = (p_{ik}) and N = (n_{kj}) in the column convention (L(e_k) = sum_i p_{ik} e_i, R(e_j) = sum_k n_{kj} e_k). Then the matrix of L o R is P N, because
(L o R)(e_j) = L(sum_k n_{kj} e_k) = sum_k n_{kj} L(e_k) = sum_k n_{kj} sum_i p_{ik} e_i = sum_i (sum_k p_{ik} n_{kj}) e_i,
while (PN)_{ij} = sum_k p_{ik} n_{kj} by the definition of matrix product. So the (i,j)-entry of the matrix of L o R equals (PN)_{ij}.

(c) Matrix of T^{-1}. Let N be the matrix of T^{-1}. Applying (b) to L = T, R = T^{-1}: T o T^{-1} = id_V has matrix M N = I. Applying (b) to L = T^{-1}, R = T: T^{-1} o T = id_V has matrix N M = I. Thus N is a two-sided inverse of M in M_d(K); in particular M is invertible and N = M^{-1}, i.e. the matrix of T^{-1} is M^{-1}.

(d) Powers. We show by induction on n >= 1 that the matrix of T^n is M^n. The case n = 1 is the definition. If the matrix of T^n is M^n, then by (b) the matrix of T^{n+1} = T o T^n is M . M^n = M^{n+1}. Likewise, the matrix of T^{-n} = (T^{-1})^n is (M^{-1})^n = M^{-n} by the same induction applied to T^{-1}.

Step 3 (matrix of G_n over K). Let A^K = (a^K_{ij}) be the K-matrix of G_n, a^K_{ij} = G_n(e_i, e_j). First record that if R in End_K(V) has matrix N in the column convention, then b(e_i, R e_j) = sum_k n_{kj} b(e_i, e_k) = sum_k s_{ik} n_{kj} = (S N)_{ij}. Applying this with R = T^n (matrix M^n by (d)) and R = T^{-n} (matrix M^{-n} by (d)),
a^K_{ij} = G_n(e_i, e_j) = b(e_i, T^n e_j) + c^n b(e_i, T^{-n} e_j) = (S M^n)_{ij} + c^n (S M^{-n})_{ij} = (S M^n + c^n S M^{-n})_{ij}.
Hence A^K = S(M^n + c^n M^{-n}). Write Q_n := M^n + c^n M^{-n} in M_d(K), so A^K = S Q_n.

Step 4 (Q_n is the matrix of T^n + c^n T^{-n}). The matrix of a sum of endomorphisms is the sum of their matrices, and the matrix of multiplication by the scalar c^n is (c^n) I_d. Therefore the K-matrix of the endomorphism T^n + c^n T^{-n} is M^n + c^n M^{-n} = Q_n.

Step 5 (the C-bilinear extension). By the definition of scalar extension along sigma, G_n^C(e_i tensor 1, e_j tensor 1) = sigma(G_n(e_i, e_j)) and G_n^C is C-bilinear; hence the matrix of G_n^C is the entrywise image A_n = sigma(A^K). Since sigma is a ring homomorphism, entrywise application respects matrix products: for all i, j,
(sigma(S Q_n))_{ij} = sigma(sum_k s_{ik} (Q_n)_{kj}) = sum_k sigma(s_{ik}) sigma((Q_n)_{kj}) = (sigma(S) sigma(Q_n))_{ij},
where sigma(S), sigma(Q_n) denote entrywise images. Hence A_n = sigma(S) sigma(Q_n). By hypothesis A_n is a positive definite Hermitian matrix, i.e. x^* A_n x > 0 (a positive real) for every nonzero x in C^d.

Step 6 (A_n is invertible). Suppose A_n x = 0. If x != 0, then on the one hand x^* A_n x > 0 by positive definiteness, while on the other hand x^* A_n x = x^*(A_n x) = x^* 0 = 0, a contradiction. Hence x = 0: A_n has trivial kernel. A square complex matrix with trivial kernel is an isomorphism C^d -> C^d (injection on a finite-dimensional vector space), so A_n is invertible and det A_n != 0.

Step 7 (descent of the determinant). From Step 5, A_n = sigma(S) sigma(Q_n), so det A_n = det(sigma(S)) det(sigma(Q_n)). The determinant is a polynomial in the matrix entries with integer coefficients, hence commutes with entrywise application of a ring homomorphism: det(sigma(S)) = sigma(det S) and det(sigma(Q_n)) = sigma(det Q_n). Since S is invertible over K (Step 2(a)), det S in K^*, and because sigma is an embedding, sigma(det S) != 0. Therefore
sigma(det Q_n) = det(sigma(Q_n)) = det A_n / sigma(det S) != 0,
being the quotient of two nonzero complex numbers. Injectivity of sigma now gives det Q_n != 0 in K.

Step 8 (conclusion). By Step 4, Q_n is the K-matrix of the K-linear endomorphism T^n + c^n T^{-n} of V, and Step 7 gives det Q_n != 0 in K. Over a field, a square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero; thus Q_n has a two-sided inverse in M_d(K), which is the matrix of (T^n + c^n T^{-n})^{-1}. Hence T^n + c^n T^{-n} is invertible over K.

Closing remark: the argument uses only the nondegeneracy of b and T in GL_K(V); the relation b(Tx, Ty) = c b(x, y) and the symmetry of b are not needed, and no diagonalizability is asserted anywhere in the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let c be in K^*, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be in GL_K(V), and let b:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y). Then the multiset of eigenvalues of T in Kbar is invariant under lambda -> c/lambda, with equal algebraic multiplicities.
proof: Let n = dim_K V. If n = 0 there are no eigenvalues and the assertion is vacuous, so assume n >= 1. We work over the algebraic closure Kbar: extend scalars from K to Kbar. Fix a K-basis e_1,...,e_n of V. Let A be the n x n matrix representing T in this basis, and let B be the n x n matrix representing the bilinear form b, i.e. b(x,y) = x^t B y for column vectors x,y in K^n. Because b is nondegenerate, the linear map x -> (y -> b(x,y)) from V to the dual V^* is an isomorphism: its kernel is 0 by nondegeneracy, and dim V = dim V^* = n, so the map is an isomorphism. Hence the Gram matrix B is invertible: det(B) lies in K^*, and therefore B is also invertible over Kbar. Because T is in GL_K(V), det(A) lies in K^*, so A is invertible over K and over Kbar. Step 1 (matrix form of the hypothesis). For all x,y we have b(Tx,Ty) = c b(x,y). In the chosen basis, Tx is A x and Ty is A y, so the left side is (A x)^t B (A y) = x^t (A^t B A) y, and the right side is c x^t B y. Since these two linear expressions in x,y agree for every pair x,y, their coefficient matrices are equal: (1) A^t B A = c B. Step 2 (a similarity). Write A^{-t} := (A^{-1})^t. Left-multiply (1) by A^{-t}; since A^{-t} A^t = I, the left side reduces to B A, and the right side becomes c A^{-t} B; thus (2) B A = c A^{-t} B. Right-multiply (2) by B^{-1}, which is invertible over Kbar: (3) B A B^{-1} = c A^{-t}. Equation (3) says that conjugation by the invertible matrix B sends A to c A^{-t}; conjugate (similar) matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, so (4) charpoly(A) = charpoly(c A^{-t}). Step 3 (transpose invariance). For any n x n matrix M over a field, charpoly(M^t) = charpoly(M), because det(tI - M^t) = det((tI - M)^t) = det(tI - M), using that the determinant is unchanged by transposition. Apply this with M = A^{-1} (an invertible Kbar-matrix) to obtain charpoly(A^{-t}) = charpoly((A^{-1})^t) = charpoly(A^{-1}). Combining with (4): (5) charpoly(A) = charpoly(c A^{-1}). Step 4 (the eigenvalue multisets). Because A is invertible, 0 is not an eigenvalue of A. Over the algebraically closed field Kbar, write charpoly(A) = prod_{i=1}^n (t - lambda_i), where {lambda_i : i = 1..n} is the multiset of eigenvalues of A (equivalently of T) in Kbar, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Let mu run over the distinct eigenvalues of A and let V_mu be the generalized eigenspace ker((A - mu I)^{r_mu}) for a suitable positive integer r_mu, so that Kbar^n is the direct sum of the spaces V_mu and A|_{V_mu} = mu I + N_mu with N_mu nilpotent. Inverting on V_mu gives A^{-1}|_{V_mu} = (mu I + N_mu)^{-1} = mu^{-1} (I + mu^{-1} N_mu)^{-1} = mu^{-1} sum_{j=0}^{r_mu-1} (-mu^{-1})^j N_mu^j, a finite (nilpotently truncated) geometric series, which has the single eigenvalue mu^{-1} on V_mu with algebraic multiplicity dim(V_mu). Hence the multiset of eigenvalues of A^{-1} is {mu^{-1} : mu a distinct eigenvalue of A}, with each multiplicity equal to the corresponding dim(V_mu), i.e. the reciprocals of the multiset {lambda_i}. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar c scales every eigenvalue by c and preserves multiplicities, so the multiset of eigenvalues of c A^{-1} is {c/mu : mu a distinct eigenvalue of A}, i.e. {c/lambda_i : i = 1..n}; therefore charpoly(c A^{-1}) = prod_{i=1}^n (t - c/lambda_i). Step 5 (conclusion). By (5) and the two factorizations obtained in Step 4, we have in Kbar[t]: prod_{i=1}^n (t - lambda_i) = prod_{i=1}^n (t - c/lambda_i). Both sides are monic polynomials of degree n over the algebraically closed field Kbar. The multiset of roots, with algebraic multiplicity, of the left side is exactly {lambda_1,...,lambda_n}, and that of the right side is exactly {c/lambda_1,...,c/lambda_n}. By the fundamental theorem of algebra (unique factorization of polynomials over Kbar), two monic degree-n polynomials over Kbar are equal if and only if they have the same multiset of roots. Hence {lambda_1,...,lambda_n} = {c/lambda_1,...,c/lambda_n} as multisets. This is exactly the assertion that the multiset of eigenvalues of T in Kbar is invariant under the map lambda -> c/lambda, with equal algebraic multiplicities. The proof is complete.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let sigma:Kbar->C be an embedding, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be in End_K(V), and let R>0 and C0>0. If |sigma(Tr(T^n))| <= C0 R^n for every integer n>=1, then every eigenvalue lambda of T in Kbar satisfies |sigma(lambda)| <= R.
proof: Let N be the dimension of V over K. If N is 0, the set of eigenvalues is empty and the assertion is vacuous. Assume N is positive. Since Kbar is algebraically closed, every linear endomorphism of a finite-dimensional Kbar-vector space admits an upper triangular matrix: choose a one-dimensional T-stable subspace (which exists because the characteristic polynomial has a root in Kbar), and induct on the quotient. Thus, after extending scalars from K to Kbar and choosing a suitable basis, T is represented by an upper triangular matrix with diagonal entries lambda_1,...,lambda_N in Kbar, counted with algebraic multiplicity. For n>=1, the matrix of T^n is upper triangular with diagonal entries lambda_i^n, so its trace is sum_{i=1}^N lambda_i^n. The trace of an endomorphism is unchanged by extension of scalars, hence for every n>=1 the element sigma(Tr(T^n)) in C equals sum_{i=1}^N sigma(lambda_i)^n. By hypothesis, the absolute value of this complex number is at most C0 R^n. Zero eigenvalues contribute 0 for n>=1, so omit them from the following discussion. Let mu_1,...,mu_s be the distinct nonzero eigenvalues of T in Kbar, and let m_j be the positive integer algebraic multiplicity of mu_j. Then for every n>=1, a_n := sum_{j=1}^s m_j sigma(mu_j)^n satisfies |a_n| <= C0 R^n. If |sigma(mu_j)| <= R for all j, then every eigenvalue satisfies the desired inequality. Suppose not, and let M = max_j |sigma(mu_j)|. Then M > R. Let J = {j : |sigma(mu_j)| = M}, and for j in J set gamma_j = sigma(mu_j)/M. Each gamma_j has modulus 1, and the gamma_j are distinct because sigma is injective. Since R/M < 1, the hypothesis gives |a_n|/M^n <= C0 (R/M)^n, which tends to 0. Also a_n/M^n = sum_{j in J} m_j gamma_j^n + sum_{j not in J} m_j (sigma(mu_j)/M)^n. For j not in J, the modulus of sigma(mu_j)/M is strictly smaller than 1, so the second sum tends to 0 as n tends to infinity. Therefore u_n := sum_{j in J} m_j gamma_j^n tends to 0. Define u_0 := sum_{j in J} m_j; this is a positive integer. We now record an elementary claim. Claim. Let z_1,...,z_t be distinct complex numbers with |z_j| = 1, let c_1,...,c_t be complex numbers, and let v_n = sum_{j=1}^t c_j z_j^n. If v_n tends to 0 as n tends to infinity, then v_n is identically zero. Proof of the claim. Put P(z) = product_{j=1}^t (z - z_j) and write P(z) = z^t - a_1 z^{t-1} - ... - a_t. For each j, P(z_j)=0 gives z_j^t = a_1 z_j^{t-1} + ... + a_t. Multiplying by z_j^n and summing over j with weights c_j yields v_{n+t} = a_1 v_{n+t-1} + ... + a_t v_n for all n>=0. Let x_n = (v_n,...,v_{n+t-1}) in C^t. Let B be the companion matrix whose first t-1 rows are 0,1,0,...,0 and 0,0,1,...,0 up to 0,...,0,1,0, and whose last row is a_t,a_{t-1},...,a_1. Then x_{n+1} = B x_n. The characteristic polynomial of B is P, so B has the distinct eigenvalues z_1,...,z_t; hence B is diagonalizable. Choose Q with B = Q diag(z_1,...,z_t) Q^{-1} and set y = Q^{-1} x_0. Then Q^{-1} x_n = diag(z_1^n,...,z_t^n) y. Since v_n -> 0, x_n -> 0 coordinatewise, so Q^{-1} x_n -> 0. But the j-th coordinate of Q^{-1} x_n has constant modulus |y_j|, because |z_j|=1. Thus every y_j is 0, so y=0 and x_0=0. Therefore v_n=0 for all n, which proves the claim. Applying the claim to u_n, we get that u_n must be identically zero. In particular u_0 = 0, contradicting u_0 > 0. Hence the assumption M > R is impossible. Therefore |sigma(lambda)| <= R for every eigenvalue lambda of T in Kbar.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth very ample geometrically connected curve on S, write H^s=H^s_et(S_k,Q_ell), fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), let L be cup product with the cycle class of Y, let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, suppose L^2:H^0->H^4 and L:H^1->H^3 are isomorphisms and F L=q^{2m} L F, put P^2=ker(L:H^2->H^4), let beta be the Poincare pairing on H^2, and let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_Y with h_Y((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^m h_Y(x,y), then for every integer N>=1 the form (x,y)->beta(x,F^N y)+q^{2mN}beta(x,F^{-N}y) is positive definite on P^2 tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C.
proof:
Assume the stated hypotheses. Let xi be the cycle class of Y after the fixed identification Q_ell(1) = Q_ell, so that L is cup product with xi and L(1) = xi, where 1 in H^0 is the unit. We first show that the stated hypotheses are inconsistent; the assumed positive definite form on H^1_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is not even needed.

Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/27640a with X = S and d = 2. Its hard-Lefschetz hypothesis requires that for every 0 <= n <= 2 the map L^{2-n}: H^n -> H^{4-n} is an isomorphism. For n = 0 this is the given isomorphism L^2: H^0 -> H^4. For n = 1 this is the given isomorphism L: H^1 -> H^3. For n = 2 this is L^0 = id_{H^2}, which is an isomorphism. Hence the lemma applies. It concludes that the restriction of the Poincare pairing beta on H^2 to im(L: H^0 -> H^2) is nondegenerate. Since H^0 = Q_ell * 1 and L(1) = xi, the image im(L: H^0 -> H^2) is the one-dimensional Q_ell-subspace Q_ell * xi. Nondegeneracy on this one-dimensional subspace is equivalent to beta(xi, xi) != 0.

Now use the Frobenius relation FL = q^{2m} L F. Apply both sides to 1 in H^0. On the left, F L(1) = F(xi). On the right, q^{2m} L(F(1)) = q^{2m} L(1) = q^{2m} xi. Therefore

F(xi) = q^{2m} xi.

Next apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/2be0a7 with X = S and d = 2. It says that for the Poincare pairing beta on H^2, one has

beta(Fx, Fy) = q^{2m} beta(x, y)

for all x, y in H^2. Taking x = y = xi gives

beta(Fxi, Fxi) = q^{2m} beta(xi, xi).

But Fxi = q^{2m} xi, and beta is Q_ell-bilinear. Hence the left-hand side is

beta(Fxi, Fxi) = beta(q^{2m} xi, q^{2m} xi) = q^{4m} beta(xi, xi).

Combining the two expressions yields

q^{4m} beta(xi, xi) = q^{2m} beta(xi, xi),

or equivalently

(q^{4m} - q^{2m}) beta(xi, xi) = 0.

Since q = p^a is a prime power with q > 1 and m >= 1, the scalar

q^{4m} - q^{2m} = q^{2m}(q^{2m} - 1)

is nonzero in Q_ell. We already proved beta(xi, xi) != 0. This is a contradiction.

Thus the conjunction of the hypotheses of the lemma cannot hold for any such surface S, curve Y, Frobenius F, pairing beta, and embedding sigma. Therefore the implication stated in the lemma is vacuously true: under the stated hypotheses, for every integer N >= 1, the form

(x, y) -> beta(x, F^N y) + q^{2mN} beta(x, F^{-N} y)

is positive definite on P^2 tensor_{Q_ell, sigma} C.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, xi its cycle class, L cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), and let beta be the Poincare pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). Then beta(y,x)=(-1)^d beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d.
proof:
Let tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace, and write the Poincare pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) as beta(x,y)=tr_X(x cup y). The divisor Y is a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, so its cycle class xi is the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, and L is cup product with xi. Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/2e4606 with r=d. In that lemma the subspace is P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}); for r=d this is P^d=ker(L^{1})=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), exactly the P^d in the present statement. The bilinear form in the lemma is beta_d(x,y)=tr_X(x cup L^{d-d}y)=tr_X(x cup y)=beta(x,y). Therefore the cited lemma gives, for all x,y in P^d,

    beta(x,y)=(-1)^d beta(y,x).

Applying the same identity with x and y interchanged, or simply swapping the arguments, yields

    beta(y,x)=(-1)^d beta(x,y)

for all x,y in P^d. This is precisely the desired conclusion. No additional hypothesis is needed; in particular, the assumed Lefschetz isomorphisms are not used in this symmetry statement.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, Y a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^m}, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on etale cohomology, sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, and t the scalar by which F acts on Q_ell(-1). If H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_Y with h_Y((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-1)}h_Y(x,y) for all x,y, then H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
Write V := H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k, Q_ell), a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. The hypothesis says that F_V := F on V satisfies: V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_Y with h_Y((F_V tensor id)x,(F_V tensor id)y) = q^{m(d-1)} h_Y(x,y) for all x,y in V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 1 (Frobenius on the twist). By definition V(-1) = V tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell(-1), and the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F acts on V(-1) as F_{-1} := F_V tensor F_{Q_ell(-1)}, where F_{Q_ell(-1)} is multiplication by the scalar t on Q_ell(-1) (this is exactly the given meaning of t, so F_{Q_ell(-1)}(tau) = t*tau for tau in Q_ell(-1)).

Step 2 (an identification). Q_ell(-1) is a one-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, so fix a Q_ell-linear isomorphism iota : Q_ell(-1) -> Q_ell (equivalently, choose any nonzero element of Q_ell(-1) and send it to 1). Its sigma-extension iota_sigma : Q_ell(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C -> C is a C-linear isomorphism. Define a C-linear map
  Phi : V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C = (V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C) tensor (Q_ell(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C) -> V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C
by Phi((v) tensor (tau)) = v tensor iota_sigma(tau). Since iota_sigma is an isomorphism, Phi is a C-linear isomorphism.

Step 3 (the intertwining relation). For an elementary tensor (v) tensor (tau) in V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C:
  F_{-1}((v) tensor (tau)) = (F_V v) tensor (F_{Q_ell(-1)} tau) = (F_V v) tensor (t*tau).
Applying Phi, and using that F_{Q_ell(-1)} acts by the complex scalar sigma(t) on Q_ell(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C and that iota_sigma is C-linear, gives
  Phi(F_{-1}((v) tensor (tau))) = (F_V v) tensor iota_sigma(t*tau) = (F_V v) tensor (sigma(t) iota_sigma(tau)) = sigma(t) * ( (F_V v) tensor iota_sigma(tau) ) = sigma(t) * ( (F_V tensor id) Phi((v) tensor (tau)) ).
Both sides extend C-linearly in each factor, so the identity holds on the whole space: for all x in V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C,
  Phi(F_{-1} x) = sigma(t) * ( (F_V tensor id) Phi x ).   (I)

Step 4 (define the form). Define h on V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C by
  h(x, y) := h_Y(Phi x, Phi y),  for x, y in V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 5 (h is Hermitian and positive definite). Hermitian symmetry: h(y, x) = h_Y(Phi y, Phi x) = overline{h_Y(Phi x, Phi y)} = overline{h(x, y)}, where we used that h_Y is Hermitian. Positive definiteness: h(x, x) = h_Y(Phi x, Phi x) >= 0; if x != 0 then, since Phi is an isomorphism, Phi x != 0, and since h_Y is positive definite, h_Y(Phi x, Phi x) > 0, so h(x, x) > 0. Hence h is positive definite.

Step 6 (the scaling). We use the following convention-independent fact about Hermitian forms: for any Hermitian form H and any scalar c in C, H(c a, c b) = |c|^2 H(a, b). Indeed, in the linear-in-first convention this is H(ca, cb) = c * overline{c} H(a,b) = |c|^2 H(a,b), and in the linear-in-second convention it is overline{c} * c H(a,b) = |c|^2 H(a,b); both give |c|^2 H(a,b). Now compute, with c := sigma(t), a := (F_V tensor id)(Phi x), b := (F_V tensor id)(Phi y):
  h( (F_{-1} tensor id) x, (F_{-1} tensor id) y ) = h_Y( Phi(F_{-1} x), Phi(F_{-1} y) )
    = h_Y( sigma(t)(F_V tensor id)(Phi x), sigma(t)(F_V tensor id)(Phi y) )        [by (I)]
    = |sigma(t)|^2 * h_Y( (F_V tensor id)(Phi x), (F_V tensor id)(Phi y) )       [Step 6 fact]
    = |sigma(t)|^2 * q^{m(d-1)} * h_Y( Phi x, Phi y )                             [hypothesis on h_Y]
    = q^{m(d-1)} |sigma(t)|^2 * h(x, y).                                          [definition of h]
This is the desired identity for all x, y in V(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Conclusion: h is a positive definite Hermitian form on H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k, Q_ell)(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C satisfying h((F tensor id)x, (F tensor id)y) = q^{m(d-1)} |sigma(t)|^2 h(x, y). QED

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let sigma:Kbar->C be an embedding, let c be in K^* with sigma(c)>0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be in GL_K(V), let b:V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y), and let C0>0. If |sigma(Tr(T^n))| <= C0 sigma(c)^{n/2} for every integer n>=1, then every eigenvalue lambda of T in Kbar satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=sqrt(sigma(c)).
proof: First treat the case dim V=0; there are no eigenvalues, so the conclusion is vacuous. Assume dim V>0. Put R=sqrt(sigma(c)), a positive real number because sigma(c)>0. Let Lambda be the multiset of eigenvalues of T in Kbar, counted with algebraic multiplicity. Since T is invertible, every lambda in Lambda is nonzero. Over Kbar, by choosing an eigenvector and using induction, T is similar to an upper triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the elements of Lambda; consequently T^n is upper triangular with diagonal entries lambda^n, and for every n>=1, Tr(T^n)=sum_{lambda in Lambda} lambda^n.
