Applying sigma gives sigma(Tr(T^n))=sum_{lambda in Lambda} sigma(lambda)^n. Next prove the reciprocal symmetry. Let V* be the dual space and let T* be the contragredient operator, T*(f)=f o T. The map phi:V->V*, phi(x)(y)=b(x,y), is an isomorphism because b is nondegenerate. For all x,y, (T* phi T)(x)(y)=phi(Tx)(Ty)=b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y)=c phi(x)(y). Hence T* phi T=c phi, so phi^{-1} T* phi=c T^{-1}. If A is a matrix of T in some basis, the matrix of T* in the dual basis is A^t, so T and T* have the same characteristic polynomial. Therefore c T^{-1} has the same characteristic polynomial as T. From the upper triangular form of T, the eigenvalues of c T^{-1} are c/lambda for lambda in Lambda. Since the characteristic polynomial of c T^{-1} equals that of T, the multiset Lambda is invariant under lambda -> c/lambda. Now prove the following elementary claim. Claim: if r>=1, u_1,...,u_r are distinct elements of the unit circle S^1, and a_1,...,a_r are complex numbers, then sum_{j=1}^r a_j u_j^n cannot tend to 0 as n tends to infinity unless all a_j are 0. Proof of claim: set x=(u_1,...,u_r) in G=(S^1)^r. Let Orb={x^n : n in Z} and let H be the closure of Orb in G; H is a compact subgroup of G. Let P={x^n : n>=0}. We first show that every tail P_N={x^n : n>=N} is dense in H. Let Pbar be the closure of P. It is enough to show Pbar=H. If x has finite order, then P=Orb, so Pbar=Orb=H. If x has infinite order, then Pbar is compact and is closed under multiplication because P is a multiplicative semigroup. The sequence x^n has a convergent subsequence x^{n_k} -> y in Pbar with n_k strictly increasing. Put d_k=n_{k+1}-n_k. Then x^{d_k}=x^{n_{k+1}} x^{-n_k} tends to y y^{-1}=1. If some positive integer d occurred for infinitely many k, then x^d=1, contradicting infinite order; hence a subsequence d_{k_j} tends to infinity. For this subsequence, x^{d_{k_j}-1}=x^{-1} x^{d_{k_j}} tends to x^{-1}, and for large j the index d_{k_j}-1 is positive, so x^{-1} lies in Pbar. Since x lies in P, the semigroup property of Pbar gives x^{-m} in Pbar for every m>=1. Hence every integer power x^m lies in Pbar, so Orb is contained in Pbar. Because P is contained in Orb, H=closure(Orb) is contained in Pbar, while Pbar is contained in H; thus Pbar=H. Now P_N=x^N P, and left multiplication by x^N is a homeomorphism of H onto H, so the closure of P_N equals x^N Pbar=H. This proves that every tail is dense in H. Let f:G->C be f(z_1,...,z_r)=sum_j a_j z_j, a continuous map to the complex field C. If S_n=sum_j a_j u_j^n=f(x^n) tends to 0, then for any y in H and any i>=1, choose n_i>=i with x^{n_i}->y, using density of the tail P_i. Then f(y)=lim_i f(x^{n_i})=0. Thus f vanishes on H. In particular, for n=0,1,...,r-1, the equations sum_j a_j u_j^n=0 hold. The Vandermonde matrix (u_j^n) with 0<=n<r and 1<=j<=r has determinant prod_{i<j} (u_j-u_i), which is nonzero because the u_j are distinct. Hence all a_j are 0. Claim proved. Return to T. Let M=max_{lambda in Lambda} |sigma(lambda)|; the maximum exists because Lambda is finite. Suppose M>R. Group the eigenvalues with |sigma(lambda)|=M according to the distinct unit complex numbers u_j=sigma(lambda)/M. There are finitely many, say u_1,...,u_r, and let a_j be the total algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalues lambda with sigma(lambda)=M u_j; each a_j is a positive integer. Let E be the set of eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, with |sigma(lambda)|<M. If E is nonempty, put M_1=max_{lambda in E} |sigma(lambda)| and let s be the number of elements of E; if E is empty, set M_1=0 and s=0, so that the sum over E is 0. For n>=1, M^n |sum_{j=1}^r a_j u_j^n| <= |sigma(Tr(T^n))| + sum_{lambda in E} |sigma(lambda)|^n <= C0 R^n + s M_1^n. Therefore |sum_j a_j u_j^n| <= C0 (R/M)^n + s (M_1/M)^n. Since M>R and M_1<M, both R/M and M_1/M are in [0,1), so the right hand side tends to 0. By the claim, all a_j are 0, contradicting that they are positive. Hence M<=R, and every eigenvalue lambda satisfies |sigma(lambda)|<=R. Finally, let lambda be any eigenvalue of T. By the reciprocal symmetry, c/lambda is also an eigenvalue of T. Applying the upper bound to c/lambda gives |sigma(c/lambda)|=|sigma(c)|/|sigma(lambda)|=sigma(c)/|sigma(lambda)|=R^2/|sigma(lambda)| <= R. Since |sigma(lambda)|>0, this is equivalent to |sigma(lambda)|>=R. Together with |sigma(lambda)|<=R, we get |sigma(lambda)|=R=sqrt(sigma(c)). This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, U the open complement of Y in X, delta:H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) the Gysin boundary, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, and t the scalar by which F acts on Q_ell(-1). Suppose F preserves im(delta), and H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 h(x,y). Let Fbar be the induced action on the quotient H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1)/im(delta). Then that quotient tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form hbar with hbar((Fbar tensor id)u,(Fbar tensor id)v)=q^{m(d-1)}|sigma(t)|^2 hbar(u,v) for all u,v in the quotient tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C.
proof: Let V = H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) and W = im(delta). Put V_C = V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C and W_C = W tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Since Q_ell is a field, tensoring with C over (Q_ell,sigma) is exact, so V_C / W_C is canonically isomorphic to (V / W) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Let T = F tensor id on V_C. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is induced by an automorphism of k, hence its pullback on etale cohomology is an invertible Q_ell-linear map; therefore T is invertible on V_C. The hypothesis that F preserves im(delta) implies T(W_C) is contained in W_C, so W_C is a T-stable C-subspace. The scalar t is nonzero because Frobenius acts invertibly on the one-dimensional Q_ell-vector space Q_ell(-1); hence R = q^{m(d-1)} |sigma(t)|^2 is a positive real number. The given form h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V_C with h(Tv,Tw) = R h(v,w) for all v,w in V_C. Now apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/d105c4 with K = C, the identity embedding C to C, the finite-dimensional C-vector space V_C, the invertible C-linear endomorphism T, and c = R. Its hypotheses are satisfied: c is in C^* and its image under the identity embedding is positive; W_C is T-stable; and h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V_C tensor_{C,id} C = V_C satisfying the stated similitude. The lemma gives a positive definite Hermitian form hbar on (V_C / W_C) tensor_{C,id} C = V_C / W_C such that hbar((T tensor id)u,(T tensor id)v) = R hbar(u,v) for all u,v. Under the canonical identification V_C / W_C with (V / W) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C, the induced action of T on the quotient is precisely Fbar tensor id. Therefore hbar, transported by this identification, is a positive definite Hermitian form on (H^{d-1}_{et}(Y_k,Q_ell)(-1) / im(delta)) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C and satisfies hbar((Fbar tensor id)u,(Fbar tensor id)v) = q^{m(d-1)} |sigma(t)|^2 hbar(u,v) for all u,v.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d and P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y) for all x,y. Then F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of F on P^d satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2}.
proof: Put V=P^d and let T be the Q_l-linear restriction of F to V. We first record two elementary consequences of the hypotheses. Since X is smooth projective over F_{q^m}, it is proper over F_{q^m}. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, applied with the prime power q^m, the group H^d_et(X_k,Q_l) is a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space. The subspace V=ker(L) is a Q_l-subspace of H^d_et(X_k,Q_l), so V is finite-dimensional. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, applied with the prime power q^m, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is a Q_l-linear automorphism of H^d_et(X_k,Q_l). The hypothesis F(P^d) subset P^d says that V is F-stable. If T(x)=0 for some x in V, then F(x)=0 in H^d_et(X_k,Q_l); since F is invertible, x=0. Thus T is injective. Because V is finite-dimensional, T is therefore bijective, so T lies in GL_{Q_l}(V) (with the usual vacuous interpretation in the zero-dimensional case). Now set c=q^{md}. This is an element of Q_l^*, and the restriction of sigma to Q_l sends c to the positive real number q^{md}. The given h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V tensor_{Q_l,sigma} C satisfying h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y)=c h(x,y) for all x,y. By Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea, T tensor id is diagonalizable over C, and every eigenvalue mu of T tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c))=sqrt(q^{md})=q^{md/2}. Next apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_408 to the same V, T, sigma, and positive real number c. Its hypothesis holds, and it says that T tensor id is diagonalizable over C if and only if T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l). Since we have already shown that T tensor id is diagonalizable over C, it follows that T is diagonalizable over overline(Q_l). Finally, let lambda be any eigenvalue of T in overline(Q_l). Choose a nonzero eigenvector v in V tensor_{Q_l} overline(Q_l). Applying sigma coefficientwise gives a nonzero vector v_sigma in V tensor_{Q_l,sigma} C and the relation (T tensor id)(v_sigma)=sigma(lambda)(v_sigma). Hence sigma(lambda) is an eigenvalue of T tensor id. By the eigenvalue modulus conclusion above, |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2}. This proves both claimed conclusions.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=3 be odd, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell), xi the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, beta the Poincare pairing on H^d, sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C with sigma(Q_ell) subset R, and bar complex conjugation on P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d, beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d, and the restriction of beta to P^d is nondegenerate. For N>=1 let G_N be the C-bilinear extension of (x,y)->beta(x,F^N y)-q^{mdN}beta(x,F^{-N}y). If for every N>=1 the Hermitian form (x,y)->G_N(x,bar y) on P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C is positive definite, then P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y).
proof:
Let V:=P^d⊗_{σQ_ℓ}C and let bar denote complex conjugation on V. We show that the form h:V×V→C given by h(x,y)=G_1(x,bar y), where G_1 is the C-bilinear extension for N=1, is positive definite Hermitian and satisfies h((F⊗id)x,(F⊗id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y). By the N=1 case of the hypothesis this h is positive definite Hermitian, so it remains to prove the equivariance.

STEP 1 (F is an automorphism of H^d and F^{-N} is well-defined on P^d). By the cited lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is a Q_ℓ-linear automorphism of H^d_et(X_k,Q_ℓ) (its inverse being the corresponding geometric operator). Hence F^{-1} is a well-defined Q_ℓ-linear operator on H^d, and so is F^{-N} for every N≥1. Because the hypothesis gives F(P^d)⊆P^d, the restriction F|_{P^d}:P^d→P^d is injective (F is injective on H^d) and its image is a subspace of P^d of dimension dim P^d, hence F|_{P^d}=P^d is an automorphism of P^d. In particular F^N and F^{-N} map P^d onto P^d for every N≥1, so for y∈P^d the elements F^N y and F^{-N}y lie in P^d⊂H^d and the formula defining G_N is a well-defined Q_ℓ-bilinear form on P^d×P^d. (The nondegeneracy of β|_{P^d} is not needed in what follows; it is part of the hypotheses only.)

STEP 2 (F-stability of the arguments used). Let B:=β|_{P^d×P^d}. The hypothesis β(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}β(x,y) for all x,y∈P^d reads B(Fu,Fv)=q^{md}B(u,v) for all u,v∈P^d. For the computation below we need B applied to pairs whose F-images lie in P^d: if y∈P^d then Fy∈P^d (hypothesis), F^2 y∈P^d (apply F(P^d)⊆P^d again), and F(F^{-1}y)=y∈P^d. Thus every argument of B below is an element of P^d, so the scaling law is legitimately applied.

STEP 3 (Equivariance of G_1 on P^d). By definition, for x,y∈P^d, G_1(x,y)=B(x,Fy)−q^{md}B(x,F^{−1}y). Then
G_1(Fx,Fy)=B(Fx,F(Fy))−q^{md}B(Fx,F(F^{−1}y)).
Apply B(Fu,Fv)=q^{md}B(u,v) to the first term with u=x, v=Fy (both in P^d and F(Fy)∈P^d): B(Fx,F(Fy))=q^{md}B(x,Fy). Apply it to the second term with u=x, v=F^{−1}y (so F(F^{−1}y)=y∈P^d): B(Fx,F(F^{−1}y))=B(Fx,y)=q^{md}B(x,F^{−1}y). Therefore
G_1(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}B(x,Fy)−q^{md}·q^{md}B(x,F^{−1}y)=q^{md}(B(x,Fy)−q^{md}B(x,F^{−1}y))=q^{md}G_1(x,y).

STEP 4 (Extension to V). Let e_1,...,e_r be a σQ_ℓ-basis of P^d; then e_i⊗1 is a C-basis of V, and the C-bilinear extension 䧠_1 of G_1 satisfies 䧠_1(p⊗1,q⊗1)=G_1(p,q) for p,q∈P^d. The map V×V→C, (u,v)↦䧠_1((F⊗id)u,(F⊗id)v)−q^{md}䧠_1(u,v), is C-bilinear. It vanishes on the C-span of the products (e_i⊗1,e_j⊗1) because (F⊗id)(e_i⊗1)=Fe_i⊗1 with Fe_i∈P^d, so its value on (e_i⊗1,e_j⊗1) is 䧠_1(Fe_i,Fe_j)−q^{md}G_1(e_i,e_j)=G_1(Fe_i,Fe_j)−q^{md}G_1(e_i,e_j)=0 by Step 3. Hence the identity holds on all V:
䧠_1((F⊗id)u,(F⊗id)v)=q^{md}䧠_1(u,v) for all u,v∈V. (Equivalently, writing u=Σ_i a_i e_i⊗1, v=Σ_j b_j e_j⊗1 with a_i,b_j∈C, C-bilinearity gives 䧠_1((F⊗id)u,(F⊗id)v)=Σ_{i,j}a_i b_j G_1(Fe_i,Fe_j)=Σ_{i,j}a_i b_j q^{md}G_1(e_i,e_j)=q^{md}䧠_1(u,v).)

STEP 5 (Conjugation commutes with F⊗id). For p∈P^d, z∈C, 䧠(p⊗z)=p⊗z̄; this is well-defined because σ(Q_ℓ)⊂R, so for a∈Q_ℓ, 䧠((ap)⊗z)=䧠(p⊗σ(a)z)=p⊗σ(a)z̄=ap⊗z̄. Hence for u=Σ_i p_i⊗z_i∈V, 䧠((F⊗id)u)=䧠(Σ_i Fp_i⊗z_i)=Σ_i Fp_i⊗z̄_i=(F⊗id)(Σ_i p_i⊗z̄_i)=(F⊗id)䧠u. So 䧠∘(F⊗id)=(F⊗id)∘䧠 on V.

STEP 6 (Definition and properties of h). Define h(x,y):=䧠_1(x,䧠y) for x,y∈V. By the hypothesis with N=1, the map (x,y)↦G_1(x,䧠y) (here G_1 denotes that C-bilinear extension) is a positive definite Hermitian form on V; since 䧠_1|_{P^d×P^d}=G_1 and 䧠_1 is its C-bilinear extension, the displayed form is exactly 䧠_1(x,䧠y)=h(x,y). Hence h is a positive definite Hermitian form on V. (It is linear in the first variable because 䧠_1 is C-linear there, conjugate-linear in the second because y↦䧠y is conjugate-linear, and it is Hermitian-symmetric and positive definite by the hypothesis.)

STEP 7 (Equivariance of h). For x,y∈V,
h((F⊗id)x,(F⊗id)y)=䧠_1((F⊗id)x, 䧠((F⊗id)y))
=䧠_1((F⊗id)x,(F⊗id)䧠y)   [by Step 5]
=q^{md}䧠_1(x,䧠y)              [by Step 4 with u=x, v=䧠y]
=q^{md}h(x,y).

Thus V=P^d⊗_{σQ_ℓ}C carries the positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F⊗id)x,(F⊗id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y), as required. (The assumption that d is odd is consistent with the setup—Poincare duality makes β on H^d skew-symmetric—but the computation above is independent of the parity of d and goes through verbatim.)

statement:
Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2 be even, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, beta the Poincare pairing on H^d, and sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C with sigma(Q_ell) subset R. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d, beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d, and sigma(beta(x,x))>0 for every nonzero x in P^d. Then P^

d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md}h(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
Let V = P^d and H^d = H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). We build h on W := V ⊗_{Q_ell,sigma} C directly from the bilinear form beta|_{V×V}.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and a basis). The group H^d is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space (standard theorem of étale cohomology: for a smooth projective variety over a finite field, the étale cohomology groups with Q_ell coefficients, ell≠p, are finite-dimensional over Q_ell). Hence V, a Q_ell-subspace of H^d, is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space; write N = dim_{Q_ell} V (N≥0) and let e_1,...,e_N be a Q_ell-basis of V. If N=0 the assertion is vacuous (the zero space carries only the zero form, which is positive definite and the equivariance is trivial), so assume N≥1. Because sigma:Q_ell→C is a field embedding, W is a C-vector space whose C-basis is {E_i := e_i⊗1 : i=1..N} (tensoring a Q_ell-basis with the extension Q_ell⊂C via sigma yields a C-basis, since V≅Q_ell^N and Q_ell^N⊗_{Q_ell,sigma}C≅C^N).

Step 2 (symmetry of beta on V). The Poincaré pairing is beta(x,y)=tr_X(x∪y), where tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)→Q_ell is the trace (Poincaré duality) isomorphism. The étale cohomology ring H^*_{et}(X_k,Q_ell) is graded-commutative: for a∈H^r, b∈H^s, a∪b=(-1)^{rs} b∪a. Taking r=s=d (x,y∈H^d) gives x∪y=(-1)^{d^2} y∪x. Since d is even, d^2 is even and (-1)^{d^2}=1, hence x∪y=y∪x. As tr_X is Q_ell-linear, beta(x,y)=beta(y,x). In particular beta restricted to V×V is symmetric.

Step 3 (definition of h). Let B=(B_{ij})∈M_N(Q_ell) with B_{ij}=beta(e_i,e_j) be the matrix of beta|_{V×V}, and set M=(sigma(B_{ij}))∈M_N(C). Since sigma(Q_ell)⊂R, M is a real matrix; by Step 2, M_{ji}=sigma(beta(e_j,e_i))=sigma(beta(e_i,e_j))=M_{ij}, so M is real symmetric. Define h:W×W→C by: for w=Σ a_i E_i and w'=Σ b_i E_i (unique a_i,b_i∈C), set h(w,w')=Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j M_{ij}. By this formula h is C-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second.

Step 4 (h is Hermitian). h(w',w)=Σ_{i,j} b_i \bar{a}_j M_{ij}, so its complex conjugate is \bar{h(w',w)}=Σ_{i,j} \bar{b}_i a_j \bar{M_{ij}}=Σ_{i,j} a_j \bar{b}_i M_{ji} (using M_{ij}∈R so \bar{M_{ij}}=M_{ij}, then renaming indices i↔j) = Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j M_{ij}=h(w,w'), where the penultimate equality uses M_{ji}=M_{ij}. Thus h(w,w')=\bar{h(w',w)}: h is Hermitian.

Step 5 (positive definiteness). We first prove that the real symmetric matrix M is positive definite.
(5a) M is positive semidefinite. Let f:R^N→R be f(r)=r^T M r; f is a real polynomial, hence continuous. Claim: f(r)≥0 for every r∈R^N. Suppose not; pick r_0 with f(r_0)<0. By continuity there is ε>0 such that f(r)<0 on the ball B(r_0,ε); take ε<||r_0|| so 0∉B(r_0,ε). The set sigma(Q_ell)⊂R is a subfield containing Q (sigma|_Q is the identity) and Q is dense in R, hence sigma(Q_ell) is dense in R, and therefore sigma(Q_ell)^N is dense in R^N. Thus B(r_0,ε)∩sigma(Q_ell)^N≠∅; choose r_1 in this intersection. Then r_1≠0 and f(r_1)<0. Write r_1=(sigma(x_1),...,sigma(x_N)) for the unique x=(x_i)∈Q_ell^N (r_1≠0 forces x≠0 since sigma is injective); x corresponds to v=Σ x_i e_i∈V, v≠0. Then f(r_1)=Σ_{i,j} r_{1i} r_{1j} M_{ij}=Σ_{i,j} sigma(x_i) sigma(x_j) sigma(beta(e_i,e_j))=sigma(Σ_{i,j} x_i x_j beta(e_i,e_j))=sigma(beta(v,v)), which is >0 by the hypothesis sigma(beta(x,x))>0 for nonzero x∈V. This contradicts f(r_1)<0. Hence f(r)≥0 for all r∈R^N, i.e. M is positive semidefinite (all eigenvalues of the real symmetric matrix M are ≥0).
(5b) M is non-singular. Suppose M were singular. The linear system M r=0 has coefficients in the field sigma(Q_ell)⊂R; performing Gaussian elimination over that field yields a nonzero solution r_* with all coordinates in sigma(Q_ell). Write r_*=(sigma(x_1),...,sigma(x_N)) for nonzero x∈Q_ell^N, corresponding to v=Σ x_i e_i≠0. Then M r_*=0, so f(r_*)=r_*^T(M r_*)=0, whereas by the computation of (5a), f(r_*)=sigma(beta(v,v))>0. Contradiction. Hence M is non-singular.
(5c) From (5a) and (5b), M is a real symmetric matrix that is positive semidefinite and non-singular, hence positive definite. Concretely, by the real spectral theorem M=O^T D O with O real orthogonal and D=diag(λ_1,...,λ_N) real; (5a) gives λ_i≥0 and (5b) rules out λ_i=0, so λ_i>0 for all i. For any nonzero a∈C^N, a^* M a=(O a)^* D (O a)=Σ_i λ_i |(O a)_i|^2>0, since O is invertible and a≠0 implies Oa≠0.
Now take w=Σ a_i E_i∈W. If w=0 then a=0 and h(w,w)=0. If w≠0 then a≠0 and h(w,w)=Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{a}_j M_{ij}=a^* M a>0. Hence h is positive definite.

Step 6 (Frobenius equivariance). Since F(P^d)⊂P^d and F is Q_ell-linear on H^d, the restriction F|_V:V→V is Q_ell-linear. Let C=(c_{ki})∈M_N(Q_ell) be its matrix in the basis {e_i}, i.e. F(e_i)=Σ_k c_{ki} e_k. For x,y∈V with coordinate columns x,y, beta(x,y)=x^T B y and beta(Fx,Fy)=(Cx)^T B (Cy)=x^T (C^T B C) y. The hypothesis beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x,y forces C^T B C = q^{md} B (the matrices are equal because the identity holds for every x,y). Applying sigma entrywise (sigma is real-valued and sigma(q^{md})=q^{md}) gives, with C̄=(sigma(c_{ki})) a real matrix and M=sigma(B), the relation C̄^T M C̄ = q^{md} M.
Now for w=Σ a_i E_i and w'=Σ b_i E_i in W: (F⊗id)w=Σ_i a_i (F e_i)⊗1=Σ_i a_i (Σ_k c_{ki} e_k)⊗1=Σ_k (Σ_i sigma(c_{ki}) a_i) E_k, so its coordinate column is C̄ a; similarly the coordinate column of (F⊗id)w' is C̄ b. Therefore
h((F⊗id)w,(F⊗id)w')=Σ_{p,q} (C̄ a)_p \bar{(C̄ b)_q} M_{pq}=Σ_{p,q,i,j} C̄_{pi} a_i C̄_{qj} \bar{b}_j M_{pq} (since C̄_{qj}∈R, \bar{(C̄ b)_q}=Σ_j C̄_{qj} \bar{b}_j)
=Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j (Σ_{p,q} C̄_{pi} M_{pq} C̄_{qj})=Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j (C̄^T M C̄)_{ij}=Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j (q^{md} M)_{ij}=q^{md} Σ_{i,j} a_i \bar{b}_j M_{ij}=q^{md} h(w,w').
Thus h((F⊗id)w,(F⊗id)w')=q^{md} h(w,w') for all w,w'∈W=P^d⊗_{Q_ell,sigma}C, completing the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, xi its cycle class, L cup product with xi, suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=n<=d, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, and beta the Poincare pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell). Then beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d.
proof: Let H^r = H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell). We prove the stronger identity for all x,y in H^d and then restrict to P^d. Let f: X_k -> X_k be the q^m-power map whose pullback f^* is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F. First determine f^* on H^{2d}. Let z be a closed point of X_k. Since X is smooth of dimension d over the perfect field k, the completed local ring at z is a complete regular local k-algebra of dimension d; in suitable formal parameters T_1,...,T_d it is k[[T_1,...,T_d]], and the pullback of the maximal ideal under the q^m-power Frobenius is the ideal generated by T_1^{q^m},...,T_d^{q^m}. Thus the scheme-theoretic fiber over z is Spec k[[T_1,...,T_d]]/(T_1^{q^m},...,T_d^{q^m}), whose length is the number of monomials T_1^{a_1}...T_d^{a_d} with 0<=a_i<q^m, namely (q^m)^d=q^(md). The same monomial description shows that f is finite; the degree of f is the length of the fiber over a closed point, and the calculation is independent of the choice of z, so the degree is q^(md). Let Fz denote the scheme-theoretic fiber of f over z. Now H^{2d}(X_k,Q_ell) is one-dimensional: H^0(X_k,Q_ell)=Q_ell because X is geometrically connected, and Poincare duality gives H^{2d}(X_k,Q_ell) = Q_ell(-d). Let deg: H^{2d}(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d) be the canonical degree map, normalized so that the cohomology class of a closed point has degree 1. Compatibility of cycle classes with pullback gives f^*(cl(z)) = cl(Fz). The 0-cycle given by Fz has degree q^(md), so deg(cl(Fz)) = q^(md). Since cl(z) is a nonzero, hence spanning, element of the one-dimensional space H^{2d}, it follows that f^* is multiplication by q^(md) on H^{2d}. Now define the Poincare pairing by beta(x,y)=deg(x cup y), where cup is the cup product H^d x H^d -> H^{2d}; if beta is taken with values in Q_ell after a fixed identification of H^{2d} with Q_ell, the same scalar calculation holds because that identification is Q_ell-linear, and if it is taken in Q_ell(-d) then q^(md) is the natural Q_ell-scalar on that twist. By functoriality of cup product, f^*(x cup y) = f^*(x) cup f^*(y). Therefore beta(Fx,Fy) = beta(f^*x, f^*y) = deg(f^*x cup f^*y) = deg(f^*(x cup y)) = deg(q^(md)(x cup y)) = q^(md) deg(x cup y) = q^(md) beta(x,y). This identity holds for all x,y in H^d. Since P^d = ker(L:H^d -> H^{d+2}) is a Q_ell-subspace of H^d, the identity holds in particular for x,y in P^d. The Lefschetz hypotheses are not needed for this scalar identity; they only specify the subspace P^d in the surrounding argument.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2 be even, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell), xi the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L cup product with xi, P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, beta the Poincare pairing on H^d, and sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C with sigma(Q_ell) subset R. Suppose F(P^d) subset P^d, beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md}beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d, and sigma(beta(x,x))>0 for every nonzero x in P^d. Then F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of F on P^d satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2}.
proof:
We work throughout with X exactly as given: a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over the field F_{q^m}, with F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell), k=overline(F_q). Crucially, X is treated as an F_{q^m}-variety from the outset: we do not assert that X descends to F_q, we do not view X as an F_q-scheme, and we never claim that F is an iterate of a q-power Frobenius. Every lemma below is stated for varieties over F_{q^m} whose Frobenius is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, so each application is made directly to the object in the statement, with the prime power Q=q^m built in.

Step 1 (existence of a positive definite Hermitian form with similitude). We check the hypotheses of the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/119876 against the present situation. That lemma assumes: q=p^a a prime power, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2 even, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}; the notation H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell); xi the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor; L cup product with xi; P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}); F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius; beta the Poincare pairing on H^d; and an embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C with sigma(Q_ell) subset R. It further assumes: (i) F(P^d) subset P^d; (ii) beta(Fx,Fy)=q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x,y in P^d; (iii) sigma(beta(x,x))>0 for every nonzero x in P^d. In the statement of the target lemma, d is assumed to be even and >=2, X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, all the objects H^s, xi, L, P^d, F, beta are defined identically, sigma is an embedding overline(Q_ell)->C with sigma(Q_ell) subset R, and conditions (i), (ii), (iii) are exactly the three suppositions of the target. Hence every hypothesis of Miner/16d24b0281973336/119876 holds, with the same similitude constant q^{md}. By that lemma, the space P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h such that
  h((F tensor id)x, (F tensor id)y) = q^{md} h(x,y)  for all x,y in P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C,
where F tensor id means (F|_{P^d}) tensor id_C. This is well-defined because F is Q_ell-linear (it is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on etale cohomology with Q_ell coefficients) and the hypothesis F(P^d) subset P^d ensures F|_{P^d}:P^d->P^d is a Q_ell-linear map.

Step 2 (diagonalizability and Weil weights). We now check the hypotheses of the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/4ac845. That lemma assumes: q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}; the notation H^s=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell); xi the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor; L cup product with xi; P^d=ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}); F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius; an embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C; and the two assumptions (a) F(P^d) subset P^d, and (b) P^d tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{md} h(x,y) for all x,y. In our situation: d>=2 even in particular implies d>=2; X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m} exactly as required; xi, L, P^d, F are the same objects as in the statement; our sigma is an embedding overline(Q_ell)->C (its extra property sigma(Q_ell) subset R is harmless and is not even needed by this lemma); assumption (a) is the first supposition of the target; and assumption (b) is exactly the form h constructed in Step 1, with the same similitude constant q^{md}. Hence all hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/4ac845 are satisfied.

Step 3 (conclusion). By Miner/16d24b0281973336/4ac845, F on P^d is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and every eigenvalue lambda of F on P^d satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{md/2}. This is precisely the required conclusion of the target lemma.

Remark on the method: both cited lemmas are applied directly to X over the prime power field F_{q^m} with the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F. No descent of X to F_q is invoked or needed, no claim is made that F is the m-th iterate of a q-power Frobenius, and the positivity of the Hermitian form is imported from Miner/16d24b0281973336/119876 rather than re-derived, so the entire argument is valid for an arbitrary F_{q^m}-variety X.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell!=p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, L cup product with the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, suppose L^{d-r}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=r<=d, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, FL=q^mLF, P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If each P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_r with h_r((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{mr}h_r(x,y), then for every n>=0, H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h_n with h_n((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{mn}h_n(x,y).
proof: Let H^n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) and V_n = H^n tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Write F_n for F tensor 1 on V_n. Denote the given positive definite Hermitian forms on P^r tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C by G_r for r=0,...,d; thus G_r(F_r u, F_r v)=q^{mr}G_r(u,v). By the usual cohomological dimension bound for a smooth projective variety of dimension d, H^n=0 for n>2d; in particular H^{2d+1}=H^{2d+2}=0. Therefore P^0=ker(L^{d+1}:H^0->H^{2d+2}=0)=H^0 and P^1=ker(L^d:H^1->H^{2d+1}=0)=H^1. Set h_0=G_0 and h_1=G_1; these are positive definite on V_0 and V_1 and satisfy h_i(F_i x, F_i y)=q^{mi}h_i(x,y). From FL=q^mLF, by induction on k we have F L^k = q^{mk}L^kF for every k>=0. The induction step is F L^{k+1}= (F L^k)L=q^{mk}L^k(F L)=q^{mk}L^k(q^m L F)=q^{m(k+1)}L^{k+1}F. Also sigma(q^m)=q^m is a positive real number, so if C is a positive rational scalar and H is Hermitian, then H(Cx,Cy)=C^2H(x,y). We first construct h_n for 2<=n<=d by induction on n. Suppose h_{n-2} has been constructed and satisfies the weight condition. Let A_n be the image of L:H^{n-2}->H^n. Since n-2<=d, the map L^{d-(n-2)}=L^{d-n+2}:H^{n-2}->H^{2d-n+2} is an isomorphism by the hypothesis. For x in H^n, L^{d-n+1}x lies in H^{2d-n+2}; choose the unique y in H^{n-2} with L^{d-n+2}y=L^{d-n+1}x. Then p=x-Ly satisfies L^{d-n+1}p=L^{d-n+1}x-L^{d-n+2}y=0, so p in P^n and x=Ly+p. If z lies in A_n intersection P^n, write z=Ly; because z in P^n, 0=L^{d-n+1}z=L^{d-n+2}y, and the injectivity of L^{d-n+2} gives y=0, hence z=0. Thus H^n=A_n direct sum P^n. Tensoring this direct sum with C gives V_n=A_n_C direct sum P^n_C, where A_n_C is the image of L tensor 1. The subspace A_n is F-stable because F(Ly)=q^mL(Fy). The subspace P^n is F-stable because if L^{d-n+1}p=0, then 0=F(L^{d-n+1}p)=q^{m(d-n+1)}L^{d-n+1}(Fp); since q^{m(d-n+1)} is invertible in Q_ell, L^{d-n+1}(Fp)=0. Define an isomorphism i_n:V_{n-2}->A_n_C by i_n(u)=(L tensor 1)u. Define h_n_L on A_n_C by h_n_L(i_n(u),i_n(v))=h_{n-2}(u,v). Well-definedness follows from injectivity of i_n; it is C-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second because i_n is C-linear and h_{n-2} is Hermitian, and it is positive definite because i_n is an isomorphism and h_{n-2} is positive definite. For u,v in V_{n-2}, (F_n)i_n(u)=(FL tensor 1)u=q^m(LF tensor 1)u=q^m i_n(F_{n-2}u); hence h_n_L(F_n i_n(u),F_n i_n(v))=h_{n-2}(q^mF_{n-2}u,q^mF_{n-2}v)=q^{2m}h_{n-2}(F_{n-2}u,F_{n-2}v)=q^{2m}q^{m(n-2)}h_{n-2}(u,v)=q^{mn}h_n_L(i_n(u),i_n(v)). Now define h_n on V_n by h_n(a+p,b+p')=h_n_L(a,b)+G_n(p,p'), where a,b in A_n_C and p,p' in P^n_C. This is a positive definite Hermitian form: if a+p is nonzero, then a or p is nonzero, and h_n(a+p,a+p) is a sum of two nonnegative terms with at least one positive. For the weight, F preserves the two summands, so if x=a+p and y=b+p' then F_n x=F_n a + F_n p with F_n a in A_n_C and F_n p in P^n_C; therefore h_n(F_n x,F_n y)=h_n_L(F_n a,F_n b)+G_n(F_n p,F_n p')=q^{mn}h_n_L(a,b)+q^{mn}G_n(p,p')=q^{mn}h_n(x,y). This gives the desired form for every 0<=n<=d. Now let d<n<=2d and put s=2d-n, so 0<=s<d. By the hypothesis with r=s, T=L^{n-d}=L^{d-s}:H^s->H^{2d-s}=H^n is an isomorphism. The form h_s on V_s has already been constructed and has weight q^{ms}. Let J:V_s->V_n be J(u)=(T tensor 1)u. Define h_n(Ju,Jv)=h_s(u,v) for u,v in V_s. Since J is a C-linear isomorphism and h_s is positive definite Hermitian, h_n is a positive definite Hermitian form on V_n. For weight, (F_n)J=q^{m(n-d)}J(F_s), so h_n(F_n Ju,F_n Jv)=h_s(q^{m(n-d)}F_s u,q^{m(n-d)}F_s v)=q^{2m(n-d)}h_s(F_s u,F_s v)=q^{2m(n-d)}q^{ms}h_s(u,v)=q^{mn}h_n(Ju,Jv). Finally, if n>2d, then H^n=0 by the same vanishing, so V_n=0; the unique Hermitian form h_n=0 is positive definite vacuously and the weight identity has no nontrivial cases. This completes the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell!=p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, and 0<=r<=2d. If H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{mr}h(x,y), then H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h' with h'((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(2d-r)}h'(x,y).
proof:
We work over K=Q_ell. Set W=H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) and W'=H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell), both finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, and let T (resp. T') denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on W (resp. W'). Arithmetic Frobenius is an automorphism of X_k, hence T in GL_K(W) and T' in GL_K(W') are invertible. By Poincare duality the two groups have equal dimension; write dim_K W=dim_K W'=n. If W=0 then the pairing used below is perfect, forcing W'=0, and the conclusion is vacuous; hence assume W!=0.

STEP 1 (spectral data on H^r from the hypothesis). Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/45d6ea with K, V=W, T, and c=q^{mr} in K^*. We have sigma(c)=sigma(q^{mr})=q^{mr}>0 because q^{mr} lies in Q and sigma restricts to the identity on Q, and the hypothesis on h is exactly the hypothesis of that lemma. Its conclusion gives: (i) T tensor id is diagonalizable over C; and (ii) every eigenvalue of T tensor id (an element of C) has complex absolute value sqrt(sigma(c))=q^{mr/2}. In particular the minimal polynomial m_T of T over K is a product of distinct linear factors over C, and the multiset of eigenvalues of T over C is {sigma(lambda)} (lambda ranging over the algebraic eigenvalues of T) with |sigma(lambda)|=q^{mr/2} for each.

STEP 2 (the Frobenius-balanced perfect pairing). By part (b) of the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 (applied to Y=X, dimension d, with n=r), the pairing beta:W x W' -> Q_ell(-d), (x,y)|->tr(x cup y), is a PERFECT K-bilinear pairing and satisfies beta(Tx,T'y)=q^{md} beta(x,y) for all x in W, y in W'. Since Q_ell(-d) is a one-dimensional K-vector space, choose a nonzero vector zeta in Q_ell(-d) and write beta(x,y)=b(x,y) zeta with b(x,y) in K. Then b:W x W' -> K is a perfect K-bilinear form and, because the scalar q^{md} acts by multiplication on Q_ell(-d), we have b(Tx,T'y)=q^{md} b(x,y) for all x,y. Set c:=q^{md} in K^* (a positive rational). Perfectness means the induced maps W -> W'^* and W' -> W^* are K-isomorphisms.

STEP 3 (linear-algebraic bridge: spectrum of T' from spectrum of T). Choose K-bases of W and of W'. Let A in GL_n(K) be the matrix of T, B in GL_n(K) the matrix of T', and C in GL_n(K) the matrix of the form b (perfectness is exactly invertibility of C; note dim W=dim W'=n). Writing column vectors x,y for elements of W, W', the relation b(Tx,T'y)=c b(x,y) reads (Ax)^T C (By)=c x^T C y for all x,y, i.e. A^T C B=c C. Conjugating: A^T C B=c C, multiply on the left by A^{-T} and on the right by C^{-1} to get C B C^{-1}=c A^{-T}; hence B is K-similar to c A^{-T}, i.e. B=c C^{-1}(A^{-T}) C. Two facts now finish the step. (a) A matrix and its transpose have the same characteristic and the same minimal polynomial, so A^{-T} has eigenvalue mu iff A^{-1} does, i.e. mu=1/lambda where lambda runs over the eigenvalues of A; and A^{-T} is diagonalizable over any field over which A is diagonalizable (equivalently, the squarefreeness of the minimal polynomial is unchanged by transpose and by inversion). (b) Similarity preserves the multiset of eigenvalues and diagonalizability over any field. Therefore, over C (where, by Step 1, T tensor id is diagonalizable with eigenvalues of modulus q^{mr/2}), the operator T' tensor id is diagonalizable over C and its eigenvalues are exactly c/lambda for lambda ranging over the eigenvalues of T, with |c/lambda|=|c|/|lambda|=q^{md}/q^{mr/2}=q^{m(2d-r)/2}=sqrt(q^{m(2d-r)}). (The computation is over C via the embedding sigma; since c=q^{md} is a positive rational, sigma(c)=c.) Thus: T' tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue of T' tensor id has complex absolute value sqrt(q^{m(2d-r)}).

STEP 4 (positive definite Hermitian form on H^{2d-r}). Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/5d27b2 with K=Q_ell, V=W', T=T', and c=q^{m(2d-r)}>0 (a positive real number). Its hypotheses are exactly those established in Step 3: T' tensor id is diagonalizable over C and every eigenvalue has complex absolute value sqrt(c). Its conclusion is that W' tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C=H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h' with h'((T' tensor id) x,(T' tensor id) y)=c h'(x,y)=q^{m(2d-r)} h'(x,y) for all x,y, which is precisely the required conclusion.

This completes the proof. (The argument is uniform in r and also covers the boundary cases r=0 and r=2d, where W or W' is one-dimensional and the same computation applies.)

statement: Let q=p^a, ell!=p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, L cup product with the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, suppose L^{d-r}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for 0<=r<=d, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, FL=q^mLF, P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)). If for every 0<=r<=d, F on P^r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}, then for every n>=0, F on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mn/2}.
proof:
Proof. Convention on Weil absolute value: an element lambda in overline(Q_ell) is said to "have Weil absolute value R" to mean that for EVERY embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C one has |sigma(lambda)|=R, where |.| is the usual complex absolute value; we will verify this property instance by instance, using only that sigma fixes Q (so sigma(q^{mj})=q^{mj}>0) and that the complex absolute value is multiplicative. Nothing is asserted about sigma-independence beyond these pointwise computations. (If the phrase in the statement is read in the weaker "for some embedding" sense, the argument below still proves the uniform statement, hence a fortiori the weaker one.)

Set-up and notation. Let H^s:=H^s_et(X_k,Q_ell). Write L for cup product with the cycle class xi of the F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, as in the statement, i.e. L:H^n->H^{n+2} with L(x)=xi cup x, and let P^s=ker(L^{d-s+1}:H^s->H^{2d-s+2}) for 0<=s<=d; for s<0 we set P^s=0 (only finitely many s occur in what follows, and for the terms L^j P^{r-2j} with r-2j<0 the summand is 0 by this convention).

Step 1 (the Lefschetz decomposition of H^r for 0<=r<=d). First a bookkeeping remark about the clause "Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), identify Tate twists with Q_ell" appearing in the two decomposition lemmas. The cycle class xi lies in H^2(X_k,Q_ell)(1); cup product with xi therefore naturally defines a map H^n->H^{n+2}(X_k,Q_ell)(1), and to regard it as a map H^n->H^{n+2}=H^{n+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell) one must fix an identification Q_ell(1)~Q_ell, equivalently a choice of a nonzero element e of Q_ell(1). Let L_e denote cup product with xi under the identifications given by some fixed nonzero e in Q_ell(1). The operator L of the statement is the same construction under some choice of identifications; if e' is the corresponding choice, then e'=a e for some a in Q_ell^x, and for x in H^n, L_{e'}(x)=a L_e(x). Hence L_{e'}=a L_e, and in particular L_e=a L for some a in Q_ell^x. Two consequences: (i) L_e^{k}=a^{k} L^{k} for every k>=0, so L_e^{d-n}:H^n->H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for a given n if and only if L^{d-n} is an isomorphism; in particular, since L^{d-n} is an isomorphism for all 0<=n<=d by hypothesis, so is L_e^{d-n} for all 0<=n<=d (hence also for 0<=n<=d-1); (ii) for every s, ker(L_e^{d-s+1})=ker(L^{d-s+1}), since multiplying a map by a nonzero scalar leaves its kernel unchanged, so both kernels equal P^s; and (iii) for every j>=0, im(L_e^{j}|_{P^{r-2j}})=im(L^{j}|_{P^{r-2j}}) as subspaces of H^r, since im(a^{j}M)=im(M). Now X is smooth of dimension d over F_{q^m}, hence of pure dimension d. Applying Miner/16d24b0281973336/ace14e (with L replaced by L_e, justified by (i) in degrees 0<=n<=d-1) we obtain, for every 0<=r<d, that the sum map
  direct_sum_{j>=0} L^{j}: direct_sum_{j>=0} P^{r-2j} --> H^r,
with P^s=0 for s<0, is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces; its image of the summand P^{r-2j} is im(L_e^{j}|_{P^{r-2j}})=im(L^{j}|_{P^{r-2j}}) by (iii). Applying Miner/16d24b0281973336/ac7db0 (with L replaced by L_e, justified by (i) in degrees 0<=n<=d) gives the same assertion for r=d (there j ranges over 0<=j<=d/2). Thus, for every 0<=r<=d:
  (*)  H^r = direct_sum_{j>=0} W_j(r),  where  W_j(r):=L^{j}(P^{r-2j}) subset H^r
with only the terms j with r-2j>=0 nonzero, each a Q_ell-subspace of H^r.

Step 2 (Frobenius commutation, stability, and similarity of the summands). Claim: for every j>=0, F L^{j}=q^{mj} L^{j} F on H^* (degree-2j operators, computed degree by degree). Proof by induction on j: j=0 is the identity. Assuming the formula for j, for x in H^n,
  F L^{j+1} x = F L^{j}(L x) = q^{mj} L^{j}(F L x) = q^{mj} L^{j}(q^{m} L F x) = q^{m(j+1)} L^{j+1} F x,
where the third equality uses the given commutation FL=q^{m}LF. This proves the claim.

First, F preserves each P^{s} for 0<=s<=d: if x in P^{s}, then L^{d-s+1}x=0, and applying the claim with j=d-s+1 and inverting the scalar (q^{m(d-s+1)} is a nonzero element of Q subset Q_ell),
  L^{d-s+1}(F x) = q^{-m(d-s+1)} F(L^{d-s+1} x) = q^{-m(d-s+1)} F(0) = 0,
so F x in P^{s}.

Second, F preserves each W_j(r): if x in P^{r-2j}, then by the claim with the same j,
  F(L^{j} x) = q^{mj} L^{j}(F x),
and F x in P^{r-2j} by the preceding paragraph, hence F(L^{j}x) in L^{j}(P^{r-2j})=W_j(r).

Third, for fixed 0<=r<=d and fixed j with s:=r-2j>=0, the map
  phi_j(r): P^{s} --> W_j(r),  phi_j(r)(x)=L^{j}x
is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces. Indeed, if s=d then r=d and j=0, so phi_j(r)=id is injective. If 0<=s<=d-1, then s+2j=r<=d implies j<=(d-s)/2<=d-s (since d-s>=0), so d-s-j>=0; write L^{d-s}=L^{d-s-j} o L^{j} as a factorization H^{s}--L^{j}-->H^{s+j}--L^{d-s-j}-->H^{2d-s}, which is legitimate because L^{d-s-j}(L^{j}x)=xi^{d-s} cup x=L^{d-s}x. The outer map L^{d-s} is an isomorphism by the hard Lefschetz hypothesis at n=s (s<=d). A left-to-right factor whose composition is an isomorphism is injective: if L^{j}x=L^{j}x', then L^{d-s}(x)=L^{d-s}(x'), so x=x'. Thus L^{j} is injective on H^{s}, in particular on P^{s}; being surjective onto its image W_j(r) by construction, phi_j(r) is an isomorphism. Finally, for x in P^{s}, using the claim and F(P^{s}) subset P^{s},
  F(phi_j(r) x) = F(L^{j}x) = q^{mj} L^{j}(F x) = q^{mj} phi_j(r)(F x),
so, as endomorphisms of W_j(r),
  F|_{W_j(r)} = phi_j(r) o (q^{mj} F|_{P^{s}}) o phi_j(r)^{-1}.
That is: the restriction of F to W_j(r) is Q_ell-similar to q^{mj} times the restriction of F to P^{r-2j}. Note we do not claim, and do not need, any Q_ell-eigenbasis of P^{s}; all eigen-basis arguments below are carried out over overline(Q_ell).

Step 3 (diagonalizability and eigenvalues of each summand, over overline(Q_ell)). Fix 0<=r<=d and j with s=r-2j>=0. By hypothesis, F on P^{s} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell): by definition this means that (P^{s}) tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell) admits an overline(Q_ell)-basis x_1,...,x_N (N=dim_{Q_ell} P^{s}) of eigenvectors, F x_i=lambda_i x_i, lambda_i in overline(Q_ell), each lambda_i having Weil absolute value q^{ms/2}, i.e. |sigma(lambda_i)|=q^{ms/2} for every embedding sigma. The map phi_j(r) extends by Q_ell-linearity... extends to an overline(Q_ell)-linear isomorphism phi_j(r) tensor 1: (P^{s}) tensor overline(Q_ell) --> (W_j(r)) tensor overline(Q_ell) (scalar extension preserves isomorphisms). Set y_i=phi_j(r)(x_i). Then y_1,...,y_N is an overline(Q_ell)-basis of (W_j(r)) tensor overline(Q_ell), and
  (F|_{W_j(r)} tensor 1)(y_i) = (F tensor 1)(phi_j(r)(x_i)) = phi_j(r)(F x_i) = q^{mj} lambda_i y_i,
where we used that F commutes with scalar extension (F tensor 1)(phi(x))=phi(F x) for Q_ell-linear phi, i.e. the computation F(L^j x_i)=q^{mj}L^j(F x_i)=q^{mj}lambda_i L^j x_i of Step 2 applied over overline(Q_ell). Hence F|_{W_j(r)} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and its multiset of eigenvalues (with algebraic multiplicities) is {mu_i := q^{mj} lambda_i : 1<=i<=N}: in the eigenbasis above, F|_{W_j(r)} tensor 1 is the diagonal matrix diag(q^{mj}lambda_1,...,q^{mj}lambda_N), whose characteristic polynomial over overline(Q_ell) is product_{i} (X - q^{mj}lambda_i), which accounts for all N eigenvalues with multiplicity.

Weil absolute values: let sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C be any embedding. Since q^{mj} in Q subset overline(Q_ell) is fixed by sigma and sigma(q^{mj})=q^{mj}>0, and the complex absolute value is multiplicative,
  |sigma(mu_i)| = |sigma(q^{mj} lambda_i)| = |sigma(q^{mj})| |sigma(lambda_i)| = q^{mj} q^{ms/2} = q^{m(s+2j)/2} = q^{mr/2}.
Thus every eigenvalue mu_i of F|_{W_j(r)}, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2} in the stated (uniform) sense.

Step 4 (F on H^r for every 0<=r<=d). Fix 0<=r<=d. Extending the direct sum (*) by Q_ell-linearity (scalar extension preserves finite direct sums),
  (H^r) tensor overline(Q_ell) = direct_sum_{j>=0} (W_j(r)) tensor overline(Q_ell).
Each summand (W_j(r)) tensor overline(Q_ell) is stable under F tensor 1 (Step 2), and Step 3 provides, for each j, an overline(Q_ell)-eigenbasis y_i^{(j)} of (W_j(r)) tensor overline(Q_ell) with eigenvalues mu_i^{(j)}=q^{mj}lambda_i, each of Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Concatenating these bases over j yields an overline(Q_ell)-basis of (H^r) tensor overline(Q_ell) consisting of eigenvectors of F tensor 1: the number of basis vectors is sum_j dim(W_j(r))=dim(H^r) by (*), and the concatenated vectors are independent because they are bases of a direct sum. In this basis the matrix of F tensor 1 is diagonal, with diagonal entries the mu_i^{(j)}; hence F on H^r is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), and the multiset of its eigenvalues (with algebraic multiplicities) is the disjoint union over j of {q^{mj}lambda_i}, each of Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.

Thus we have established: for every integer r with 0<=r<=d, F on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.

Step 5 (all degrees n>=0). Since X is smooth of dimension d, it is of pure dimension d, so the hypotheses of Miner/16d24b0281973336/49d581 are satisfied (with the same X, d, F, and the same convention for Weil absolute values, which is verified pointwise as above). Its conclusion states exactly that for every integer n>=0, F on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mn/2}; this includes n>2d, where H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell)=0. This is the desired conclusion. QED.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell!=p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d over F_{q^m}, Y a smooth very ample geometrically connected divisor on X, i:Y->X, F the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C. If H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((F tensor id)x,(F tensor id)y)=q^{m(d-1)}h(x,y), then the induced action of F on coker(i^*:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma}C carries a positive definite Hermitian form hbar with hbar((F tensor id)u,(F tensor id)v)=q^{m(d-1)}hbar(u,v).
proof:
Proof. Set q' := q^m = p^{am}. Then q' is a prime power of characteristic p, and ell != p. Since F_{q'} is a finite extension of F_q inside k and k is algebraically closed, k = overline(F_q) is simultaneously an algebraic closure of F_{q'}. Everything below is a scheme over F_{q'} unless stated otherwise: write X_k = X x_{F_{q'}} Spec(k), Y_k = Y x_{F_{q'}} Spec(k), i_k = i x_{F_{q'}} id_{Spec k}: Y_k -> X_k, and let s: k -> k be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, s(x) = x^{q^m}. No identification of X_k or Y_k with a base change through F_q is used or needed anywhere.

Step 1 (V is finite-dimensional and carries the Frobenius automorphism). Since Y is a smooth very ample divisor on the projective F_{q'}-scheme X, Y is a closed subscheme of X (cut out by one global section of a very ample line bundle). The structure morphism Y -> Spec(F_{q'}) is the composition of the closed immersion Y -> X with the projective morphism X -> Spec(F_{q'}); a closed immersion is proper and properness composes, so Y is proper over F_{q'}. Hence Y is a proper (indeed smooth, of pure dimension d-1) variety over F_{q'}. We now apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob directly over F_{q'}: in its hypotheses take the prime power q' = q^m in place of its q, the proper F_{q'}-variety Y in place of its X, the field k = overline(F_q), which is at the same time an algebraic closure of F_{q'}, in place of its k, and the same prime ell != p. We take K = Q_ell, the constant sheaf on Y_k, equipped with the natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism psi: F_Y^* Q_ell -> Q_ell mentioned in that lemma, where F_Y = id_Y x s: Y_k -> Y_k is the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism on Y_k. The lemma gives directly — without passing through F_q, so no disjoint-union argument is involved — that H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell and carries a canonical Q_ell-linear arithmetic Frobenius automorphism, namely the pullback F_Y^* on etale cohomology. This is exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F appearing in our statement. Write V := H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell). Since F_Y: Y_k -> Y_k is an isomorphism of schemes (an automorphism), its pullback functor on etale sheaves is an equivalence, so the induced map T := F_Y^* on V is a Q_ell-linear automorphism, i.e. T in GL_{Q_ell}(V). By hypothesis, V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = q^{m(d-1)} h(x,y) for all x,y in V tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 2 (Frobenius stability of the image of i^*). Let F_X = id_X x s: X_k -> X_k be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on X_k. As morphisms of F_{q'}-schemes (equivalently of k-schemes), F_X o i_k and i_k o F_Y are equal by a purely formal computation: since i_k = i x id and F_X = id_X x s, F_Y = id_Y x s, we have F_X o i_k = (id_X o i) x (s o id) = i x s = (i x id) o (id_Y x s) = i_k o F_Y; on points of Y_k both compositions send (y,t) to (i(y), s(t)). No computation about the base field is involved, and nothing is asserted about the q-power Frobenius. Contravariance of pullback on etale cohomology (pullback reverses the order of composition) then gives i_k^* o F_X^* = (F_X o i_k)^* = (i_k o F_Y)^* = F_Y^* o i_k^*. The pullback map i^*: H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k, Q_ell) appearing in the statement of the lemma is precisely i_k^*, the pullback induced by the F_{q'}-morphism i after base change to k (functoriality of pullback: base-changing the morphism i base-changes its pullback map). Now let W := im(i^*) subset V. For any a in H^{d-1}_et(X_k, Q_ell), we have F_Y^*(i^* a) = i^*(F_X^* a) by the commutation relation, which lies in W; hence W is a T-stable Q_ell-subspace of V. (W is automatically finite-dimensional, being a subspace of the finite-dimensional V.)

Step 3 (a form on the quotient). Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/d105c4 with K = Q_ell (a field of characteristic 0), sigma|_{Q_ell}: Q_ell -> C (the restriction of the given embedding; it is still an embedding, and it fixes Q, hence fixes the positive rational number q^{m(d-1)}), c = q^{m(d-1)} in Q_ell^* (with sigma(c) = q^{m(d-1)} > 0), V as in Step 1 (finite-dimensional), T = F_Y^* in GL_{Q_ell}(V), and h the form of the hypothesis, which satisfies h((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = q^{m(d-1)} h(x,y) = sigma(c) h(x,y) for all x,y, together with the T-stable subspace W from Step 2. The lemma yields a positive definite Hermitian form h_W on (V/W) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C such that h_W((T tensor id)x,(T tensor id)y) = sigma(c) h_W(x,y) = q^{m(d-1)} h_W(x,y) for all x,y in (V/W) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Step 4 (identification with the cokernel and its induced Frobenius action). By the very definition of the cokernel, coker(i^*) = V / im(i^*) = V/W as Q_ell-vector spaces; thus h_W is, without further transport, a positive definite Hermitian form on coker(i^*) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C. Because W is T-stable (Step 2), T = F_Y^* descends to a well-defined Q_ell-linear map of V/W, [v] -> [T v] (well-defined since if v - v' in W then T(v - v') in W); this descended map is precisely the induced action of F, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, on coker(i^*) that the conclusion refers to. Renaming h_W as hbar, we conclude that coker(i^*) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form hbar with hbar((F tensor id)u,(F tensor id)v) = q^{m(d-1)} hbar(u,v) for all u,v in coker(i^*) tensor_{Q_ell,sigma} C.

Edge cases, stated explicitly: if W = V, then coker(i^*) = 0, the zero space carries the zero Hermitian form (vacuously positive definite, and the scaling identity holds trivially), and the assertion is vacuous; if W = {0}, then coker(i^*) is canonically V itself and hbar = h. Both cases are in any case covered by the application of Miner/16d24b0281973336/d105c4 in Step 3. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let sigma:Kbar->C be an embedding, let a,b be in K^* with sigma(a)>0 and sigma(b)>0, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let T_V in GL_K(V), let T_W in GL_K(W), and let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with T_W phi = a phi T_V. If V tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T_V tensor id)x,(T_V tensor id)y)=b h(x,y) for all x,y, then W tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h' with h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y)=a^2 b h'(x,y) for all x,y.
proof:
We prove that W tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h' with h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y) = (a^2 b) h'(x,y) for all x,y, where the scalars from K are viewed in C through sigma.

Step 1: Restrict the embedding to K. Since sigma: Kbar -> C is a field embedding and K is a subfield of Kbar, the restriction sigma|_K: K -> C is itself a field embedding (a K-linear injection into C; being nonzero and multiplicative, it is injective). Write sigma_K := sigma|_K. Note that the C-vector spaces V tensor_{K,sigma} C and W tensor_{K,sigma} C depend only on the ring map K -> C used in the base change, namely sigma_K, because the tensor product over K only evaluates the embedding on K. Thus the statement with sigma: Kbar -> C is literally the statement with sigma_K: K -> C applied to the same underlying C-vector spaces, and the operators T_V tensor id, T_W tensor id are the same C-linear automorphisms in both notations.

Step 2: Reinterpret the hypothesis on h with a real scalar. The hypothesis says that h((T_V tensor id)x,(T_V tensor id)y) = b h(x,y) for all x,y in V tensor_{K,sigma} C. Both sides are complex numbers (h is C-valued), and the element b of K acts on the complex number h(x,y) through the embedding sigma_K: K -> C; i.e., the right-hand side is sigma_K(b) h(x,y). Since sigma(b) = sigma_K(b) > 0 by assumption, setting lambda := sigma(b) is a positive real number. Therefore the hypothesis is exactly: V tensor_{K,sigma} C carries a positive definite Hermitian form h with h((T_V tensor id)x,(T_V tensor id)y) = lambda h(x,y) for all x,y. All remaining hypotheses of the target (K of characteristic 0; V, W finite-dimensional K-vector spaces; T_V in GL_K(V), T_W in GL_K(W); phi: V -> W a K-linear isomorphism with T_W phi = a phi T_V, with a in K^*) are verbatim the hypotheses of the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/54dead with the choices c := a and lambda := sigma(b) > 0.

Step 3: Apply Miner/16d24b0281973336/54dead. The proved lemma (with sigma = sigma_K, c = a, lambda = sigma(b)) yields a positive definite Hermitian form h' on W tensor_{K,sigma} C such that for all x,y in W tensor_{K,sigma} C,
  h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y) = |sigma(a)|^2 lambda h'(x,y).
(Concretely, the lemma produces h' as the pullback h'(u,v) = h(phi^{-1}u, phi^{-1}v), which is positive definite because phi is an isomorphism and h is, and for which the displayed identity follows from the computation h(a T_V u', a T_V v') = sigma(a) overline{sigma(a)} h(T_V u', T_V v') = |sigma(a)|^2 h(T_V u', T_V v') for u' = phi^{-1}x, v' = phi^{-1}y, using phi^{-1} T_W = a T_V phi^{-1}, which is equivalent to T_W phi = a phi T_V by conjugation with phi.)

Step 4: Compute the constant. By assumption sigma(a) > 0, so sigma(a) is a positive real number and |sigma(a)| = sigma(a); hence |sigma(a)|^2 = sigma(a)^2. Substituting lambda = sigma(b), the identity from Step 3 becomes
  h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y) = sigma(a)^2 sigma(b) h'(x,y).
Since sigma: K -> C is a field homomorphism, sigma(a)^2 sigma(b) = sigma(a) sigma(a) sigma(b) = sigma(a^2 b). Therefore
  h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y) = sigma(a^2 b) h'(x,y) = (a^2 b) h'(x,y)
for all x,y in W tensor_{K,sigma} C, where on the last equality the element a^2 b of K is viewed in C through sigma, as in the statement.

Conclusion. The form h' is a positive definite Hermitian form on W tensor_{K,sigma} C (by Step 3) and satisfies h'((T_W tensor id)x,(T_W tensor id)y) = (a^2 b) h'(x,y) for all x,y (by Step 4). This is exactly the assertion to be proved. Edge cases: none require separate treatment, since K^* guarantees a and b are nonzero scalars, sigma(a), sigma(b) > 0 guarantee the constants are positive real numbers, and phi being an isomorphism guarantees W tensor_{K,sigma} C is a well-defined C-vector space of the same dimension as V tensor_{K,sigma} C so that pulling back h along phi is legitimate. QED

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K, let sigma:Kbar->C be an embedding, let a be in K^*, let V and W be finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, let T_V in GL_K(V), let T_W in GL_K(W), let R>0, and let phi:V->W be a K-linear isomorphism with T_W phi = a phi T_V. If T_V is diagonalizable over Kbar and every eigenvalue lambda of T_V in Kbar satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=R, then T_W is diagonalizable over Kbar and every eigenvalue mu of T_W in Kbar satisfies |sigma(mu)|=|sigma(a)|R.
proof:
Fix the data of the statement: a field K of characteristic 0, an algebraic closure Kbar, an embedding sigma:Kbar -> C, an element a in K^*, finite-dimensional K-vector spaces V and W, invertible K-linear operators T_V in GL_K(V) and T_W in GL_K(W), a real number R>0, and a K-linear isomorphism phi:V->W satisfying T_W phi = a phi T_V (where a on the right denotes multiplication by the scalar a, which is a K-linear automorphism of V and of W since a in K^*). We must show T_W is diagonalizable over Kbar and that every eigenvalue mu of T_W in Kbar satisfies |sigma(mu)| = |sigma(a)| R. The argument also covers the degenerate case dim_K V = 0 (hence dim_K W = 0 since phi is an isomorphism): then all assertions about eigenvalues are vacuous and the construction below uses the empty basis, so we present it uniformly.

Step 1 (T_W is a scalar multiple of an operator similar to T_V). Because phi is a K-linear isomorphism, its inverse phi^{-1}:W->V is K-linear, and the map c_phi:End_K(V)->End_K(W), S |-> phi S phi^{-1} (composition of linear maps), is an isomorphism of K-algebras: c_phi is K-linear and c_phi(S S') = phi S S' phi^{-1} = (phi S phi^{-1})(phi S' phi^{-1}) = c_phi(S) c_phi(S'), with c_phi(id_V) = id_W, and c_phi(c_phi^{-1}(T)) = T. The hypothesis T_W phi = a phi T_V is equivalent, after right-composing with phi^{-1}, to T_W = a (phi T_V phi^{-1}), i.e. T_W is the product of the scalar map a id_W with the operator phi T_V phi^{-1} which is K-similar to T_V.

Step 2 (scalar extension to Kbar). Write Vbar = V tensor_K Kbar and Wbar = W tensor_K Kbar, which are finite-dimensional Kbar-vector spaces. The map phi extends Kbar-linearly to phi_bar := phi tensor_K id_{Kbar}:Vbar->Wbar, and since phi is an isomorphism with inverse phi^{-1}, phi_bar is a Kbar-linear isomorphism with inverse phi^{-1} tensor_K id_{Kbar} (standard fact: tensoring an isomorphism with id over a field preserves being an isomorphism). Multiplication by a likewise extends to the Kbar-linear maps a id_{Vbar} and a id_{Wbar}, and phi_bar (a id_{Vbar}) = a id_{Wbar} phi_bar by Klinearity/bilinearity. The hypothesis T_W phi = a phi T_V extends by Klinearity to (T_W tensor_K id)(phi_bar) = (phi_bar)(a (T_V tensor_K id)) on Vbar.

Step 3 (T_V diagonal over Kbar with complete list of eigenvalues). By hypothesis, T_V is diagonalizable over Kbar, meaning the Kbar-linear operator T_V tensor_K id on Vbar is diagonalizable. So there exist a Kbar-basis v_1,...,v_n of Vbar (n = dim_K V = dim_K Vbar) and scalars lambda_1,...,lambda_n in Kbar such that (T_V tensor id)(v_i) = lambda_i v_i for i=1,...,n. In this basis the matrix of T_V tensor id is the diagonal matrix diag(lambda_1,...,lambda_n). Hence the characteristic polynomial of T_V tensor id is prod_{i=1}^n (t - lambda_i) in K[t] (the characteristic polynomial does not depend on the chosen basis, and a fortiori the monic polynomial whose roots in Kbar are the eigenvalues is this one). Since Kbar is algebraically closed, every root of the characteristic polynomial in Kbar is an eigenvalue, so the multiset of all eigenvalues of T_V in Kbar, counted with algebraic multiplicity, is exactly {lambda_1,...,lambda_n}. In particular each lambda_i is an eigenvalue of T_V in Kbar, so by the hypothesis on T_V we have |sigma(lambda_i)| = R for every i=1,...,n.

Step 4 (a T_V is diagonal with eigenvalues a lambda_i). For each i, (a (T_V tensor id))(v_i) = a (T_V tensor id)(v_i) = a lambda_i v_i. Thus the same basis (v_1,...,v_n) diagonalizes a (T_V tensor id), and its matrix in that basis is diag(a lambda_1,...,a lambda_n), all entries in Kbar. Since a in K^* and the lambda_i are arbitrary complex-absolutely-valued scalars, the numbers a lambda_i are simply scalars in Kbar; note a lambda_i is nonzero for every i, consistent with invertibility.

Step 5 (transport the eigenbasis to Wbar). Set w_i := phi_bar(v_i) in Wbar for i=1,...,n. Because phi_bar is a Kbar-linear isomorphism and (v_1,...,v_n) is a Kbar-basis of Vbar, the family (w_1,...,w_n) is a Kbar-basis of Wbar. Now compute the action of T_W tensor id on w_i. Using the extended relation from Step 2 and then Step 4:
(T_W tensor id)(w_i) = (T_W tensor id)(phi_bar(v_i)) = phi_bar(a (T_V tensor id)(v_i)) = phi_bar(a lambda_i v_i) = a lambda_i phi_bar(v_i) = a lambda_i w_i,
where the second equality is (T_W tensor id) phi_bar = phi_bar a (T_V tensor id) from Step 2, the third is linearity of phi_bar, and the fourth is linearity of phi_bar and of scalar multiplication. Hence w_1,...,w_n is a Kbar-basis of eigenvectors for T_W tensor id, so T_W tensor id, and equivalently T_W viewed over Kbar, is diagonalizable. Moreover, in this basis the matrix of T_W tensor id is diag(a lambda_1,...,a lambda_n), so its characteristic polynomial is prod_{i=1}^n (t - a lambda_i) in K[t], and since Kbar is algebraically closed, the multiset of all eigenvalues of T_W in Kbar, counted with algebraic multiplicity, is exactly {a lambda_1,...,a lambda_n}. In particular, T_W is diagonalizable over Kbar, which establishes the first half of the conclusion.

Step 6 (Weil-type absolute value of the eigenvalues of T_W). Let mu be any eigenvalue of T_W in Kbar. By Step 5, mu = a lambda_i = a lambda for some i, where lambda = lambda_i is an eigenvalue of T_V in Kbar. The map sigma:Kbar -> C is an embedding of fields, hence a ring homomorphism and in particular multiplicative: sigma(xy) = sigma(x) sigma(y) for all x,y in Kbar. Since a in K^* subset Kbar and lambda in Kbar, both lie in the domain of sigma, and sigma(a) in C^* (sigma(a) neq 0 because sigma is injective and a neq 0), while sigma(lambda) in C. Therefore
sigma(mu) = sigma(a lambda) = sigma(a) sigma(lambda).
The complex absolute value is multiplicative, i.e. |xy| = |x| |y| for all complex numbers x,y (this is standard: |xy|^2 = (xy)(xy-bar-conjugate) ... more concretely, writing the numbers in polar form or using |xy|^2 = (x y)(\bar{x} \bar{y}) = |x|^2 |y|^2 gives |xy| = |x| |y| since both sides are nonnegative). Applying multiplicativity:
|sigma(mu)| = |sigma(a) sigma(lambda)| = |sigma(a)| |sigma(lambda)| = |sigma(a)| R,
where the last equality uses Step 3, which gave |sigma(lambda)| = R because lambda is an eigenvalue of T_V in Kbar. Since mu was an arbitrary eigenvalue of T_W in Kbar, every eigenvalue mu of T_W satisfies |sigma(mu)| = |sigma(a)| R.

Combining Step 5 (T_W diagonalizable over Kbar) and Step 6 (absolute value of every eigenvalue of T_W in Kbar), the desired conclusion holds. No properties beyond the stated hypotheses were used, and the degenerate zero-dimensional case is covered vacuously by the same argument with the empty basis, completing the proof.

statement: Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), let X be a smooth projective variety over F_{q^m} that is a disjoint union over F_{q^m} of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties X_1,...,X_s, and let r>=0. Suppose the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et((X_j)_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) for every j and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(X_k,Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.
proof:
Fix the notation: q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), X smooth projective over F_{q^m} with X = disjoint union over F_{q^m} of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties X_1,...,X_s (s>=1), and r>=0. For each j write V_j = H^r_et((X_j)_k, Q_ell) and let F_j be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V_j; write V = H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V. Hypothesis: for every j, F_j is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue of F_j, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2} (i.e. for every embedding sigma:overline(Q_ell)->C, |sigma(lambda)|=q^{mr/2}).

Finiteness of dimensions. Since each X_j is smooth projective (hence proper) of finite type over the field F_{q^m}, the standard finiteness theorem for etale cohomology of smooth varieties of finite type over a field with coefficient Q_ell gives that V_j is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space; the same argument (or the decomposition proved next, summing finite-dimensional spaces) shows V is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. Also, overline(Q_ell) is an algebraic closure of Q_ell.

Step 1: the decomposition into components is canonical and Frobenius-equivariant. First note that the X_j are exactly the connected components of the scheme X_{F_{q^m}}. Indeed: each X_j is open and closed in X (it is one of the members of a finite disjoint union over F_{q^m}), and because X_j is geometrically connected over F_{q^m} it is connected over F_{q^m}. Since X is of finite type over a field, X_{F_{q^m}} is locally Noetherian, so its connected components are open. Let C be a connected component of X_{F_{q^m}}. The family {C cap X_j} is a decomposition of C into relatively open and closed subsets; since C is connected, at most one C cap X_j is nonempty, so C is contained in a unique X_j. Then C is a connected subset of X_j, hence C is contained in some connected component C' of X_j; conversely X_j is a connected subset of X_{F_{q^m}}, so X_j lies in a connected component C'' of X_{F_{q^m}}, and by the uniqueness above C'' is contained in X_j; combining inclusions gives C = X_j. Thus the X_j are precisely the connected components.

Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_13 with the base field F_{q^m} in the role of its F_q (the lemma's statement is unchanged by the change of prime power q -> q^m; its algebraic closure is the same field k=overline(F_q)), and the connected components X_1,...,X_s found above. For i=r it states that the restriction-to-components maps give a canonical isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces
    phi: V = H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) --=--> direct sum_{j=1}^s V_j,
and this isomorphism is equivariant for the arithmetic Frobenius x -> x^{q^m}; i.e. phi o F = (direct sum_{j=1}^s F_j) o phi.

Step 2: invertibility. For each j, F_j is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell), so V_j decomposes into a direct sum of eigenspaces. Every eigenvalue lambda of F_j satisfies |sigma(lambda)|=q^{mr/2} for every embedding sigma, in particular lambda != 0 (since q^{mr/2} != 0). Thus F_j has no zero eigenvalue; a diagonalizable endomorphism whose eigenvalues are all nonzero is invertible, so F_j in GL_{Q_ell}(V_j). The direct sum T := direct sum_{j=1}^s F_j is then in GL_{Q_ell}(direct sum V_j), and by the equivariance phi o F = T o phi, F = phi^{-1} o T o phi lies in GL_{Q_ell}(V). So F is an invertible Q_ell-linear operator, as required for applying the direct-sum lemma below.

Step 3: induction on s. We prove by induction on s that: the operator T_s := direct sum_{j=1}^s F_j on W_s := direct sum_{j=1}^s V_j is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue of T_s, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.

Base s=1: T_1 = F_1 and this is exactly the hypothesis.

Inductive step s>=2: Let W_1 := direct sum_{j=1}^{s-1} V_j and W_2 := V_s. Consider the variety X' = disjoint union_{j=1}^{s-1} X_j over F_{q^m}, a disjoint union of s-1 smooth projective geometrically connected varieties. Applying the inductive hypothesis to X' (and using again eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_13 to identify H^r_et((X')_k,Q_ell) with W_1 in a way equivariant for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius), the operator T_{s-1} := direct sum_{j=1}^{s-1} F_j on W_1 is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue of T_{s-1} has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. For W_2 = V_s, the operator F_s is diagonalizable with all eigenvalues of Weil absolute value q^{mr/2} by the original hypothesis. Both W_1 and W_2 are finite-dimensional over Q_ell.

Now fix an embedding sigma: overline(Q_ell) -> C and set R := q^{mr/2} > 0. Apply the proved lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/8bfe65 with K = Q_ell (characteristic 0), Kbar = overline(Q_ell), the chosen sigma, V_0 := W_s = W_1 direct sum W_2, the Q_ell-linear decomposition V_0 = W_1 direct sum W_2, and T = T_s, which lies in GL_{Q_ell}(W_s) (product of the invertible F_j) and preserves both W_1 and W_2 by construction. The lemma's two induction conditions hold: T|_{W_1} = T_{s-1} is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue of T|_{W_1} satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = R (Weil absolute value implies this for our particular sigma); likewise T|_{W_2} = F_s satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = R for every eigenvalue. The lemma Miner/16d24b0281973336/8bfe65 then concludes that T_s is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue lambda of T_s satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = R = q^{mr/2}. This completes the induction on s (the base case s=1 having no sigma-dependence, and at each step any fixed sigma serving equally well).

Step 4: transfer to V and conclude. We have: T_s is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and for every embedding sigma (the argument of Step 3 worked with an arbitrary fixed sigma), every eigenvalue lambda of T_s satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = q^{mr/2}. Since F = phi^{-1} o T_s o phi with phi an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces, F is similar to T_s: if T_s = P D P^{-1} is a diagonalization over overline(Q_ell), then F = (phi^{-1} o P) o D o (phi^{-1} o P)^{-1} is a diagonalization of F over overline(Q_ell), so F is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell). The eigenvalues of F in overline(Q_ell) are exactly the eigenvalues of T_s: if T_s v = lambda v with v != 0 in (direct sum V_j) tensor_{Q_ell} overline(Q_ell), then F(phi^{-1}v) = lambda phi^{-1}v, and conversely by applying phi; similarity also shows the multisets coincide. Hence every eigenvalue lambda of F, viewed in overline(Q_ell), satisfies |sigma(lambda)| = q^{mr/2} for the chosen sigma; because sigma was arbitrary, this is precisely the statement that every eigenvalue of F, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}.

Thus the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) is diagonalizable over overline(Q_ell) and every eigenvalue, viewed in overline(Q_ell), has Weil absolute value q^{mr/2}. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field, let c be a nonzero element of K, let epsilon be 1 or -1, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let b: V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with b(y,x) = epsilon b(x,y), let T be in GL_K(V) with b(Tx,Ty) = c b(x,y) for all x,y in V, and let N >= 1. Put G_N(x,y) = b(x,T^N y) + epsilon c^N b(x,T^(-N) y). Then G_N(y,x) = G_N(x,y) for all x,y in V.
proof:
We prove G_N(y,x)=G_N(x,y) for all x,y in V by an explicit adjoint computation. All steps are valid over an arbitrary field K (no characteristic, positivity, embedding, or diagonalizability assumption is used); we rely only on the bilinearity of b, its nondegeneracy, the symmetry b(y,z)=epsilon b(z,y), the similitude b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y), and the elementary facts epsilon^2=1 and c^N c^{-N}=1 (with epsilon in {1,-1} and c in K^*).

STEP 0 (Existence, uniqueness, and linearity of the adjoint). Because b is nondegenerate, the map V -> V^*, w -> (x -> b(x,w)), is injective: if b(x,w)=0 for every x then w=0. Since V is finite-dimensional, an injective endomorphism of the finite set of basis-functionals is an isomorphism, so for every K-linear functional f:V->K there is a unique w with f(x)=b(x,w) for all x. Define T^*:V->V to be the unique endomorphism satisfying
    b(Tx,y) = b(x, T^* y)      (†)
for all x,y in V. Indeed, for each fixed y the linear functional x -> b(Tx,y) equals x -> b(x,w) for a unique w; set T^* y = w. Linearity of T^*: for y1,y2 in V and a,b in K, the functional x -> b(Tx, a y1+b y2) equals x -> a b(x,T^* y1)+b b(x,T^* y2) = x -> b(x, a T^* y1+b T^* y2), so uniqueness in (†) forces T^*(a y1+b y2)=a T^* y1+b T^* y2. Hence T^* in GL_K(V) is well defined. (We use the convention b(Tx,y)=b(x,T^* y).)

STEP 1 (Compute T^* from the similitude). Apply (†) with u=x, v=Ty: b(Tx,Ty)=b(x, T^*(Ty))=b(x, T^* T y). The similitude gives b(Tx,Ty)=c b(x,y). Hence b(x, T^* T y)=b(x, c y), i.e. b(x, (T^* T - c) y)=0 for every x,y. For each fixed y, the functional x -> b(x, (T^* T - c) y) is identically zero, so by nondegeneracy (injectivity of w -> (x -> b(x,w))) we get (T^* T - c) y=0. Since y was arbitrary, T^* T = c I. Because T is invertible, multiplying on the right by T^{-1} gives T^* = c T^{-1}.

STEP 2 (The adjoint is an anti-automorphism). For any endomorphisms A,B and all x,y,
    b((AB)x,y) = b(A(Bx),y) = b(Bx, A^* y)      [by (†) with u=Bx, v=y]
                = b(x, B^* A^* y)               [by (†) with u=x, v=A^* y].
So the functional x -> b((AB)x,y) equals x -> b(x, (B^* A^*)y). By uniqueness in the defining property of the adjoint (with A replaced by AB), (AB)^* = B^* A^*.

STEP 3 (Adjoint of powers). Iterating Step 2, (T^N)^*=(T^*)^N=(c T^{-1})^N=c^N (T^{-1})^N=c^N T^{-N} (a scalar commutes, so (c T^{-1})^N=c^N(T^{-1})^N). For the inverse powers, note (T^{-1}T)^*=I^*=I (since b(Ix,y)=b(x,y)=b(x,Iy), so I^*=I), while by Step 2 (T^{-1}T)^*=T^* (T^{-1})^*. Hence T^* (T^{-1})^*=I, so (T^{-1})^*=(T^*)^{-1}=(c T^{-1})^{-1}=c^{-1} T. Iterating again, (T^{-N})^*=((T^{-1})^*)^N=(c^{-1} T)^N=c^{-N} T^N.

STEP 4 (Symmetry of G_N). We have G_N(x,y)=b(x,T^N y)+epsilon c^N b(x,T^{-N} y) and G_N(y,x)=b(y,T^N x)+epsilon c^N b(y,T^{-N} x). Compute the two summands of G_N(y,x).
  Summand A: b(y,T^N x). Using the symmetry b(v,u)=epsilon b(u,v) with u=T^N x, v=y: b(y,T^N x)=epsilon b(T^N x, y). Using (†) with the operator T^N (i.e. b(T^N u,v)=b(u,(T^N)^* v)) and Step 3: b(T^N x, y)=b(x, c^N T^{-N} y)=c^N b(x,T^{-N} y). Hence A = epsilon c^N b(x,T^{-N} y).
  Summand B: epsilon c^N b(y,T^{-N} x). First by symmetry, b(y,T^{-N} x)=epsilon b(T^{-N} x, y). Then by (†) with the operator T^{-N} and Step 3, b(T^{-N} x, y)=b(x, c^{-N} T^N y)=c^{-N} b(x,T^N y). Hence B = epsilon c^N (epsilon c^{-N} b(x,T^N y)) = epsilon^2 b(x,T^N y) = b(x,T^N y) (since epsilon^2=1 and c^N c^{-N}=1).
  Adding, G_N(y,x) = A+B = epsilon c^N b(x,T^{-N} y) + b(x,T^N y) = b(x,T^N y)+epsilon c^N b(x,T^{-N} y) = G_N(x,y).

The argument uses only epsilon^2=1 (valid since epsilon in {1,-1}) and the given symmetry relation, so it is valid simultaneously for epsilon=1 and epsilon=-1. No property of the characteristic of K, no positivity, no embedding, and no diagonalizability is invoked anywhere. Therefore G_N(y,x)=G_N(x,y) for all x,y in V, as required. (Note the computation yields symmetry P^t=P of the matrix of G_N in any basis; it does not give P^t=epsilon P, and it concludes nothing about diagonalizability.)
